The result, according to Apple, is “richer, more detailed sound across an even wider range of ear geometries.” Sound, again, is one of those things you have to hear to believe, but clearly Apple paid attention to improving the sound quality in this generation, so you should expect a step up over the last generation. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Battery life Battery life is where things get a little more complicated. While the base model of AirPods 5 has the same battery life as its predecessor—a pretty pedestrian four hours on a single charge when ANC is activated—you can actually shell out a bit more money for a different tier with some extra juice. The $149 AirPods 5 (that’s $20 more than the base) will get you an extra hour of battery life with ANC on. That’s still not great in the scheme of most wireless earbuds (about six hours is pretty standard), but if you’re strictly comparing between generations of non-Pro AirPods, then the more expensive model of AirPods 5 definitely take the cake. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Features While both generations share a lot of the same features, there are some subtle differences to note outside of ANC. In addition to better ANC, the AirPods 5 also have next-gen Adaptive EQ, according to Apple. Thanks to this upgraded Adaptive EQ, the AirPods 5 can tune sound to the specific shape of your ears across a larger range of frequencies. The result, Apple says, is a “more immersive and accurate sound.” AirPods 4 do have Adaptive EQ, for the record, but Apple claims that the new generation just does it better. The differences continue to pile up when you consider the more expensive tier of AirPods 5. By shelling out $149, you get two things that neither the base tier of AirPods 5 nor the AirPods 4 have: wireless charging and stem controls. For the first time, the more expensive tier now lets you swipe on the wireless earbuds to control volume. Not groundbreaking, but it can be better than reaching for your phone every time. Similarly, wireless charging in the charging case isn’t mind-blowing, but it’s nice to have. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Fit This is one area where not much has changed. In its announcement, Apple didn’t say much about any kind of physical redesign, so the AirPods 5 likely look and feel pretty similar to the AirPods 4. These are still semi-open-ear, meaning they nest in your outer ear instead of being inserted like AirPods Pro.

item.title: Here’s When You Can Finally Download iOS 27 and Siri AI
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.18
Apple’s white whale, the AI-enhanced Siri, will finally be available to download later this month. The entire software suite, including iOS 27, macOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and more, should be available starting Sept. 14. If you haven’t already tried either the developer or public betas, iOS 27’s big feature is the new AI assistant tied to Siri. You can talk with Siri as normal, but now the chatbot has access to “personal context,” which means users can allow it access to your calendar and emails if you want it to complete tasks on your behalf. Siri AI is rolling out as a “beta” on Monday, Sept. 14. It’s only available in English to start. French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish should be along in October, with other languages following later. The rest of the Apple Intelligence features should be available in more languages to start. Gizmodo’s Senior Editor of Consumer Tech, Raymond Wong, has been rather positive about the experience from beta testing, but there are more updates to care about as well. iOS 27 introduces a Liquid Glass slider to make your translucent icons a little more legible. There are several more minor upgrades besides, including a fix to that one optical illusion that caused such a ruckus at the launch of iOS 26. If you know, you know. Apple’s macOS 27 Golden Gate includes those same Siri features, which we’ve found occasionally helpful as an assistant or alternative to the ever-degrading Google Search. Golden Gate also adds several helpful AI features, like the ability to prompt Shortcuts to make you an easy-to-use macro. These features will be available to all M-series MacBooks, though not all iPhones will see the Siri enhancements. Furthermore, if you were hoping to use Siri from your wrist, you have to own a more recent Apple Watch. For instance, even the Apple Watch Ultra from 2022 won’t support AI Siri. Other software updates may be a little less exciting. iPads with more recent A-series and M-series chips and the Apple Vision Pro are all getting access to Siri. At least, you won’t have to wait long to find out if there are any features you most appreciate or anything you don’t enjoy. Just know one thing—love it or hate it—Liquid Glass is here to stay.

item.title: Apple Launches Feature to Prove iPhone 18 Photos Are Not AI Generated
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.04
As AI gets better at outputting photorealistic images, tech companies have been rolling out tools to identify when an image was generated by AI. Now, Apple is taking a different approach, with a new feature designed to prove when a photo is real. The tech giant announced Apple Reference Image on Wednesday at its event unveiling a slate of new products, including the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. “Users can now prove the authenticity of a photo taken on iPhone 18 Pro models with Apple Reference Image, powered by the new sensor in the Main camera that can sign every pixel it sees,” Apple said in a press release. When a user takes a photo using the new Reference mode on an iPhone 18 Pro, the camera captures signed sensor data. That data is then processed using Apple’s Private Cloud Compute to create what the company says is an unalterable reference image. The reference image can then be viewed in the Photos app alongside the regular photo. Apple compares it to a “digital negative” that lets users see what the camera originally captured and compare it with any altered images. Apple is making APIs for the feature available in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS 27 to allow third-party apps to view reference Images. The company is pairing Reference Image with other tools meant to make AI-generated and edited images easier to spot. Apple says image metadata and upcoming support for the SynthID standard will help users identify images that have been generated or edited with AI. SynthID is an AI watermarking tool developed by Google DeepMind. It works by embedding an invisible digital watermark directly into AI-generated images, audio, text, or video that can later be detected using SynthID tech. SynthID is already used across Google’s generative AI products, as well as by OpenAI for images generated through ChatGPT, Codex, and its API. “Together with Apple Reference Image, this set of features represents a multifaceted approach to image authenticity — vital for photojournalists, photographers, and everyday viewers,” Apple said. Interestingly, Reference Image won’t be available everywhere at launch. In China, the feature won’t be available initially because of what Apple describes only as “regulatory requirements.” Meanwhile, in the European Union, iPhone 18 Pro users won’t be able to capture Reference Images at launch, although users with iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27 will still be able to develop and view them. Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Circular’s Ring 3 Series Beats Oura to Adding Contactless Payments
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.00
Circular is trying to stand out from its smart ring competition by making its next wearables more than just health trackers. The Circular Ring 3 Pro and Circular Ring 3 Slim feature sensors for health and fitness tracking but also manage to squeeze in NFC chips for contactless payments and haptic motors that can wake you up or guide you through breathing exercises. Design-wise, both rings are slimmer than the Circular Ring 2, but the company now offers the Ring 3 Slim as an even thinner alternative. Either Series 3 ring can track your activity, heart rate, blood pressure, sleep (including sleep stages), stress, and menstrual cycle through a combination of PPG sensors (the green and red lights on smartwatches and rings), skin temperature sensors, and accelerometers. Besides thickness, the key advantage the Ring 3 Pro offers over its slimmer sibling is support for ECG readings and AFib detection. The larger ring also gets 12 days of battery life compared to the Slim’s 10 days. What’s more interesting is what the rings can do outside of health and fitness. Circular says both rings support “Circular Pay,” its take on an Apple Pay or Google Pay-style contactless payment system. Anyone who buys a Ring 3 model will be able to add a Visa or Mastercard to their ring and use it to complete payments. The company has also brought the haptic motor of the original Circular Ring back to the Ring 3 series. Haptic vibrations in the ring can be used as a silent alarm, to notify of a health alert, or as a non-visual guide through a breathing exercise. For the most part, smart rings like the Galaxy Ring or Oura Ring 5 compete closely on software features because they tend to use similar sensors to track the same aspects of your health. Circular is playing that game, too, and even has an AI assistant called “Kira,” but the addition of NFC makes the Ring 3 series legitimately more useful than its competition. That might matter less if the ring’s other features are found lacking, but paying with a smart ring definitely sounds better than pulling out a smartwatch or your phone. The Circular Ring 3 Pro and Circular Ring 3 Slim will be available in U.S. sizes 6-14 in gold, silver, rose gold, and black finishes. Circular hasn’t announced the price of the ring, but you can join a waitlist to purchase one now, and the company plans to open pre-orders in December.

item.title: What Will Apple Call Its Foldable iPhone?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.58
Nobody knows what Apple will call its first foldable iPhone. We’ll get the official name at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event tomorrow. But since I’m in an antsy mood, let’s debate about it. The one name leading the pack is iPhone Ultra. “Everyone calls it the Ultra internally,” reported Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. Of course, an internal name does not necessarily mean that’s the final name that will be printed on the foldable iPhone’s box. As Creative Strategies analyst Max Weinbach noted last month, iPhone Ultra seems off. What about the foldable, besides the screen, would be ultra? It’s not expected to have a telephoto lens, so it wouldn’t even meet the definition of “Pro” compared to the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. It won’t have the longest-lasting battery of any iPhone. It’s also going to be missing Face ID and the Action button. It probably won’t even have the same vapor cooling chamber in the Pro iPhones to keep performance from throttling under heavy loads. Everyone calls it the Ultra internally. We’ll see what happens. — Mark Gurman (@markgurman) August 11, 2026 iPhone Duo and iPhone Folio are also names that have been thrown around. Before today, I felt iPhone Duo could be a strong possibility, even if Microsoft already used it for its failed own dual-screen, folding phone and poor sequel. iPhone Folio or iBook has never passed the sniff test for me. It implies the main use for the device is for reading, which I don’t think is how Apple will market it. Apple will likely tout the benefit of the inner widescreen for watching videos, playing games, and running multiple apps simultaneously. Besides, Apple already used iBook for a previous laptop line, and then reused it for its digital books app, before renaming it to Apple Books. iFold, iPhold, iPhone Fold. Not a chance. I can’t see Apple using a name that’s so synonymous with Android foldables, like Samsung’s Galaxy Fold series. So, what then will Apple call the foldable iPhone? I’m going to just throw this out there. I see two paths Apple could take. The first is to just call it iPhone Plus or iPhone Max. Apple has ascribed both descriptors to iPhones before to emphasize a larger screen size. Apple first used Plus for the iPhone 6 Plus through the iPhone 8 Plus. Then, switched over to iPhone Max to describe the bigger model with the iPhone XS Max. When Apple introduced the first “Pro” iPhone, the iPhone 11 Pro, the bigger screen model was christened iPhone 11 Pro Max. Since then, the larger Pro iPhone has always been called “Pro Max.” Apple also brought back “Plus” for the iPhone 14 through iPhone 16 series. The iPhone 16 Plus was replaced with an iPhone Air last year. What if foldable iPhone is called: iPhone Max It’s not a “Pro” because it doesn’t have telephoto or the longest battery or Face ID or action button Just the biggest iPhone screen ever Just iPhone Max — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 8, 2026 Which brings me to the next possibility: what if the foldable iPhone is actually viewed as part of the iPhone Air family? It’s supposed to measure around 4mm when open, which would make it thinner than the 5.6mm iPhone Air. It’d definitely qualify to be an “Air” device. If that’s how Apple sees it—as an iPhone Air with a huge screen—then I think it could be called the iPhone Air Max, iPhone Air Pro, or iPhone Air Plus. Nike would probably not be okay with Apple using “Air Max” branding. As some of my followers have astutely pointed out, Tim Cook may be on the Nike board and use every chance to wear Nike sneakers in public, but that may be a line too far. That leaves us with iPhone Air Pro or iPhone Air Plus. Or iPhone Air Duo, even. So here are my final name bets: - iPhone Max - iPhone Plus - iPhone Air Pro - iPhone Air Duo Who wants to take bets? Fight me in the comments 😛

item.title: Silicon Valley’s AI Agent Push Has Been Paying Off—for Cybercriminals
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.44
AI companies have made a lot of noise about the technology supercharging healthcare, scientific discovery, education, productivity, and just about everything else worth caring about. But so far, probably the most dramatic change wrought by the AI race has been the sudden appearance of dangerous new cybersecurity threats. The most infamous of these are the autonomous hacks launched by swarms of AI agents, the most recent of which was first reported last week (even though OpenAI, the company behind the agents, had reportedly been aware of the incident for quite a while longer). But it’d be a mistake to think that new cyber threats in the age of AI are only coming from mindless, reward-hacking bots; there are still plenty of good ol’ fashioned human hackers, for whom new AI tools have been a godsend. A new report from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)—a research team within Google monitoring emerging cyberthreats—found that threat actors, many of them with direct ties to the United States’ geopolitical foes, have been leveling-up the sophistication of their AI usage, transitioning from basic chatbots to more agentic, autonomous systems. “Over the past quarter, threat actors have moved beyond simple prompt-based LLM interactions to integrate AI capabilities into multiple stages of an attack lifecycle,” GTIG wrote in its report, which was published online Tuesday morning. “While traditional script-based automation has long been a staple of threat actor operations, groups are increasingly upgrading these workflows, creating highly autonomous systems capable of reasoning through complex tasks and making dynamic decisions without the need for human oversight.” In plain English: the technology that leading AI companies (including Google) have been building into their AI systems, giving them the ability to handle complex tasks without constant hand-holding, is also making hackers’ dirty work a whole lot easier. Some of the “adversaries” that GTIC identified in its new report appear to be backed by China, Russia, and Iran. One group, which GTIC first reported earlier this year and identified only as “UNC6508,” has been targeting American academic, medical, and military research institutions in a manner “aligned with the strategic interests of the People’s Republic of China.” According to Tuesday’s report, UNC6508 has been observed using an open source AI model within its targets’ cloud environments to steal compute without leaving the kind of trail that would be left if they’d been using a commercial, publicly available AI model. “[UNC6508] continues to research how to set up and use AI tools, including using open models locally, and researching vulnerabilities in AI models themselves,” GTIC wrote in its new report. In another case reported by GTIC, threat actors traced to Iran used Gemini to generate realistic deepfakes to be used in social engineering campaigns. Rather than entering one prompt after another to fine-tune the deepfakes’ appearance, they deployed the AI model to autonomously define “granular technical parameters—including camera angles, studio lighting, and realistic facial textures—to achieve photorealistic visual outputs.” GTIC also reported “coordinated campaigns” being carried out “on a regular basis” to distill its proprietary AI systems, which it said is a violation of Google’s terms of service and could be subject to legal action. Though distillation has long been a widely used practice within the AI industry to develop new models, it’s recently become a political flashpoint. Leading American developers including OpenAI and Anthropic have accused their Chinese rivals of distilling their AI systems in an effort to gain a competitive edge, and the White House has vowed to crack down on what it’s described as “deliberate, industrial-scale campaigns to distill U.S. frontier AI systems.”

item.title: This Photon Survived an ‘Impossible’ Journey to Earth. To Explain it, Physicists Had to Break Einstein
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.00
In 2022, astronomers detected an absurdly bright and long-lasting gamma ray burst, GRB 221009A—nicknamed “BOAT,” for “Brightest of All Time” (seriously). The shower of photons was so old and powerful that, theoretically, it shouldn’t have reached Earth. And yet, it clearly has. But how? In a paper published yesterday in Physical Review Letters, a pair of physicists offer a puzzling solution to a puzzling problem: hypothetical particles from the cosmic dawn. Specifically, the researchers propose that photons could temporarily transform into axion-like particles, which are extremely light, paired with a separate tweak to account for photon behavior at extreme energies. It’s this second piece that technically violates something called Lorentz invariance, a key tenant of Einstein’s special relativity. But here’s the thing—using this model, the pair predicted a secondary effect that would arise from the photon’s journey. And, it turns out, a completely unrelated observatory actually had observed exactly this. In other words, there’s actually empirical support for this theory. “We started from a very simple question: how did this photon survive a journey that, according to known physics, should have destroyed it?” Giorgio Galanti, the study’s co-author and an astrophysicist at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics, said in a statement. “We therefore looked for a theoretical scenario capable of consistently describing what we observe, without resorting to arbitrary corrections to the equations.” ‘B.O.A.T.’ Because GRB 221009A was so powerful, it “temporarily blinded most space-based gamma-ray instruments,” according to a NASA explainer—hence the nickname, “BOAT.” But the signal was also exceptionally long, at about 10 minutes. The flash remained detectable for the next 10 hours, and soon astronomers were able to lock down some key statistics of the BOAT. Originating roughly two billion light-years from Earth, it exerted energies around 300 teraelectronvolts (TeV). For context, 1 electronvolt is the kinetic energy of 1 electron in a 1-volt vacuum; 1 teraelectronvolt is equivalent to 1 trillion electronvolts. At the time, experts with NASA surmised that the burst of light came from the birth of a new black hole, and subsequent investigations of the signal deemed that such luminous events would occur once in every 10,000 years. A broken signal? Then, astronomers had to reckon with the elephant in the room: the logistics of GRB 221009A’s journey to Earth. In the paper, Galanti and co-author Marco Roncadelli, of the Italian National Institute for Nuclear Physics, explained that GRB 221009A was “in tension” with conventional physics. According to the physics rulebook, photons at similar energy levels should have collided with the cosmic microwave background—traces of radiation from the universe’s earliest days—and been annihilated in the process. In the statement, the team likened this to “shooting an arrow through an extremely dense forest stretching for two billion light-years and expecting it not to hit a single tree.” So, if the signal got here—and we know it did—the photons must have found a way either to dodge all of these trees or disregard them altogether. The pair believes the answer is the latter. Some models of quantum gravity allow for slight flexibility in one of the fundamental rules of Einstein’s special relativity for matter at the highest energy levels. The pair coupled this mechanism with axion-like particles. As a result, what you get are what the researchers call the universe’s “fast lane,” through which super light, very powerful particles zip through obstacles as if they didn’t exist. Cheat code Understandably, this might sound like an ad hoc solution to the problem; after all, it’s not like we have concrete proof that axion-like particles exist. The team recognized this in the paper, explaining that its proposal is just one out of many ideas to probe this unexplained signal. That said, the latest calculations predicted a one-hour gap between a shower of lower-energy photons and the 300 TeV photon’s arrival on Earth. And, remarkably, this was precisely what one Chinese observatory caught at the time. “The most interesting aspect of our work is that, for the first time, it brings together two ideas that until now had been developed separately,” Roncadelli said in the statement. “If future observations confirmed this scenario, the universe would become a natural laboratory for studying quantum gravity at energies enormously higher than those achievable by any accelerator built on Earth.”

item.title: Report: Roughly Half the World’s Governments Underestimated Covid Deaths by the Millions
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.80
Aside from maybe a few blinkered members from some of society’s more fortunate demographics (e.g., white-collar remote workers, monied introverts, etc.), most people don’t particularly recall the covid-19 pandemic fondly. But new research from social scientists in London and Jerusalem is now providing strong indications that the scope of this tragedy was far worse than many governments let on. Moses Shayo and Ariel Karlinsky, two researchers who specialize in political and health economics, compiled an unusually comprehensive dataset from “all-cause mortality” reports, taken across 134 countries and territories both before and during the covid-19 pandemic. They then compared this more concrete data, some of it obtained by local journalists via freedom of information laws, to contemporaneous official government pronouncements during the heights of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021. As many as 45% to 55% of these nations, Shayo and Karlinsky found, misreported covid’s death toll—in most cases underplaying the severity of the crisis. Compared to the 5.08 million deaths attributed to covid-19 by state officials during this two-year period, the researchers determined that the actual number of covid-related deaths (based on these governments’ own hard numbers) was more than twice that: about 12.47 million. “Our evidence shows that manipulation was remarkably widespread and large in magnitude,” Shayo and Karlinsky said in a press statement. In the 62 countries where they found covid deaths were underreported, aspiring and successful “informational autocrats” managed to avoid counting 14.5% of the expected covid deaths on average, they found. Means, motive, and opportunity Shayo and Karlinsky devoted considerable effort in their study, published in the Journal of Economic Growth, to dissecting and delineating between possible explanations for why a given country might have underreported its covid-19 deaths. Plenty of nations, they noted, simply did not have the resources to adequately keep up with the punishing deluge of deaths, whether in terms of medical diagnostics, hospital access, or sheer personnel. But, as they adjusted for these factors, the researchers found a troubling correlation indicative of multiple premeditated efforts to minimize the scope of the pandemic’s impact. Shayo and Karlinsky used state-level data on the share of adults with either a college education and/or internet access, alongside information collected by the United Nations’ Human Development Education Index, to craft a metric for each nation’s relative “audience sophistication.” The measure—when viewed alongside the structural checks and balances reining in each government’s executive power—tended to mirror the scale of underreported covid deaths. “In countries where formal and informal checks and balances are weak, executives tend to act as ‘informational autocrats,’” Shayo and Karlinsky said. “The most important set of constraints appear to be institutional constraints on the executive. Additionally, the severity of underreporting drops significantly the more sophisticated the domestic audience is,” the pair wrote in their study. “We find less evidence relating it to cultural factors and to macroeconomic incentives to underreport.” A tyranny of small decisions Shayo and Karlinsky stopped short of claiming causality, however, merely framing it as “probably noteworthy” that states with the most accurate covid-19 reporting were “strongly associated with constraints on the government’s ability to effectively manipulate information.” More benign institutional policies might lead certain state bureaucracies to repeatedly err on ambiguous deaths, leading edge cases to either be always or never logged as covid-related, they noted. “[Some] countries may be reluctant to report a given death as Covid unless they are absolutely certain the death was due to Covid, even though this violates [U.N. World Health Organization] WHO guidelines, [independent] of capacity or intention to obfuscate,” according to the pair, who are currently based at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel. (Shayo is also a professor at King’s College London). In perhaps the duo’s most unsurprising finding, Shayo and Karlinsky uncovered signs that incumbent politicians somehow succumbed to the temptation to skew government data in their favor: “There is also evidence that misreporting is higher in countries holding elections during the pandemic,” they wrote.

item.title: Anthropic Builds Model to Predict Economy in 2030, Leaves Off the ‘Everybody Dies’ Outcome
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.67
Life as a member of the communications team for frontier AI labs must be fascinating. Imagine you’ve got this big report ready to go out on the extremely elaborate model your economics team built that you want to position as a tool for policymakers and academics to understand how AI is going to impact the workforce, and the night before it publishes, your colleagues just casually (and publicly) declare that there’s a greater than 10% chance that your technology kills everyone within the next decade. Is that in the model? Do you address that? Anthropic went with no to both of those questions, but it did, in fact, release its Economic Index growth model, which is designed to project what the economy could look like by the end of the decade, based on different levels of AI functionality and adoption. You’ll be shocked to learn that the big takeaway from the model is that everything is going to be a-okay in most cases—though the outcomes that aren’t on the chart are probably as noteworthy as the ones that are. Per Anthropic, as long as we stay within the parameters of somewhere between “business as usual” and an economy where “AI increases growth to about twice the normal rate,” we can expect unemployment to stay within historically normal ranges and wages to “remain flat or rise depending on the industry.” However, if we reach growth that is “faster than anything in economic history,” then there will be “adverse impacts on wages and job prospects for knowledge workers.” But don’t worry, because even when it’s bad, it’s good! “In those scenarios, society is far wealthier, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are broadly shared.” And since we’ve historically been so great at wealth distribution, there are certainly no red flags to raise there. The model is interesting, at least. As the AI lab explained it, it sought to effectively break down jobs into bundles of tasks, then determine how the availability of AI might impact those tasks—what can be automated, what new work will be created because of AI, and what will likely remain human labor. Then it scales AI adoption levels to each job to determine how different industries and the economy as a whole will be affected by the technology. It ultimately spits out a model that, at the extreme end of the spectrum, projects an economy that is 50% larger than it is today and has a nearly 30% unemployment rate. For what it’s worth, the furthest you can push the model the other way is zero AI adoption, which amounts to the economy functioning as usual. It doesn’t account for a potential AI bubble and how its popping may impact workers and the economy, which is currently wildly overleveraged on the idea that the AI boom is for real. Even the model’s most extreme edges also don’t account for everyone dying, which is apparently within the internal parameters for possible outcomes. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, posted on Twitter yesterday that, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” and put the odds at greater than 10% over the next decade while admitting, “we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Feels like that’d probably result in some economic shrinkage, but maybe eliminating humans would just get rid of inefficiencies. Guess we’ll just plow forward unimpeded until we find out!

item.title: Apple’s Biggest AI Advantage: It’s Not Trying to Build God
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.49
Apple had a lot to talk about during its “Surprise and Shine” product launch event on Wednesday: a new CEO, revamped AirPods, an Apple Watch that can record your conversations, and of course, a much-anticipated foldable iPhone. The only thing missing was grandiose proclamations about how AI is going to revolutionize everything in the world, and maybe even kill us all. Not so long ago, believing such a thing would’ve been considered at the very least fringe, even within the sci-fi-indoctrinated ranks of Silicon Valley. It wasn’t until the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022 that people started accepting the idea that AI—long an intellectual taboo in tech circles—could in fact become a mainstream tool, and perhaps have as big a cultural impact as the iPhone or the internet. And while people have been warning about the danger of runaway AI for decades, those fears escalated sharply earlier this year, following a series of autonomous hacks which showed how frail our existing cybersecurity infrastructure can be in the face of swarms of self-coordinating agents that tech companies seem unable (or unwilling) to control. Anxiety about the future reached a new height this week after an AI safety researcher at Anthropic named Evan Hubinger wrote in a social media post that the very technology his company is racing to build has a greater than ten percent chance of wiping out humanity. It got the world’s attention. In a sign that AGI fears had breached the mainstream, Sheryl Crow, of all people, wrote on Instagram that she was “begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent [unconstrained AI development] from going forward.” U.S. lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle called on Congress this week to rein in the race to build artificial “superintelligence”—a term that started as a warning but has since, in a strange trick of rhetorical alchemy, been embraced as a marketing buzzword by the biggest American AI labs. Hubinger’s views on the apocalyptic potential of AI can seem confounding: Why would he help to build something he thinks could exterminate every one of us? But that idea is hardly unusual in his industry. Many of the most powerful players in the AI race have long said, quite plainly and in public, that the technology could go terribly wrong and be the agent of our extinction, whether that’d be through some engineered doomsday virus, a cybersecurity takeover, an AI-triggered nuclear exchange, or some other machine-made catastrophe our mortal minds can’t even hope to fathom. (The whole idea behind superintelligence, after all, is that it’ll be playing hyperdimensional chess while we humans are still struggling to play checkers.) Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s cofounder and CEO, has said there’s as high as a 25% chance that AI goes “really, really badly.” (Read: that humanity is toast.) Elon Musk believes there’s about a 10%-20% chance that things could go terribly wrong. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been reluctant to assign a specific probability to that outcome, but he doesn’t believe it’s zero. In a perverse but very real way, the world-killing power of superintelligent AI is, for tech leaders, a feature, not a bug. You can’t have an all-powerful machine God capable of curing cancer and freeing us from drudgework without some risk that it’ll turn on us. That will seem deeply inhuman to most sane people who don’t have any prospect of becoming uber-wealthy from the AI boom. But make no mistake, it is a fundamental presupposition these companies are operating from, and they don’t even try to keep it a secret. The language they use is typically more dialed-down, but the bottom line, they’ll say, is that humanity should accept some chance of annihilation for a shot at the golden age they believe AI can lead us into. All of which makes Apple’s rather muted approach to AI stand out. The company has been widely regarded as a slowpoke since the debut of ChatGPT, focusing on its hardware business while just about every other tech giant did an about-face to make AI a top priority. Its launch of “Apple Intelligence” in 2024 was more of a whimper than a bang, and to this day its AI muscle is largely dependent upon models from Google, its erstwhile competitor. AI wasn’t completely absent from its Wednesday product launch event, but it was more of a background theme than the shiny center of attention. No doubt freshly minted Apple CEO John Ternus has been keeping a watchful eye on the public backlash to AI data centers and fears over an AI-pocalypse, and thinking that perhaps the best way to win over people’s hearts and minds is not to talk about AI as if it were some omnipotent God we’re summoning into being, but just another tool to help you do the things you already do, like touching up photos and getting walking directions from Siri. And for millions of people who are increasingly fearful of the future, that’s likely to be a sales pitch they can actually get behind. READ MORE:

item.title: Google-Backed Nuclear Plant Gets Nearly $2 Billion Loan From the Energy Department
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.34
The AI boom is driving up electricity demand, helping fuel a revival of nuclear power. And the Trump administration is fully on board. The U.S. Department of Energy announced Tuesday that it closed a loan of up to $1.9 billion to help finance NextEra Energy’s plans to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa. The nuclear plant operated for more than 45 years before shutting down in 2020. NextEra had already planned to close the plant later that year, but a storm damaged parts of the facility and forced it offline several months early. Google announced last October that it was working with NextEra to restart Duane Arnold and explore deploying more nuclear power around the country. Under the deal, Google signed a multi-year agreement to buy power from the plant, helping make the investment needed to restart it financially viable and cover the cost of energy production. “We expect Duane Arnold to be back online in early 2029, and the plant will provide more than 600 MW of clean, safe, “always-on” nuclear energy to the regional grid,” Google said in a blog post at the time. The electricity will help support Google’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure in Iowa. The company also announced last year that it was investing an additional $7 billion in the state over two years, including in new and expanded cloud and AI infrastructure. Once restarted, the Energy Department says Duane Arnold will add 615 megawatts of power to the grid, enough to power nearly 500,000 homes. The department also says the project will help drive down electricity costs. Google isn’t the only tech company turning to nuclear power to fuel its AI ambitions. A Microsoft-backed project to restart Constellation Energy’s Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania, formerly known as Three Mile Island Unit 1, received a $1 billion Energy Department loan last year. Meanwhile, Meta announced earlier this year that it had reached agreements with several companies to support up to 6.6 gigawatts of new and existing nuclear power by 2035. Major tech companies like Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Google are all pouring billions of dollars into data centers and other infrastructure needed to train and run increasingly powerful AI models. All of that infrastructure requires a lot of electricity. The Trump administration has also gone all-in on expanding nuclear power to help meet growing electricity demand. President Donald Trump signed several executive orders last year aimed at speeding up nuclear development. One of them directed the Energy Department to stop most of its previous plans to dilute and dispose of surplus plutonium and instead establish a program to process the material and make it available to private companies. Even Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, has gotten in on the action, announcing last year that it would merge with private nuclear fusion company TAE Technologies in an effort to help “America win the A.I. revolution.” NextEra Energy and Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Live Updates From Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ iPhone Event 🔴
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.14
A new era at Apple is upon us. Newly appointed CEO John Ternus is now at the helm of the $4.75 trillion-dollar company, and the first foldable iPhone is reportedly going to be announced this Wednesday, Sept. 9, at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event at Apple Park. While the foldable iPhone will likely steal the show, we’re also expecting to see the rumored iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Raymond Wong, Gizmodo’s Senior Editor of Consumer Tech, and Adriano Contreras, Gizmodo’s Social Media Editor, will be reporting live from the Steve Jobs Theater before, during, and after the keynote, which kicks off at 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT. In an internal memo sent to staff on his first day as CEO, Ternus said the launch “is going to be phenomenal.” Let’s see if Apple can change the world again. Be sure to bookmark this page and check back often as we live blog it all. Don’t get too upset by any headlines you read that say the new Apple Watch Series 12 screen is smaller than previous models. However, MacRumors pointed out that the Series 12 specs page lists the screen surface area as 1,196 sq mm. The Apple Watch Series 11 watch face was 1,220 sq mm on the 46mm version. The 42mm version has dropped from 989 sq mm to 970 sq mm. That’s about a 2% difference for both versions of the Series 12. The casing is now also slightly larger, resulting in an almost imperceptible growth in the screen borders. I don’t imagine most users would be able to spot the difference, though I may be more intrigued to see screen size shrinking instead of growing, for a change. —Kyle Barr the Apple tiktok team is once again killing it (last one is insane tho 😭) pic.twitter.com/HFAGJnzWiG — Dylan (@DylanMcD8) September 10, 2026 Apple’s new Instagram and TikTok scrolling promos for the iPhone Duo are tongue-in-cheek in the way I find surprising for the Cupertino tech giant. One of the ads shows somebody at a coffee shop with their laptop and a large cup of joe, while somebody with a Duo sits next to them and receives a proportional, Alice in Wonderland-sized coffee. Another ad shows an iPhone having a nice dinner date with an iPad mini. As one of the shrinking number of tiny tablet fans, I feel almost like the crochety father who does not want my precious child mingling with the likes of iPhone. —Kyle Barr If you were wondering what the difference is between this generation of AirPods and the last generation, I got you. Spoiler alert: AirPods 5 are improved in pretty much every way. —James Pero The iPhone 18 Pro is a very similar phone to the iPhone 17 Pro, from the screen to the shape and everything in between. However, the biggest differences are more than skin deep, with some promising improvements to the iPhone’s cooling and chip design. It’s also the first iPhone with a mechanical aperture, something that will only get a few people excited. Luckily for Apple, I’m one of those people. —Kyle Barr The new Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra and their new audio recording features have people talking, and let’s just say people keep bringing up always-recording smart glasses in the same sentence. Siri Recap is supposed to listen to you throughout the day and offer a summary of what you did and who you talked to. Live Rewind is a user-activated feature that can summarize conversations you just had. Apple’s support document detailing Siri Recap and Live Rewind mentions that they’re exclusive to the S11 processor inside the new watches. That’s partly because they have a “secure exclave” that processes this audio on-device. The document reads, “Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by watchOS, apps, the user, or Apple.” The data in the exclave is not stored or transcribed, but the encrypted file is processed for transcription on your iPhone’s own secure exclave. Users can choose to save these summaries on their iCloud accounts. You can read the full explanation for yourself here. Apple seems to know this is a sore spot for privacy-centric users, so we’ll see how well they take to it when the Series 12 watches hit the scene later this month. —Kyle Barr Both the exterior and interior displays of the iPhone Duo rely on a 1:4 aspect ratio. That’s very different than what you’re used to with most candy bar-style phones, but it also means these devices are much, much better for watching content you don’t get on TikTok. Apple showed the device playing games at its full-screen height without any black bars around the content. For movies, it’s going to get interesting. Despite some dubious X post you may have seen, IMAX films use either a 1.90:1 or 1.43:1 aspect ratio. Sure, that fits the Duo’s screen better than you would on a regular mobile phone, but it would still require some black bars to make it fit. Did Christopher Nolan ever want you to watch The Odyssey on your phone? I imagine the very idea would give him a migraine. —Kyle Barr BREAKING: Apple's Polishing Cloth is compatible with the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4/Series 12 pic.twitter.com/0yxMME2qur — Aaron (@aaronp613) September 9, 2026 Okay, everybody calm down. It’s official, your Apple polishing cloth (which recently had its price slashed to $9) is indeed compatible with both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Go ahead and feel free to smooth that folding phone until it’s as smooth as glass. Oh wait, it’s already made of metal and glass. Whatever, just keep scrubbing. Apple commands it. —Kyle Barr How much are you willing to pay for the return of the Ceramic Apple Watch? A Series 12 ceramic model starts at $809 at the 42mm size in either pearl white or night blue colorways. The watches come with both GPS and cellular connectivity, but they’re easily the most expensive version of the Series 12. Meanwhile, an Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $719. —Kyle Barr Burgundy happens to be my favorite color, which means, of course, I’m very smitten with the iPhone 18 Pro. Burgundy is also a modern region in France that’s today known for its wine-making. During the Medieval period, it was a duchy that proved to be one of the most important regions for the late Medieval political field. In the 15th century, Duke Charles the Bold tried his damndest to create an independent kingdom of Burgundy through diplomacy and war. He was a known patron of the arts, and his nascent kingdom also became a center of chivalric etiquette. Unfortunately, Chrales’ dream of a revived Burgundian kingdom died at the Battle of Nancy against the Swiss Confederation. Still, Burgundy lives on thanks to Charles’s epic motto, “Je L’ay Emprins,” which translates to “I have dared it.” —Kyle Barr It’s THIN. It’s VERSATILE It’s DURABLE. It fits in your pocket. And it FOLDS. Meet iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/lVpBmC36hx — Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) September 9, 2026 All the videos showcasing the iPhone Duo include this slick-looking animation where it seems the exterior screen bleeds over into the interior display. I want to believe this is how it will look in-person, but there’s another side of me that wonders if the look of this animation will depend on whether you’re staring at the device straight-on. Also, I want to know if it works on other apps, not just the home screen. —Kyle Barr Netflix made a special version of its app for the iPhone Duo that makes use of both the exterior and interior displays. On the outside, you’ll scroll through clips from some of the streamer’s shows, and then opening it up, you’ll be greeted with a larger screen-filling video. Apple does want you to use its device for watching shows and content, though it’s also partnered with Zoom and Slack for making use of the larger 7.58-inch interior display. —Kyle Barr Apple imagines you’ll treat your iPhone Duo like a miniature, pocketable tablet. That makes sense, given the Apple Pencil compatibility and the consistent bezels. To that end, Apple’s also making a Folio case for the Duo with a built-in gumstick kickstand. It also covers up the exterior screen in this mode, but you weren’t looking at it anyway. The Folio case is only available in a tan taupe color and navy blue. —Kyle Barr iPhone Duo prices. $3200 for 2TB model. pic.twitter.com/aopePNw1nx — Mark Gurman (@markgurman) September 9, 2026 Foldable phones are expensive—there’s no doubt about that—but if you want the top-of-the-line iPhone Duo, you’re going to have to really shell out. The iPhone Duo with 2TB of storage costs $3,200 before tax, which is a ton of money (but somehow less than a Vision Pro). Still, I think I speak for most wallets when I say… ouch. —James Pero Apple says that, starting Sept. 14, you’ll be able to download the next OS update to all your Apple devices, including iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, watchOS 27, and so on. Just know that all the new Siri AI capabilities are still listed as a “beta,” which is how Apple plans to wash its hands when the chatbot inevitably makes a mistake. Additionally, some anticipated features, like the Apple Watch “Audio Intelligence” features, won’t be available until later. —Kyle Barr The new Apple Watch doesn’t seem all that different from the Series 11, at least on the surface. Beyond a whole slew of new health metric tracking, the big additions are all in how these watches now include extra AI features that use audio capture. The most important ones you’ll get to know are “Siri Recap” and “Live Rewind.” Siri can use your data and combine that with your audio to give you a rundown of what you did that day. Live Rewind can enable users to see a summary of what somebody just said to you when you weren’t listening. Those specific features won’t be available until a beta comes out this October. —Kyle Barr That foldable iPhone won’t be available until Oct. 23, more than a month after the iPhone 18 Pro hits the scene. Preorders start Oct. 16. Here’s the big news: the iPhone Duo will start at $1,999. At the very least, $2,000 is a lot less than the $2,500 rumors originally suggested. —Kyle Barr Apple’s new C2 modem supports 5G mmWave. For reference, previous modems, the C1 and C1X, both in-house products, didn’t have that. Apple says the C2 also allows for 50% faster uploads, which is nothing to scoff at. —James Pero The iPhone Duo is using a special screen layer that Apple promises is doing a few things, but the most important aspect is how it may reduce the chance you’ll see the crease. We’ll have to see that for ourselves, considering the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts life with minimal crease, but it becomes more apparent the more you open it up. —Kyle Barr Naturally, multitasking on the iPhone Duo looks very iPad-esque. You can stack apps vertically or horizontally, and it looks like there’s some intuitive dragging and dropping. In a way, Apple has been making foldable phone software for years, just not on a foldable phone. —James Pero Apple says using the iPhone Duo won’t be restricted to your digits. You’ll be able to use an Apple Pencil with USB-c on the interior or exterior screen. However, Apple makes no mention of the more versatile Apple Pencil Pro, which may remain only usable on an iPad. —Kyle Barr Apple’s first foldable phone also has a FaceTime camera built into the screen on the right side when it’s opened up. This means you can have your phone open and have multiple people take up different parts of the screen. What we really want is to take video calls while—hopefully—being able to keep using your device. —Kyle Barr There’s a whole lot of new features coming to Apple Watch Series 12, but at least it doesn’t cost any more than before. It starts at $399 and now—finally—comes with ceramic options. —Kyle Barr Apple has two new versions of AirPods 5. Both have better ANC, but only the more expensive model has swipe controls and wireless charging. You’ll also have to shell out more money for one more hour of battery life. The base model gets four hours with ANC on, and the more expensive model gets five hours with ANC on. —James Pero Look at those specs. As you might’ve expected, the Watch Series 12 is better in basically every way imaginable, with better sensors, of course. —Matt Wille Apple’s updated AI will now synthesize all your health information, like sleep data, exercise, and heart rate, and give you a “Health Age” score. What if I don’t actually want to know that much about myself? —Matt Wille The new Apple Watch will take your heart rate up to 24x more than its predecessor. Apple says it’s now the “most accurate heart rate sensing” available in a wearable. —Matt Wille The AirPods 5 now feature better ANC, which promises around five hours of battery life thanks to a reengineered power cell. And despite everything getting more expensive, they still cost the same $129 as the AirPods 4. The AirPods 5 with a wireless charging case will now cost $149. —Kyle Barr That’s right, RAMageddon has come for the iPhone. The new iPhone 18 Pro will start at $1,200, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max will ask for $1,300. That’s both $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, respectively. Let’s just admit that—considering today’s memory prices—it could have been way worse. —Kyle Barr Apple’s planning to support Google’s SynthID watermarks for AI-generated images, but it’s now also trying to beat deepfakes with a reference photo future. Essentially, Apple will host an original image in its Private Cloud Compute servers that doesn’t have any modifications. —Kyle Barr The iPhone Pro’s camera is getting more professional with additional controls. Now, with Pro Camera controls, you can adjust things like aperture, white balance, shutter speed, and more. The Pro controls also work with video, allowing you to adjust shutter speed for more motion blur. You can also maintain focus on moving subjects with AI. For anyone who takes iPhone photography seriously, I assume these will be pretty rad. —James Pero But it’s still pretty damn cool. Apple has added a mechanical aperture to its 48-megapixel main “fusion” camera lens, which means that you’ll have much more control over depth of field for your shots. It’s going to be a very pro-centric feature, but at least it’s one of those features that will potentially make amateur photogs more willing to reach for their phone instead of their camera in a pinch. —Kyle Barr The iPhone 18 Pro is supposed to offer much better performance, and a big reason for that is because the iPhone should be much better at keeping cool. Apple said the phone now has a 3X larger vapor chamber, which is important because the redesigned A20 chip now has its silicon die placed next to its memory, which means the 2nm chip can seat closer to the thermal system. All this means that, maybe—finally—the iPhone 18 won’t be as toasty as usual. —Kyle Barr The A20 Pro is Apple’s newest high-end iPhone chip and comes with two “neural engines.” That equates to quite a few improvements, according to Apple, including “2x more compute.” There’s also a 50% increase in memory bandwidth. Whether you really feel the results will depend on what you’re doing, of course, but it looks impressive on paper. —James Pero Apple mentioned that some of Siri’s capabilities may be rate limited but didn’t offer more details during its event. We’ll just have to find out for ourselves if Apple wants us to buy into an iCloud subscription to get the most use out of AI. —Kyle Barr Siri’s AI enhancements are finally here. They were in the latest betas, but if you’ve been waiting for the full release, know that Siri has more “personal context” that allows it to understand what you’ve been posting in your emails or messages, and it can take some actions on your behalf. Siri also has several “expressive” options for voice, but only on the more recent iPhone models. This has all been well-established since WWDC, but we’ll see how well it performs on the millions of iPhones that can use it. —Kyle Barr There it is: Burgundy is the new color for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Other colors for the iPhone 18 Pro: Deep Black, Glacier (light blue), and a new silver. The glass panel on the backside is also color-matched to the aluminum frame. —Raymond Wong iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Check out the new color with color matched back. Burgundy is the new color#appleevent pic.twitter.com/1maaD28lsw — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 John Ternus really had us going there for a second. “Intelligent Personal Hub?” I mean, come on, we were all thinking smart home hub, right? —James Pero While the folks in Cupertino, California are greeting John Ternus, the rest of us plebs watching the livestream are greeted with a very Apple-ish opening trailer, or perhaps multiple trailers. And suddenly, Tim Cook’s voice, then Tim Cook, who reveals he’s no longer the head honcho. It’s John Ternus, y’all. They’re really making a big deal out of this. —Kyle Barr Ternus didn’t say the signature “Good Morning,” like Tim Cook always did. Guess he’s doing things his own way. He said Apple has been doing a lot of imagining and we’ll see some of those things today. —Raymond Wong John Ternus is out on stage and attendees gave him a loud ovation. So much love for the new guy. —Raymond Wong Standing ovation for John Ternus! #appleevent pic.twitter.com/kXPDk3NLNt — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 New Executive Chairman Tim Cook sighted! Where is John Ternus? Probably behind the stage getting ready to hop on and “Good Morning” us all. —Raymond Wong New Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook sighted! #appleevent pic.twitter.com/KMQXtQWqMs — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Thanks to the iPhone 17 Pro’s 8x zoom, I was able to scope on Apple’s head of marketing Greg Joswiak and chief of software engineering, Craig Federighi. Dude’s hair still still looks incredible. Gotta find out what conditioner he uses to get that kinda volume. —Raymond Wong I spy Craig Federighi and Greg Jozwiak at the #appleevent pic.twitter.com/QAW9wUSz64 — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 I’m seated inside of the Steve Jobs Theater. If you’ve never been here, know this: the theater has plush leather (?!) seats, outlets for each one, and the speaker system is one of the very best I’ve ever experienced. —Raymond Wong 15 minutes until the #appleevent keynote! pic.twitter.com/Cpjopg4iIT — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Apple’s new leader woke up super early and shared this teaser to his X account. But what is it? The variable aperture for the iPhone 18 Pro Max? Some glimpse of a close-up of the foldable iPhone? Make your guesses in the comments. —Raymond Wong — John Ternus (@johnternus) September 9, 2026 Here’s my food review of the breakfast for invited media: B. I’m wolfing down this mini chocolate croissant and an apple tart. I’m going to need the sugar to power me through the long day. The coffee is mid, too. Edible, but nothing special. I’m old enough to remember when the food and drinks situation was amazing. Of course, this was in the early days when the Steve Jobs Theater had just opened. —Raymond Wong We just picked up our badges and have arrived at the Steve Jobs Theater. The current temperature is 72 degrees Fahrenheit in Cupertino, and it’s supposed to reach a high of 96 degrees by the late afternoon. I’m definitely feeling a bit antsy, but I can’t wait to see the so-called iPhone Duo. Is this the foldable that will make foldable phones mainstream? We shall see. —Raymond Wong Got my #AppleEvent badge! Ready to see the foldable iPhone pic.twitter.com/vhcDNwJoVH — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Maybe I should have stuck to my prediction that Apple will call the foldable iPhone the “iPhone Duo.” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said on X last night that he believes Apple has decided to call it the iPhone Duo, with the device starting at $2,000 and shipping in September. A storage option with 2TB could cost around $3,000 he said. The Apple sleuth also said that the iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil and launch in dark blue and white colorways. John Ternus could do the funniest thing ever and not call it the iPhone Duo just to screw with Gurman, though. That would be pretty funny. —Raymond Wong Well, no regular iPhones, that is. Rumor has it Apple will only be announcing the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max today, with no iPhone 18 in the mix. It’s an interesting choice from Apple, a company that usually hopes to offer something lower-end for users who aren’t ready to shell out $1,000+ on a new phone. But hey, we are expecting to see the foldable iPhone today. That’s basically two phones in one, right? —Matt Wille Apple has just released a firmware update for a product that does not exist yet Beats 360 Firmware 4A203 is out. It confirms the Beats 360 name and the 4 colors: Black, Pink, White, Cloud It also includes HD images of the upcoming products pic.twitter.com/a24FDZcu1m — Aaron (@aaronp613) September 8, 2026 AirPods aren’t the only audio product that should be on your Apple radar right now. According to leaks, Beats has a new pair of wireless headphones in the works called the Beats 360. There are even some HD images leaked along with them, and they look… very Beats-y. Whether these are announced at today’s event is another story, but the timing of the leak is certainly interesting. —James Pero Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are likely going to cost at least $100 more, according to Bloomberg’s ever-consistent Apple leaker Mark Gurman. So what kinds of hardware upgrades will Apple try to suggest are worth the ballooning cost of memory? Gurman says there should be some big camera upgrades this year that will include a mechanical aperture on at least one of the new lenses. This grants more fine-tuned control over your photos, and it may be my main reason for personally opting for the bar-style phone instead of the upcoming foldable. The other big upgrade may be Apple’s downsizing of the Dynamic Island. It could appear smaller on your phone without any content on it, but Gurman suggested users will be able to toggle between up to three live activities at one time. Compared to something like the relatively pointless Camera Control switch, the Dynamic Island has proved itself a worthwhile feature over time, and it’s nice to see it with more usability. —Kyle Barr It’s looking like AirPods with cameras in them are a long shot on today’s laundry list of releases, but AirPods 5 might make an appearance. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, AirPods 5 will bring a few perks over the last generation, including better active noise cancellation (ANC). There will be two models, according to Gurman, and one of them will have wireless charging in the case while the other won’t. Sure, it’s not as mind-blowing as wireless earbuds that can remember where you left your keys, but it’s something. —James Pero You shouldn’t expect any massive hardware update from Apple’s wearables this year. Instead, the main reason Apple wants you to be excited may be for new software updates—and of course that means AI. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman suggested The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will have a feature that summarizes your day, and that may include conversations. This AI Siri-enabled feature may be called “Recaps,” according to Gurman. The big question is whether Apple will have it run all the live-long day or if you can set it to only start recording at certain times or in certain locations. Apple will, of course, try to emphasize how it will keep your data secure, but I don’t imagine many users are still that enticed by more self-surveillance features. Also, don’t expect this feature to come to any past Apple Watches, which is especially annoying considering how many recent Apple Watch models can’t even get watchOS 27. —Kyle Barr One of the less-anticipated product reveals for the “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday may be a new version of the Apple TV 4K set-top box. It’s a good thing too, since the old one was looking a little long in the tooth. A new box necessitates a new processor upgrade, and MacRumors claims—based on some pre-release code—that we may see an A19 or A19 Pro chip. This six-core SoC was first built for the iPhone 17 generation, but that means Apple may also be upgrading the RAM spec from 4GB to 8GB or more. We’d hate to see what that does to the price. A current-gen Apple TV 4K went from $130 to $200 in Apple’s big across-the-board price hike back in June. —Kyle Barr We’ve been reading purported details about the foldable iPhone, iPhone 18 Pros, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5 for months now. Here are all the major rumors on what to expect from John Ternus and company tomorrow. Spoiler alert: it’s full of spoilers! —Raymond Wong Guys, I’ve been in Cupertino for 24 hours, and let me tell you, it’s dry out here. I’m very excited to see Apple’s first foldable iPhone. Can’t say the same about my skin drying up. Today is a planning day with the Consumer Tech Team. We’re gonna be working like maniacs to bring you all fast and accurate coverage of everything that Apple announces tomorrow. —Raymond Wong

item.title: The Fight Over OpenAI’s Math Breakthrough Is a New Kind of Scientific Arms Race
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.92
In the past 24 hours, Silicon Valley has erupted in bitter debate over what may seem from the outside to be an esoteric, trivial issue: the solution to a longstanding math problem which, despite its importance among academics, doesn’t have any clear practical applications. And yet it raises urgent new questions about the nature of competition—not only between humans, but also between humans and machines—in the age of AI. On Tuesday morning, OpenAI published a blog post claiming it had used an unreleased AI model “significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra” to solve the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, which is related to the physics of water and other fluids. It’s one of seven “Millennium Problems” laid out by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the year 2000, each of which offers a $1 million prize for the first correct solution. OpenAI wrote in its blog post that it doesn’t intend to accept the prize for its result, which it said was discovered by human researchers collaborating with around 10,000 AI agents working for a little under ninety hours. The company’s announcement has largely been overshadowed by controversy around how its result was reached. OpenAI said in its blog post that its work on the Navier-Stokes problem started Tuesday of last week, “after hearing a rumour” that two independent mathematicians, Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, had achieved a breakthrough in another area, called forced Euler, related to Navier-Stokes. The company says it then reached out to the duo “to offer a concurrent release of our result and to recognize their priority in a joint announcement.” The previous evening, Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at NYU, published a statement confirming he and Alpöge had been contacted by OpenAI after the company learned of their work on forced Euler, but that the company had played hardball to make sure it wasn’t scooped. Buckmaster said that he first learned about OpenAI’s approach during a Friday call with OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck, which he said sounded suspiciously familiar to the approach he and Alpöge had taken with forced Euler, for which they had used multiple AI models, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. (Alpöge was not on the call.) Buckmaster says he asked Bubeck if the model OpenAI had used to solve the problem had access to his and Alpöge’s Codex logs. “I was told the model did not look up user data,” Buckmaster wrote. “I asked again, about training, and I did not get an answer.” OpenAI wrote in its blog post that neither its researchers nor its AI agents saw the two researchers’ work before it was published, but also that it “cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.” Buckmaster claims Bubeck offered him two potential paths forward to ensure he shared the credit with OpenAI for the pathway that led to the Navier-Stokes solution, both of which involved completely removing Alpöge’s name from the solution; Alpöge has been employed with Anthropic, OpenAI’s biggest competitor, since 2024. Buckmaster says he declined both offers and told Bubeck that if OpenAI opted to move forward with its announcement, he would publish an account of the conversation. According to Buckmaster, Bubeck replied: “Why would you ruin your career?” In a reply posted Tuesday on X, Bubeck said he “could not consider Levent to be an independent academic” after he learned that Anthropic’s AI models had been used as part of his work with Buckmaster. He also apologized for the threatening-sounding question he posed to Buckmaster, calling it an “extremely poor choice of words” and “the opposite of what I was trying to convey.” A new era for competition Historically, the formalizing of a new mathematical proof—even one that doesn’t have any obvious practical application—was a cause for celebration. Science is a collaborative enterprise, and friendly competition is a vital engine for fresh discoveries. There has, of course, been controversy and infighting over the matter of who reached a breakthrough first. But at the end of the day, it was humans bickering among one another, all operating within human limits. Until now. With the Navier-Stokes solution controversy, we’ve entered a strange new era of scientific competition: one where humans compete not only with one another, but also with deep-pocketed tech companies wielding powerful AI models, hell-bent on being the first to tout major technical breakthroughs, and operating under the assumption that anything published on the open internet—and perhaps shared with their proprietary AI tools—is fair game. Money isn’t the issue here. Even if OpenAI were to accept the Millennium Prize for its Navier-Stokes solution, it has no need for the $1 million reward. The computing power required by the agents working on the problem cost millions of dollars, according to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown. “[OpenAI] didn’t do this for the bounty,” one X user wrote on Tuesday. “They needed a headline that says ‘our AI solved one of the hardest problems in mathematics’ and they needed it before someone else got credit.” Terence Tao, a Fields Medal recipient who’s widely regarded as the greatest living mathematician, had a similar response to the controversy. If humanity’s collective endeavor to understand the universe—which relies not only on friendly competition, but on the free and open exchange of ideas—is subsumed by competition between jealous and power-hungry tech titans, the total store of shared human knowledge is doomed to shrink, rather than expand, contrary to what the AI companies themselves have promised over and over again their technology would deliver. “We have now seen that even the rumor of someone working on a problem can trigger a massive amount of AI-powered effort to flatten it before the original research project has time to reach its full potential,” Tao wrote in a Tuesday post on Mastodon, responding to the Navier-Stokes controversy. “The incentives may now be pointing in the direction of no longer sharing any promising research directions with the broader community, which would reverse centuries of traditions of open science and do serious long-term damage to the future of the field.”

item.title: LG TVs Are Capable of Listening to More Than Your Screen, Report Claims
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.73
Smart TVs are built to siphon your data and sell it to advertisers or whomever else wants to know your viewing habits. LG, a screenmaker already coming off of a monitor adware scandal, has reportedly given its screens the ability to capture audio from your living room, even if the TV seems like it’s turned off. In a two-hour-plus video by Gamers Nexus, fellow YouTuber Wendell from Level1Tech says, in his testing, LG TVs were capturing six-second bursts of audio from the TV and surrounding environment. This could be used for the purpose of advertising as a form of Automatic Content Recognition, or ACR. It’s important to recognize is that LG isn’t necessarily reviewing this audio data. This data essentially creates a fingerprint that is then sent to LG, which can cross-reference a database to show what you’re watching. LG’s TVs can be sending this data even if the screen is off, according to the YouTubers’ findings. LG’s privacy policy explicitly gives the company consent to send data to advertising partners or law enforcement. LG also says it “may collect audio, electronic, visual, or similar information, such as video recordings” through its ThinkQ app. In an email statement provided to Gizmodo, LG said its TVs only record voice data when you’re using the remote or using the TV’s wake word. In addition, the company said that its ACR features alongside “Voice Recognition for hands-free control and Interest-Based Advertising to deliver relevant advertisements” provide “a more tailored and convenient experience.” Here is LG’s statement in full: “The claims made in the recently published video are not true. LG TVs process voice data only when the voice button on the remote control is pressed and held, or when a wake word such as ‘Hi LG’ is recognized after the user has activated the Far-Field voice recognition feature. Other than these instances, the TVs do not collect or record ambient conversations. (If the wake word is not recognized, no voice data is transmitted to the server; the audio processing for wake word detection is performed locally on the device and is immediately deleted.) Additionally, to provide smart TV functionalities, LG TVs feature the ability to scan for and connect to nearby devices on the same network. This is a standard function commonly provided by smart TVs and smart home devices. The ACR (Automatic Content Recognition) feature is provided on an opt-in basis to deliver personalized content recommendation, services, and advertisements. If a user does not consent to the applicable optional agreement, ACR data is not used for advertising purposes.” The video describes how, with a few changes, these TVs are apparently able to identify devices using the home network, even those that aren’t actually connected to the TV itself. That includes the ability to identify several smartwatches and phones all on the same network. The screens are capable of monitoring all neighboring Wi-Fi networks, which could be used for geolocating users even if the data is anonymized. Security researchers who analyzed Gamer’s Nexus findings suggested that users disconnect their LG TVs from the internet. That’s not necessarily out of privacy considerations but more so for all the potential vulnerabilities hackers could potentially exploit. Users could instead rely on a set-top box or TV stick, but those have their own data privacy considerations. Opting out of tracking on these streaming sticks could also disable certain smart features, so no matter what, you’re going in with some risk. All smart TVs are voracious data snakes that are likely to unhinge their jaws and absorb every bit of data that comes their way. Most of the time, this comes up with ACR. It’s essentially how TVs identify what you’re watching and then tie that data to your habits. But as Rtings recently identified, the majority of modern TVs track every other device you plug into your TV, including game consoles. It’s also incredibly difficult to opt out, even if you wanted to. Gamers Nexus has a tendency to bury the lede. The bigger problem isn’t necessarily how some ne’er-do-well could hack your home screen to spy on you while it’s off; it’s the fact your data isn’t just used by advertisers. U.S. law enforcement has been caught buying advertising data from data brokers as yet another form of surveillance. That data can be linked directly to individuals, where such voice transcripts would be invaluable information for any law enforcement or government agency keeping tabs on U.S. residents. LG’s data collection may be especially egregious. Still, every TV owner is essentially giving up their privacy for the sake of buying a cheaper screen. This post was updated to include a statement from LG.

item.title: This one Linux setting is capping your Wi-Fi speed far below your router's rating
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.83
A Wi-Fi router can advertise hundreds of MBs, yet your Linux laptop may deliver a fraction of that speed. Before replacing the router, changing channels, or blaming the wireless adapter, there is one Linux setting worth checking. Linux puts a wireless interface into power-saving mode to optimize battery life. On a laptop, that can make sense when battery life matters more than maximum network performance. The problem is that power-saving behavior can also introduce latency, reduce responsiveness, and, with some wireless hardware and drivers, interfere with achieving the best possible throughput. Check your actual Wi-Fi configuration first Do not confuse router ratings with negotiated link speed Before changing anything, inspect the connection itself. It can be done using: iw dev Then check the negotiated connection: iw dev wlp3s0 link The output provides details such as signal strength, frequency, channel width, and negotiated RX and TX rates. For example, a connection might report: Frequency: 5200 MHz Channel: 36 Width: 80 MHz Signal: -35 dBm RX bitrate: 866.7 Mbit/s TX bitrate: 390.0 Mbit/s That number is the PHY link rate, not the speed you will necessarily see in a browser download or speed test. This is important because Wi-Fi introduces protocol overhead, retransmissions, encryption overhead, and other inefficiencies. A connection reporting a PHY rate of 866.7 Mbit/s cannot normally deliver that exact figure as usable application throughput. The same command also shows the channel width and frequency being used, which helps establish how the wireless connection is actually configured. In my case, the Intel Wireless-AC 8265 is connected to the fiber network on the 5GHz band at 5200MHz, using an 80MHz channel. The signal is strong at -35 dBm, while the negotiated RX and TX rates are 866.7 Mbit/s and 390.0 Mbit/s respectively. These figures give us a much clearer picture of the actual Wi-Fi connection before investigating whether another configuration is responsible for slower real-world speeds. See whether Wi-Fi power saving is enabled iw gives you the answer immediately
To find if Wi-Fi power saving is on, the command is very simple: iw dev wlp3s0 get power_save An enabled configuration reports: Power save: on To perform a quick test, disable it temporarily: sudo iw dev wlp3s0 set power_save off Then verify: iw dev wlp3s0 get power_save You should now see: Power save: off You do not need to reboot to perform this test. Once power saving is disabled, run the same speed test you used before. Ideally, perform several tests against the same server or service and compare the results rather than relying on a single measurement. I used iperf3 for benchmarking: In my test, enabling Wi-Fi power saving reduced sustained throughput from about 159Mbps to 138Mbps, a drop of roughly 13%, which is entirely plausible on an 802.11ac connection, although the exact impact varies considerably between adapters, drivers, access points, and traffic patterns. The 159 Mbps result with power saving disabled is also reasonable for a 2x2 Wi-Fi 5 connection operating under real-world conditions, where application throughput is well below the theoretical PHY rate. More interestingly, the enabled test recorded 283 TCP retransmissions, while the disabled test recorded none, suggesting that power-saving behavior was contributing to additional buffering or delayed transmission in this particular setup. That does not mean every Linux system will behave the same way, however. Some laptops may see almost no throughput difference, while others can experience noticeable changes in latency, retransmissions, or sustained transfer performance. In practice, the biggest benefit of disabling power saving may therefore be more consistent network behavior and lower latency, rather than a dramatic increase in peak download speed. Make the change persistent with NetworkManager Update the connection profile The iw command changes the current wireless interface state. If NetworkManager later reconnects the interface, that setting may be restored according to the connection profile or global defaults.
