NetworkManager provides its own Wi-Fi power-saving property: 802-11-wireless.powersave First find the connection name: nmcli connection show Then disable power saving for that profile: nmcli connection modify "Your UUID" 802-11-wireless.powersave 2 Reconnect: nmcli connection down "Your UUID" nmcli connection up "Your UUID" Finally, verify: iw dev wlp3s0 get power_save The interface should report: Power save: off Test before you change hardware Before spending money on a new wireless card or router, it is worth checking whether the problem is actually coming from the software stack. Linux gives you enough visibility into the wireless interface to investigate these issues yourself. For many, that also makes this kind of troubleshooting a worthwhile first step. A setting buried in the operating system can be changed in seconds, tested under normal workloads, and reverted just as easily. That is considerably easier than replacing hardware only to discover that the original problem was somewhere else.

item.title: The invisible PC killer from the '90s is still around—and most people don't know it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.82
The early days of people having internet in their homes were pretty wild. Viruses were pretty much everywhere, and unlike now, many users had no clue what to do with them. I was a tween in the early '00s, but I remember intervening when my mom's PC had what felt like hundreds of them, with pop-ups and ads covering up the entire desktop, impossible to remove. Annoying and potentially hazardous as those viruses were in the '90s and the '00s, there was a much bigger PC killer in town, and it's one that's still around to this day. I'm talking about static electricity. You could carry thousands of volts without realizing it Your PC could feel a shock that you couldn't I'm one of those people who get zapped by static electricity each time I touch a doorknob, so I'm no stranger to the concept. Even then, static electricity is easy to underestimate, because you mostly just notice these tiny little zaps, if anything at all. But under the right conditions, your body can build up thousands, even tens of thousands, of volts. This is especially easy in a dry climate, or in a moderate climate during the winter when the heaters are running. That was a particularly nasty combo in the '90s, when beige PCs were often sitting in carpeted bedrooms and offices. (Did you know that you shouldn't keep your PC on carpet? No? Well, you do now.) Weather conditions aside, the important part is that this doesn't make static electricity dangerous to you (phew), because the amount of energy involved is tiny, and each zap lasts a split second. Your PC's components are a different story. Sensitive electronics can get damaged by electrostatic discharge (ESD), at voltages that are nowhere near what you can actually feel. You might not notice static discharge, but your PC can be affected at a tiny fraction of what it takes for you to experience that sensation. The TL;DR is you could touch a part of your PC and discharge static into it without knowing. This makes static a super-stealthy ninja PC killer that was a big threat back in those days, arguably bigger than most viruses. Static didn't have to kill a component immediately Sometimes the PC kept working At the risk of making a blanket statement, most modern viruses can be pretty stealthy compared to the stuff we dealt with in the '90s and '00s. Back then, many were up in your face, just the way I described above. Some still are, too, but most scams involve trying to fool the user into thinking they're on a legitimate platform, or working in the background without being detected. So, viruses kind of announced themselves back then. If you had one, you probably knew. But static damage can be much sneakier. A sufficiently strong ESD event might kill a component outright, and with component prices as they are right now, that can quickly turn into a $2,000+ mistake. It's not always so dramatic, though. Your PC or your components may sustain some damage, but not enough to stop working outright. They might throw errors or fail earlier than they otherwise would've, though. The PC upgrade boom gave static plenty of opportunities Every new RAM stick meant touching exposed electronics The other reason static was such a perfect '90s PC killer is that people were opening their PCs up quite a lot. Not everyone, of course. But there was just more to be done inside a PC compared to now; you could add a sound card, add a modem, replace drives ... Still doable now, but much less necessary. Every such upgrade meant handling exposed parts, circuit boards, and contacts. Often in that carpeted environment I talked about above. Viruses needed infected files or disks to get in, but static discharge only needed you to touch the wrong thing without grounding yourself. That's why manufacturers and repair pros took anti-static precautions so seriously. RAM sticks, expansion cards, and motherboards were all supposed to be handled by the edges, kept in anti-static bags, and installed while you were grounded to the chassis. Those rules still apply to this day. The invisible PC killer never actually went away Ground yourself before reaching inside You'll often find me going on and on about how cleaning your PC is the best $0 upgrade you can give it. That was true in the '90s when PCs were beige and loud, and it's true now when they're filled with RGB lighting and cooled with AIOs. The problem is that doing this the wrong way can still very much damage your PC. It's not like magically, over the years, static became a non-issue. It's just that most people who actually open up their PCs are more aware of it now than they may have been back then. I'll say it again: Please, do clean your PC. Just ground yourself properly first. The scariest PC threat was 100% invisible At a time when viruses were less than sneaky, static electricity was the cause of death for many a PC. These days, the tables have somewhat turned; many viruses are far from obvious, and static is the same way, as ever. In both cases, exercise caution and you'll never have to worry about either one of those two, vastly different, issues.

item.title: 7 ways to repurpose an old or broken smart doorbell
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.80
Smart video doorbells can be incredibly useful, but they don't last forever. If you have an old or even broken video doorbell, you don't need to throw it away. There are plenty of ways you can put it to good use. Use your smart doorbell as a security camera A battery-powered doorbell can be placed almost anywhere If your video doorbell is still in full working order, but you've replaced it with a different model, then there are plenty of things you can do with it. A video doorbell is effectively a security camera with a button, so if you stop using it as a doorbell, you can use it just like any other security camera. If your video doorbell is battery-powered, this is even better. It means you can place your security camera almost anywhere you want. Turn it into a smart button You can still use it even if the camera doesn't work If your video doorbell is broken, you may still be able to put it to good use. If the camera is no longer working, it may still be the case that the doorbell ringer is functional. If this is the case, then you can repurpose your video doorbell as a smart button. Many smart home systems allow you to use doorbell rings as a trigger for automations. This means that when you press the doorbell ringer, you can run whatever automations you want. Set up a dedicated wildlife camera See what critters visit your backyard If you don't need your video doorbell to work as a doorbell anymore, it can make a great way to track local wildlife. Most video doorbells can detect motion, and many can record motion-triggered video and offer night vision features. You can set up your old doorbell in the backyard and have it record video whenever motion is detected. You can then watch back the recordings of all the animals that have snuck into your yard at night. Use it as a 3D printer monitor Keep tabs on your print remotely One of the biggest benefits of a smart video doorbell is that it allows you to see who is at your door even when you're not at home. You can access the live doorbell feed remotely to see who just rang your bell. This feature makes an old video doorbell a great fit as a 3D printer monitor. When you start a print, you can walk away and leave your doorbell focused on your printer. You can then use your phone at any time to see how your print is getting on. Leave it mounted somewhere as a deterrent Even a broken doorbell can give you protection If your doorbell is completely broken and no longer functions at all, you might think that all you can do is dispose of it. However, it could still serve a useful purpose. Security cameras only have limited views, so a single camera is never enough to cover the entire exterior of your home. The more cameras you have, the fewer blind spots you have. If you mount your broken video doorbell outside your home in a prominent position, it's hard to tell at a glance that it's not a working device. This may be enough to deter people who might otherwise see your home as an easy mark. Repurpose it as a dedicated pet camera Keep tabs on your pet inside your home If you have pets, an old video doorbell can make a great dedicated pet camera. Most video doorbells have motion detection, and some have pet or animal detection too, so that you can receive alerts when your pet is spotted by the doorbell. You might place the doorbell pointing at your pet's food or water bowls. You can then track when they eat or drink and monitor the bowls remotely to see when they need refilling or if there's been a spillage. You could also monitor a cat flap, or place the doorbell externally to track when your pet has gone outside. Use the housing to hold your own smart doorbell Keep an ESP32 doorbell protected If the internals of your smart video doorbell are completely dead, that doesn't mean it's useless. Many video doorbells have high-quality weather-resistant housings to protect the electronics from the elements. You can use these housings for your own projects. For example, you can build your own video doorbell using an ESP32-CAM board that combines an ESP32 with a camera module. The problem is that you can't stick an exposed circuit board to your front door. By using the housing from your old doorbell, you can keep your DIY doorbell protected, and it will look smart, too. Video doorbells don't have to become e-waste There are plenty of reasons why you might want to upgrade or replace a video doorbell, but you don't need to throw your old ones away. Repurposing old tech can save you money and help to reduce unnecessary e-waste.

item.title: These Bash shortcuts save me hours of terminal typing every month
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.70
If you type a lot of commands in Bash, it can be time-consuming to navigate, correct, and add strings to achieve the desired output. I've found my fair share of typing errors, multi-instruction commands, and complex interpreters. There are ways to speed up the typing process without wearing you out or giving you headaches, from short codes and hotkeys to cool shortcuts and hidden features. Navigate Bash commands fast without reaching for your mouse Clever cursor movement by page, word, or even section using your keyboard When dealing with the terminal, there are certainly some Linux commands you should never use. If you know what you are doing and have a couple of simple mistakes in your instructions, navigational hotkeys can save you time, such as pressing Alt + B to move backward word by word, or Alt + F to move forward. It's much quicker than repeatedly pressing the arrow keys to get where you need in your commands. For an even faster approach, try pressing Ctrl + A to jump to the beginning or Ctrl + E to go to the end. I've also used Ctrl + XX to jump to the beginning of a command line, and I repeat it to return to the previous cursor position. Let's say you're typing a sudo command and forgot to add "sudo" at the beginning; you can use this shortcut to jump to the start, add the short code, then return to where you were and finish your command. Forget speed reading; try speed typing in Bash Auto-finish, multiply, repeat, and append commands quickly If you need to reuse the last typed word (often a filename or path) in your previous command, you can type !$ in the Bash console to use it again in your new command before pressing Enter — you won't see it until you execute it, but it's fast and simple. To insert it visually, type Alt + . to paste it into your command, then continue typing before pressing Enter. If you enclose the path, filename, or group of words in double quotes ("example of using quotes"), both options will consider it all to be the last word. This little trick allows you to run different commands for a specific path or filename by auto-pasting it into the new command, as long as it was at the end of the previous one. This is handy for copying code that contains spaces and switches. Some more really cool shortcuts you may not know include an actual undo function (pressing Ctrl + _), yank — pasting back (Ctrl + Y), and Ctrl + R to autocomplete from history — you can press again to cycle through your history matches. You can also command multiple items using brace expansion, such as sudo apt upgrade {Upwork,Timeshift,Inkscape} or mkdir ~/Documents/"New Folder"{1..3}, , which creates three new folders in the Documents folder named New Folder1, New Folder2, and New Folder3. When using sudo, I've had times when I copied a command from somewhere and executed it, but it failed because it required admin privileges. To correct it quickly and efficiently, I'd type sudo !! so it starts the new command with "sudo" and pastes the last command I entered. You can also use !! to copy the last command, and then type whatever you need along with it. This little trick can save you 10–30 seconds per command. Autocomplete is also a nifty shortcut in Bash, and it only takes one key to launch it. If you press the Tab key while typing your command, folder path, or filename, Bash tries to autocomplete it based on previous command history. When there is more than one possible match, press it again to view the next option—you can repeat as needed to get what you want. This makes typing commands twice as fast because it auto-populates based on your history, and it helps prevent mistyping incidents that cause you headaches and consume time rather than save it. If you want to go bigger and better, and prevent accidental Enter presses or command errors on long strings, a full text editor has you covered. Whenever I have complex or long-winded commands to type, I press Ctrl + X then Ctrl + E to open my command in Nano. I make changes or add to it, then I press Ctrl + O, then Enter to save it, followed by Ctrl + X to exit, and it magically executes the command in the terminal. Don't worry, Nano saves to a temp folder and deletes the contents after rebooting, unless you intentionally load a specific file to edit. Using Nano is also a safe and secure way to prevent auto-execution. Sometimes, I copy code from a website that would otherwise execute when pasted into the terminal — it does happen. Launching a temp Nano session allows me to paste it and review it before transferring it to the terminal. It's also a simple option to prevent command errors in the terminal, especially for long lines of code or advanced command sessions that include pipes, multiple actions, loops, or more. You wouldn't want to execute an advanced command with errors or have to go back to fix something it performed that was not correct. You may also need it to create an actual file — you can load the editor with a new filename like nano myscriptname.sh and create your new file with the necessary code or script, then write it out. Correct typos, delete segments, and fix long strings efficiently Quick Linux Terminal editing at its best When typing away in the terminal, I easily make mistakes and have to correct them as I go, from misspellings or wrong directories to forgotten switches or case-sensitive issues. I speed up the editing process by using hotkeys rather than arrows, backspaces, or delete. A quick way to erase a whole section of your command or code is to press Ctrl + U to delete everything from your cursor to the start of the command line (moving left). Ctrl + K does the same but deletes from the cursor to the end (moving right). This also comes in handy if you copy your previous command into your new line using !!. Place the cursor where you want to erase everything to the right, use Ctrl + K, then type the new characters at the end. It's a quick way to use the beginning of a command and create the rest. Another fabulous editing shortcut is to delete the word or segment before or after the cursor's position. If you catch an issue with your command that is one word before the current cursor location, press Ctrl + W to cut the word. You can also press Alt + D to cut the one after the cursor position. Don't forget you also have the Ctrl + Y (the yank feature) mentioned earlier to paste back what you cut. Become a multitasking pro in Bash without losing anything Suspend, switch, move to the background, and repeat or append previous commands easily Bash terminal operations can get rather complex at times, leading to multiple processes like archiving and downloading, numerous command sessions, or Nano editing within one terminal. Sometimes, I need to switch between directory locations to use commands, which is where I use the pushd and popd short codes. It's not like using cd where you can only reside in one directory, although there are great replacements for Linux cd commands these days. These two commands help manage a list of directory locations (a directory stack), where you pick which location you want as the active directory. The "pushd" command adds your current directory to the stack, so to speak. The "popd" removes it from the stack and returns you to the previous directory. If your current CLI directory is set to "~/Documents" and you type pushd in the command line, it will add that location to the temporary folder stack and go to it — you can repeat for each new directory location or insert pushd before a location to not only add it but go to it. When I have more than two directory locations, I add "+0" or "-0" to the command to select the current directory — counting starts at 0 from the left for "+" and 0 from the right for "-" of the stack. I'll type pushd +1 , and it goes to the second folder from the left in the stack, whereas pushd -1 goes to the second one from the right in the stack. When typing popd in the command line, it removes the current location from the library. Numbers work the same, so typing popd +1 means it will remove the second folder from the current stack. If no more exist, it ignores the command and stays in the current directory. Another task-efficient trick is to multitask in the same terminal. To save time, I use Ctrl + Z to suspend the running process and bg to let it run in the background while working on another task. I also use the fg short code when I need to bring it back to the front of the terminal. All these shortcuts and commands are tied to one terminal session — just avoiding confusion here. You can also use the "&" operator to launch an app while keeping the terminal active and usable, such as typing & brave-browser in your active session. Without the operator, your terminal freezes up, and that is not a lovely experience. Create shorthand aliases for command strings you commonly use Abbreviate complete lines of code, parts of commands, or shorthand common words Aliases are excellent time-savers, enabling you to use your own short codes to create partial or full commands. I like to open ".bashrc" using Nano to add my aliases so they are usable in any terminal, but you can also type them in your current session for temporary use. I type sudo nano ~/.bashrc and then add my aliases at the bottom. I press Ctrl + O to save it, then Ctrl + X to exit and return to the terminal. This feature can save hours of typing, allowing you to use short code in the terminal for long or specific commands or scripts. Yes, you can make Bash easier to use and spend less time in agony Linux is better than Windows for scripts and coding in many ways, but it can be tedious at times. Using short codes and hotkeys can cut your typing time in half, but there are so many shortcuts to learn that I suggest practicing a few first, then branching out to others as they become second nature. From quick typing and editing shortcuts to navigating and multitasking, Linux will be easier to use — less headaches and more free time for other projects or activities. You may want to bookmark this page so you can return later as you master each skill or shortcut like a pro.

item.title: Android's private DNS feature solves a problem most people don't know they have
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.69
If you care about protecting your privacy online, you've probably seen an ad for VPNs. You likely also know to seek out private messaging apps like Signal and Proton Mail. But there's another change you need to make in order to protect your phone's web traffic from prying eyes, and it's a relatively simple fix. Your DNS isn't private by default It's time to change this DNS stands for Domain Name System. It's what enables you to get somewhere by typing a website name rather than having to enter an exact numerical IP address. Without DNS, typing howtogeek.com would only yield an error message. Out of the box, your phone's DNS activity is quite likely neither encrypted nor private. Your internet service provider (such as Comcast or Verizon) or carrier (Verizon, T-Mobile, or AT&T) can see every site you visit. If you’re on a public Wi-Fi network, you run the risk of a snoop taking a peek at your activities as well. Third-party DNS providers like Cloudflare, NextDNS, and Mullvad offer a way to browse the web while hiding your domain name requests from your ISP. It does so by encrypting your DNS activity, just as encrypted email masks the content of your messages and HTTPS hides what data a website is transmitting to your device. How to enable Private DNS on Android It only takes a couple taps To keep your phone from leaking your domain name requests, you'll need to dive into your network settings. You can do so by swiping down from the top of the screen and tapping on the gear icon that opens your phone's Settings app. Then navigate to "Network & internet." Towards the bottom, you'll see an option for "Private DNS." Tapping here provides you with three options: Off, Automatic, and Private DNS provider hostname. You’ll likely see “Automatic” enabled by default, which means your phone will use DNS encryption when it detects the option available. This leaves you at the whim of your ISP or carrier, who may prefer to track and monetize your browsing activity rather than protect it. “Off” disables DNS encryption entirely. For a continuous private connection, you'll want to select a private DNS provider hostname, and you will then need to enter an address in order for the changes to take effect. If you don't yet know one to put here, you can find several options in our list of the best DNS servers for secure browsing. Just keep in mind that you will need to enter a hostname into this field, not an IP address. In other words, you’ll need to enter the private web address your provider offers, rather than a series of numbers and periods. Once you've entered your selection, you can confirm whether things are working using the Safer.com Browser Privacy Test. That said, there are circumstances where this fix may not be the one you’re looking for, and you’d actually be better off leaving the default setting in place. Private DNS does not fully mask your web activity There is still a lot your ISP can learn about you DNS encryption, whether via DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT), doesn’t fully prevent your ISP from seeing what you do online. While you’re shielding your DNS lookups, all the traffic that follows still happens over their connection. This means the ISP can see the destination IP address you connected to and how much data was transmitted. The company can also see how much time you spend on the site before switching to another. You’ll need to take other steps if you sincerely wish to prevent others from gaining insights into what you do online. The more technically minded who are interested in self-hosting can rent a cheap VPS, install Wireguard, and tell all of their devices to use this VPS as a full-tunnel VPN endpoint. Those of us who aren’t interested in that whole song and dance can look into commercial VPN options. They often provide mobile apps that make encrypting a connection as simple as possible, often requiring only a single tap and granting some permissions. Just know that if you opt to use a commercial VPN, such as Private Internet Access or ProtonVPN, they tend to offer their own encrypted DNS. In that situation, you’ll want to leave the private DNS setting on your phone set to “Automatic” and trust the VPN connection to shield your DNS lookups instead. There’s no way to go online without leaking at least a little Private DNS encrypts your DNS lookups, but it doesn’t mask the resulting web traffic. VPNs may go a step further, but your ISP can tell you’re using one, and you must trust your VPN provider not to abuse your trust. It’s even possible to tell someone is using TOR, even if that may be all you’re able to tell. In other words, don’t start browsing the web with the false assumption that everything you do is private, but by reducing your online footprint as best you can, you reduce how much information can be monetized or used for online attacks.

item.title: My Android notifications kept arriving late—these settings were the problem
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.23
I've had problems with Android notifications arriving late for years. Usually, it's not a huge deal—if someone needs me urgently, they'll just call instead of texting me. But not all notifications are equal. An Instagram Reel shared by my friend can wait an hour for a reaction, but an important work email about a meeting that's been canceled or moved up a few hours can't. Since I can't afford to miss notifications like those anymore, I finally decided to figure out what was causing the delays and fix the problem. Battery Saver is delaying your notifications Battery life comes at a cost Some people like to keep Battery Saver (aka Power Saving Mode on some devices) permanently enabled on their devices for a few good reasons. Modern phones are plenty fast, so sacrificing a fraction of a second for apps to load to extend the battery life of your phone by up to a few hours is a worthwhile tradeoff. However, on top of throttling the CPU's maximum clock speed and disabling various other performance optimizations to reduce power draw, Battery Saver actually does a number of other things to your phone. The most important thing for us today is that it heavily restricts or outright stops background sync for non-essential apps. Some apps might work just fine, but others might fail to sync for hours. Fortunately, the fix is super easy. Head over to Settings > Battery and disable Battery Saver or switch to Balanced mode, depending on what brand your phone is. Battery optimization is stopping apps from syncing in the background Give specific apps more freedom Android has a pretty clever feature that optimizes battery use on a per-app basis. It allows your phone to throttle apps you don't use and prioritize background activity for your most-used ones. It's a pretty clever system for the most part, but it's also one of the most common sources of delayed notifications because apps are optimized by default. This includes your email app of choice, Slack, Asana, and other important work-related apps that you might only use for a few minutes a day but can't afford to miss notifications from. At the same time, social media apps will probably get more priority if that's what you use the most on your phone. Fortunately, you can adjust this default behavior fairly easily. Go to Settings > Apps > See all apps. Find an app on this list that's experiencing delayed notifications and tap on Battery usage, then switch it from Optimized to Unrestricted. The exact wording varies from brand to brand, but since it's built directly into Android, the setting is there—and it's most likely what's causing your delayed notifications. Your app is being cut off from the internet in the background Let your important apps use data Data Saver is another core Android feature that optimizes cellular data usage. It's disabled by default, but if you enabled it at some point and forgot to turn it back off, you might not even be aware of it. Some phones display a persistent notification at the top, but not all (or the option to do so might be disabled by default). In any case, it only takes a few seconds to check. Go to Settings > Network and Internet (or equivalent) > Data usage > Data Saver and disable the feature. If you must keep it on because you're on a limited plan, there's an option to leave data unrestricted for some apps, which is the perfect compromise. Again, the wording differs between brands, so just poke around until you find it. Android is restricting an app you haven't opened lately Even unused apps deserve notification access Pause app activity if unused is another semi-problematic core Android feature that was introduced with Android 12. It's surprisingly aggressive at what it does: it puts an app into complete hibernation, kills notifications, revokes permissions, and wipes cache data if it hasn't been used in 3 months. This can be problematic if the app in question is something you access very infrequently but still need to keep up with, like a specific smart home app, security alert app, travel app, or similar. Unfortunately, there's no global setting to switch off app hibernation, but what you can do is disable it on an app-by-app basis. Go to Settings > Apps > See all apps, find the app you suspect got disabled, and disable Pause app activity if unused. On my phone, it's the Manage unused apps toggle that needs to be turned off. Like with the settings I discussed previously, the exact wording might differ between brands, but if your phone runs Android 12 or newer, it's there. A manufacturer-specific setting is restricting apps on its own Your phone might have a hidden battery saver Everything I've discussed so far has been general fixes that you can use on every Android phone. However, some brands have their own additional battery management features and optimizations on top of those built into Android. Unfortunately, since there are so many brands and things are constantly changing with updates, going over all of them here could quickly turn into its own article. So, if you're still experiencing delayed notifications after trying all of the fixes above, I recommend doing a little research on your specific device to see if there's a hidden toggle or feature that you can change to force background sync for problematic apps. Most notification delays have a simple explanation I'm sure that most Android owners can relate to the frustration of delayed notifications that happen here and there. The majority of the time, the cause is some data- or battery-saving feature that's built into Android, and luckily, the fix is often as simple as changing a single option.

item.title: 3 physical Home Assistant projects to try this weekend (Sep 11-13)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.92
We live in an increasingly digital world, but as Olivia Newton-John said, sometimes you just need to get physical. Here are three projects that let you interact with Home Assistant in a physical way. Scan empty grocery packaging straight to your shopping list An ESP32 barcode scanner makes life easier Home Assistant is not just able to help you control your smart home. It can be useful in many different aspects of your life. I use Home Assistant to help with everything from reminding me to take my medication to gamifying chores for my kids. Home Assistant can also help make the mundane things a little easier, such as grocery shopping. Having to figure out what to buy each week feels like a never-ending nightmare, but there's a clever Home Assistant project that can make things a little easier. The BeepBasket project lets you build a system for scanning the barcodes from real products and automatically adding those products to your Home Assistant shopping list. It uses an R35C-B barcode scanner hooked up to an ESP32 that can transfer the data to Home Assistant. BeepBasket then looks up the product using the Open Food Facts API and adds the item to your shopping list. If the product isn't found, the barcode itself is added to your list instead. There's even a dedicated BeepBasket card for keeping track of products through a Home Assistant dashboard. The idea is that you place your scanner next to your trash can. When you finish a product and throw away the wrapper, you scan the barcode and the product is automatically added to your shopping list. It's one less thing to think about. Let Home Assistant press the buttons on your car keys An ESP32 can control a car that wouldn't otherwise integrate with Home Assistant Many modern cars offer smart features that let you control things remotely via an app, such as unlocking the doors and turning on the heated seats. Home Assistant offers integrations such as the Tesla Fleet integration that allow you to perform these actions through Home Assistant. Not every car has these smart features, and not every car that does can integrate with Home Assistant. One user came up with an alternative solution for giving Home Assistant some measure of remote control over their car without the need for apps or APIs. The user took a spare key fob for the car, opened it up, and wired its button contacts to an ESP32. Home Assistant is then able to send commands to the ESP32 that activate the different buttons on the key fob. The battery was removed, so that the fob is only powered by the ESP32 when a command is received, reducing the risk of a relay attack. Obviously, you're limited to what your key fob can do, but the user was able to set up an automation that automatically locked their car at 9:30 PM. If anyone is detected in their driveway between 12:30 AM and 5:30 AM, Home Assistant triggers a different button, which causes the lights to flash and the horn to beep. This project comes with significant risks, since an error in your automation or a problem with Home Assistant could leave your car unlocked and vulnerable. It's worth taking precautions to ensure that any similar projects consider these risks. Turn Home Assistant data into a moving analog needle See your data the old-school way Home Assistant can display data on dashboards in a wide range of different ways, from simple numbers to dials or charts. The data is usually displayed on a digital screen such as a wall-mounted tablet, but one Home Assistant user wanted to create something more physical. The project involved creating a physical needle display built around an ESP32 and an X27.168 stepper motor. The ESP32 retrieves the data from Home Assistant, and the stepper motor moves a physical needle to a specific position related to the value it is trying to display. There are even addressable LEDs built in to show different colors depending on the values. One example of the gauge in action shows the user turning down their heating. The needle turns counterclockwise to a lower position, and the LEDs change from red to blue. The whole thing is built into a laser-cut acrylic enclosure, which looks awesome. The user shared a prototype on Reddit and got some very useful feedback from the community. They are now selling ready-made gauges that are hand-built by the user. There's nothing to stop you from building something of your own using a similar concept. Sometimes we all need to get physical While Home Assistant is highly digital, there are plenty of ways you can make it more analog, from using physical knobs to turning your lights on by snapping your fingers. It's worth exploring what's possible beyond the same old dashboards.

item.title: I upgraded my Excel PivotTable with these 3 simple features
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.49
I'm probably guilty of making Excel spreadsheets more complicated than they need to be, but I have one rule I keep coming back to: if I'm going to build a PivotTable, I want to actually enjoy using it. The basic summary is useful, but a few small additions can make a surprisingly big difference. After converting my data into a table with Ctrl+T, creating a PivotTable in a new worksheet via Insert > PivotTable, and dragging fields into the different areas of the PivotTable Fields pane, it's easy to stop there. But that's only the start. I usually add three simple features—slicers, timelines, and PivotCharts—to make the results easier to filter, explore, and understand. For the examples in this article, I'm using a fictional 500-row sales ledger. You can download a free copy of this worksheet to try the three features yourself. When you click the link, you'll find the download button in the top-right corner. Slicers make my PivotTables much easier to control I like being able to see my filters The first thing I tend to add to a PivotTable is a slicer. I like being able to see exactly how I've filtered my data, rather than opening a small drop-down menu and trying to remember which options I've selected. I also like that I can use a slicer to filter by a field that isn't actually visible in the PivotTable, giving me another way to explore the same summary. For my sales ledger, I started with a PivotTable showing Revenue by Category. I clicked inside the PivotTable, went to PivotTable Analyze > Insert Slicer, and selected Salesperson. Excel added a set of buttons for the eight salespeople in my dataset, and clicking Ava Patel, for example, immediately filtered the PivotTable to show only her sales. I can select multiple salespeople by holding Ctrl while clicking, or clear my selection using the Clear Filter button in the top-right corner of the slicer. Slicers aren't exclusive to PivotTables—you can add them to a regular Excel table—but I find them particularly useful with PivotTables because one slicer can control multiple PivotTables based on the same source data. In my case, I created a second PivotTable showing Revenue by Region. I then right-clicked my Salesperson slicer, selected Report Connections, checked the box for my Region PivotTable, and clicked OK. Now, whenever I click a salesperson, both PivotTables update at the same time. That's the part I really like. Instead of opening separate filter menus for each PivotTable, I have one set of visible buttons that lets me control the summaries I'm looking at. A timeline makes date filtering much less fiddly It gives me a better way to explore a year's worth of sales Dates are one of the first things I often want to filter when I'm looking at my data, but the standard PivotTable date filter isn't my favorite way to do it. When I have a whole year's worth of records, scrolling through individual dates feels cumbersome. That's why I usually add a timeline. I went back to my first PivotTable and clicked PivotTable Analyze > Insert Timeline. I then selected Date, clicked OK, and Excel added a timeline showing the 2025 sales data. Because I had two linked PivotTables, I also right-clicked the timeline, selected Report Connections, and checked the box for my Revenue-by-Region PivotTable. Timelines let you filter the PivotTable by Years, Quarters, Months, or Days. I usually stick with Months for a dataset like this. Then, instead of opening a filter menu and selecting individual dates, I can simply click a month or drag across several months to create a date range. For example, I can drag from April through July and immediately see how my PivotTables change to reflect those four months. The timeline also works alongside my slicer. If I select Ava Patel in the Salesperson slicer and then drag across a few months in the timeline, I can quickly narrow both connected PivotTables down to Ava's sales during that particular period. I find that much easier to work with than repeatedly opening filter menus. The timeline also makes it obvious which period I'm looking at, which is particularly useful when I come back to the spreadsheet later. PivotCharts show me what my numbers are actually doing Sometimes a table of numbers needs a picture I like being able to see the actual figures in my PivotTable, but sometimes I want to spot a trend without having to study a column of numbers. That's when I add a PivotChart. For this example, I wanted to see how my sales changed throughout 2025, so I went back to my Revenue-by-Category PivotTable, clicked PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart, and chose a Line chart. I then removed Category from the Rows area and used Date instead, while keeping Revenue in the Values area. This gave me a single line showing total sales for each month of 2025. Keep an eye on the Rows area of the PivotTable Fields pane when adding a Date field. Excel can add things like Days (Date) to your PivotTable. If you don't want them included, drag them out of the Rows area. The useful thing about a PivotChart is that it stays connected to the PivotTable. I can use the field buttons around the chart to change what I'm viewing, and those changes are reflected in the PivotTable too. My Salesperson slicer and timeline are connected as well. If I select Ava Patel in the slicer, the chart immediately changes to show only her sales. I can also use the timeline to narrow it down to a few months. That means I don't have to create a separate chart every time I want to look at a different slice of the data. I can use the chart controls, slicer, or timeline to change what I'm looking at, while the PivotChart gives me an immediate visual representation of the result. A few small additions can make a big difference A basic PivotTable is only the starting point. Slicers make filtering easier, timelines make date ranges easier to explore, and PivotCharts help me spot trends at a glance. Once everything is set up, I can use PivotTable conditional formatting to highlight the numbers that matter. I also make use of a few little-known PivotTable tricks to take them to the next level, like generating separate worksheets for each category, using distinct counts to track unique values, and calculating month-over-month growth without using any formulas.

item.title: There's a tiny computer hiding in most USB-C cables (and it isn't always used for good)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.43
Two USB-C cables can look identical, cost wildly different amounts, and behave nothing alike. The reason sits inside the connector housing: a chip that talks to your devices before any power moves. It's genuinely useful engineering. It's also a convenient place to hide something nasty. What is that tiny computer about? The e-marker chip that negotiates power and speed The component is called an e-marker, short for electronically marked cable, and it lives inside the connector shell rather than the cable itself. It communicates with chargers and devices over the Configuration Channel (CC) pin, telling connected hardware what the cable can actually do. It draws its own power from the VCONN pin—up to about a watt—which is what lets a passive-looking cable participate actively in a negotiation without any external supply. That negotiation happens before anything else. Power Delivery transactions begin by addressing the cable itself in a stage known as SOP prime, and only once the cable's capabilities are established does the rest of the process continue between source and sink. The chip publishes its specification as a set of 32-bit values called Vendor Defined Objects, or VDOs, covering things like the manufacturer and model, the signalling protocol and maximum transfer speed, whether the cable's controller can communicate independently with the charger or device, and the hardware and firmware version. Not every cable has one. Cables rated at or below 3A aren't required to carry an e-marker chip; anything expected to handle more current needs one. In practice, a cable carries an e-marker if it is rated above USB 2.0 speeds or above 60W. Either one, not necessarily both. Given that USB Power Delivery now reaches 240W, and that pushing that much energy down an unrated cable risks overheating or fire, the chip functions as a safety mechanism as much as a feature flag. Plug in a cable with no chip and both ends assume the worst case, capping you at 60W and 480Mbps regardless of what your laptop and charger are capable of. What are its downsides? Opaque specifications and a perfect hiding place The first problem is honesty. Charging capability and data capability are separate fields in the e-marker, and manufacturers set them independently: a genuine, spec-compliant 240W cable can declare its data capability as 480Mbps, the same speed as a cable from 2001. Buyers reasonably assume that an expensive, high-wattage cable is also a fast one. The chip cheerfully says otherwise, in a format nobody without a protocol analyzer can read. The second problem is worse. If a connector housing can accommodate a microcontroller, flash storage and firmware, it can accommodate other things. Security researcher Mike Grover built the O.MG cable as a penetration-testing tool for red teams and awareness training. Hidden inside the connector is a web server, a keylogger and a keystroke-injection engine reachable over Wi-Fi, so the cable can type commands, capture what's typed back, and be driven remotely from across the room. Elite models store up to 650,000 keystrokes, support geofencing to trigger payloads by location, and can self-destruct to render the cable inert. In December 2024, industrial CT scanner manufacturer Lumafield imaged an O.MG cable and found sophisticated electronics and an antenna packed into the connector, alongside a second set of wires connecting a secondary die hidden beneath the primary microcontroller. Those bond wires are roughly the thickness of a human hair, and the arrangement would evade inspection techniques that can't assess an assembly volumetrically. Even an X-ray image can't reliably show whether a cable has been tampered with, because the additional electronics are so small and so cleverly integrated that they're nearly indistinguishable from regular components. Should you worry? Real risk, modest odds, and defenses worth knowing Proportion matters here. No real-world juice jacking attack has ever been publicly documented, though researchers keep proving it's technically possible, most notably at USENIX Security 2025, where Graz University of Technology researchers presented ChoiceJacking, the first family of USB attacks to bypass existing juice jacking mitigations by injecting input events while a data connection is being established. It let a malicious charger spoof user input and enable data transfer or code execution on eleven Android and iOS devices without consent. Apple and Google have since shipped fixes in iOS 18.4 and Android 15, and on current iPhones connecting a new USB device requires a passcode or Face ID. The standards body's answer has existed for years and gone largely unused. The USB-IF launched its Type-C Authentication Program with 128-bit cryptographic verification of chargers, devices, cables and power sources, managed through DigiCert. It remains optional, with no mandatory requirement for OEMs to adopt it. Practical defense is therefore about provenance rather than detection. Use your own cables, buy from the manufacturer or an authorized seller, and label what's yours. Keep your phone locked when charging in public and decline connection prompts you didn't initiate. A Malicious Cable Detector exists for around $40, using side-channel power analysis to flag the electrical signature of an implant, but its own documentation frames it as a first-line screen rather than a forensic instrument, and it can never prove a cable is clean. Weight and feel tell you nothing. Cables are computers now, so treat them accordingly The e-marker exists for good reasons, and it makes modern fast charging possible. But it normalized the idea of silicon inside a connector, which is exactly what makes malicious implants so hard to spot. Buy your own cables, from people you trust.

item.title: These are the 7 greatest Kindle mods of all time
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.25
Like most of its products, Amazon has locked down its Kindle devices so that you can't easily make changes. Thankfully, some clever people have figured out ways to hack Kindles over the years. These are some of the very best mods of the past and present. KOReader The document viewer that puts the stock Kindle firmware to shame This is perhaps the most significant Kindle mod there is, because it's essential to the core purpose of a Kindle: reading books. KOReader turns a standard Kindle into a much more capable eReader that can coexist with Amazon's normal software without replacing it. With KOReader, you can read a huge number of formats that a standard Kindle doesn't support, including comic formats such as CBZ and even Word documents. The PDF support is particularly impressive; the Reflow feature can effectively transform a messy PDF into an eBook format that's a breeze to read. There's so much more too, with OPDS support, Calibre integration, progress sync, and a wide range of plugins. I can't imagine using a Kindle without KOReader now. Duokan EPUB support and comics, while it lasted Duokan was one of the most impressive early Kindle mods. Instead of just another reading app, it was an entire alternative OS for a Kindle. Duokan enabled you to do things that a standard Kindle couldn't, such as reading EPUB files and ZIP-based comics, and it offered strong support for Chinese-language books. Sadly, Duokan abandoned the Kindle some years back, but not before it showed just what was possible to do on the Kindle hardware. KUAL The launcher that lets you run almost anything on your Kindle The Kindle Unified Application Launcher (KUAL) is an important component of the Kindle hacking ecosystem. It's not as exciting as other hacks, but it's arguably more useful. KUAL gives your Kindle a graphical interface that you can use to launch various applications. Instead of running a single mod on your Kindle, KUAL lets you access multiple different packages and use the interface to launch or control them. The best part is that developers can create their own extensions, which means that you can build your own Kindle mods that you can run through KUAL. If there's something you wish your jailbroken Kindle could do, even with no coding experience, you can ask an AI chatbot to build it for you and have your very own Kindle mod running in KUAL. The original KUAL no longer works on Kindle firmware 5.19.4 or later. You'll need to use an updated version called KUALA for newer firmware. USBNetwork Bringing networking and SSH to the Kindle This is another mod that doesn't sound all that exciting, but it makes doing almost anything to your jailbroken Kindle so much easier. USBNetwork creates a network connection between your Kindle and computer and, most importantly, allows you to connect to the Kindle over SSH. This means you can connect your Kindle to your computer and get a root shell, allowing you to browse and edit the filesystem, run commands, and much more. USBNetwork became an invaluable tool for developing mods for the Kindle. It's a lifesaver on older Kindles, where trying to type anything is a horrific nightmare, because you can make all the changes from your computer. Custom screensavers Making the most of the E-Ink display This was one of the popular early Kindle hacks. A Kindle spends far more time sleeping than it does awake, but in its wisdom, Amazon didn't let owners use their own images as the sleep screen. The community created screensaver hacks that allowed you to replace the stock Kindle images with user-selected images instead. This may sound like a minor change, but it allowed users to take advantage of the Kindle's E-Ink display. Since an E-Ink display doesn't need power to maintain a static image, it makes a Kindle a great way to show off images and artwork when it's not being used for reading. These mods have developed over time, with KOReader now having screensaver options of its own. Some screensaver hacks can also be configured through KUAL. Collections Manager Giving the Kindle the nested collections it lacked This is another classic mod that was first designed for the original Kindle Touch and Paperwhite models. It was intended to give users far more control over how they could organize large libraries of books on their Kindles. The key feature was the ability to create nested collections. A stock Kindle let you create collections, but you couldn't place one collection inside another, making larger libraries an organizational nightmare. Using the Collections Manager mod, you could set up a collection for a specific author, which contained other collections of their different book series, with each of those collections containing the relevant books. It was then far easier to navigate to the book you needed. Sadly, firmware updates broke the nesting mechanism that Collections Manager used. More than a decade after the Collections Manager mod appeared, you still can't create proper nested collections on a standard Kindle. Custom fonts A classic hack that made reading on a Kindle better This is another mod that sounds fairly trivial, but it's one of the most important because it directly improves the Kindle's main purpose: displaying text. Older Kindles offered very little control over fonts, so community hacks soon appeared to try to fix this problem. Some of these hacks didn't even need a full jailbreak; the "Font Hack Lite" for the Kindle 3 and Kindle 4 models let you use hidden features already in the Kindle firmware. Modern Kindles allow you to install custom fonts, so this is something that is far less of an issue. However, even today, options such as KOReader give you far more control over exactly how your text is displayed than is possible on the stock firmware. The best Kindle mods solve genuine restrictions There are plenty of weird and wonderful Kindle mods that let you do everything from running Doom to working as an external monitor. The best mods, however, are those that make it easier to do what the Kindle was intended for: reading books.

item.title: There's a problem with DLSS 5, and it's not even the AI slop
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.33
When Nvidia first announced DLSS 5 neural rendering, many were quick to label it "AI slop." And I get it. We're definitely getting some uncanny valley vibes. Now that it's here, the AI slop allegations persist, but I'd say we're all focusing on the wrong thing entirely. The problem with DLSS has nothing to do with the all-too-realistic-but-also-not-realistic faces in games. The problem lies entirely elsewhere, and it's arguably bigger than just liking the aesthetic. The frame rate hit is real And it hurts a lot I'm not here to debate whether Nvidia's DLSS 5 looks good. For some people, it's great. For others, it's awful. Some say they can barely see a difference. No matter where you land in that particular conversation, there's one downside to DLSS 5 that's undeniable: the performance hit. It's real. It's too real, even. I personally own an RTX 4080 Super, so the only way I can test it is with DLSS Swapper, and yes, I've noticed the performance difference—but that makes sense. Nvidia didn't officially release DLSS 5 for the RTX 40-series, after all, so forcefully injecting it into a game that was never meant to have it on my GPU should result in performance issues. Naturally. Only, it's not just me. Some of my colleagues here at How-To Geek have tried it on RTX 50-series cards, including the ever-overpriced RTX 5090, and we're all united with the same opinion: DLSS 5 results in a massive performance hit across the board. No, it's not just us. Nvidia itself has said that turning DLSS 5 on will result in a 50-60% performance reduction. But some reviewers notice it doing even worse: TechSpot saw the RTX 5080 falling from 185 fps to 53 fps at 4K, which is a 71% drop. Even the RTX 5090 ran 60% slower at 4K, matching Nvidia's worst-case scenario. So, is it playable? It depends. You can't tune your way out of it Nothing can save you from an fps drop In the last few years, or should I say, last few generations, Nvidia's gotten really good (and shall I say, really reliant) at letting you optimize your GPU with the help of AI. Upscaling helps you "cheat" a little. Frame gen helps you "cheat" a lot. We're all allowed to believe that our GPUs are better than they actually are, while also offsetting for the fact that these days, frame gen and AI come baked into the software and the hardware. Performance expectations are built around the idea that you'll be using these features, and you'll be using them a lot. So, we've all gotten used to the idea that the DLSS section is the place to go when your game isn't running as smoothly as you'd like. But with DLSS 5, that's no longer true. Although DLSS 5 lives in the same menu, it won't up your frame rates; it'll drastically reduce them. Moreover, lowering the other settings to make up for those precious AI-generated faces isn't going to help you much. TechSpot found that on an RTX 5090 at 4K, dropping from max settings all the way down to low gives you a measly 9 fps back. There's no universe where that's ever going to be worth it. That's because DLSS 5 is largely tied to your output resolution, and it runs on the finished frame after upscaling rather than before it. Enabling upscaling doesn't help either; the gains are negligible. You can't cheat your way out of the performance tax on this one. Nvidia's own launch benchmark hides the real problem 'Fake frames' to the rescue Nvidia's own launch benchmarks are super encouraging. The RTX 5090 scores 370 fps with DLSS 5 on, ray tracing on, on the ultra preset. This is in NBA 2K27, which is the only game that currently officially supports DLSS 5. The RTX 5080 pulls off an impressive effort, too, hitting 233 fps on average. You know what I'm getting at, right? These figures have been captured with 6x multi-frame generation and DLSS Super Resolution set to Performance. So, the game was being upscaled from 1080p, and five out of six frames have been interpolated. I've learned to embrace the "fake frames" to the point of believing this type of tech is the future of GPUs. Even then, we can't treat these numbers as absolute, as the GPUs are getting a lot of AI-powered help here. If we strip the frame gen away, the RTX 5090 is rendering at around 62 fps, and the RTX 5080's 233 result works out to roughly 39 fps. You might say that fps is fps, and if it works, it works. Sure, but frame gen multiplies frames, not responsiveness, and a 39 fps base fps still feels like 39 fps. Input latency makes games feel sluggish when played with DLSS 5 on, and that's something that doesn't show up on benchmarks. Whether it's unplayable depends on your resolution And your GPU, of course In all fairness, DLSS 5 is very much playable. At 4K, sure, TechSpot's testing shows the DLSS 5 pass alone takes longer than 16.7ms. That's on every GPU in the RTX 50 lineup, by the way. Dropping down to 1440p, or better yet, 1080p, makes things much less grim, obviously. Even an RTX 5060 can do some type of successful work with DLSS 5 if you play at 1080p. Meanwhile, the RTX 5090, when propped up by all the fancy stuff Nvidia has to offer, will still do a good job. Is DLSS 5 worth it right now? The problem is that this "good job" isn't anywhere close to being an across-the-board type of experience. You should try it, because why not, but will it feel good to actually game with DLSS 5 on? Probably not. But it's still early days—I expect the tech to improve over time.

item.title: Loaded dice, card cheaters, and other unethical board game parts you can 3D print
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.08
The great thing about 3D printers is that they can make almost anything these days. The bad thing about 3D printers is that you can make almost anything with them. There are some obvious, actually illegal things that will get you in trouble if you print them. Though I won't mention them here, you can get on a watchlist on your own without my help! Then there are things that are legal, but they're a bad idea to 3D print. But what about things that aren't necessarily illegal, and are technically fine to print, but are also really unethical? Loaded dice If you've seen the movie "Casino", you know to leave these at home In case you somehow don't know, "loaded" dice are designed to fall on a specific number almost every time. In a fair die, there's an equal chance of landing on any given number, but if you change the weight distribution of the die to favor a specific number on the bottom, then you can control which number shows at the top. Traditionally, this is done using metal weights inside the dice, but with a 3D printer, where you can design the interior structure precisely, all you have to do is determine where the weight of the infill is. Indeed, with RevK's Loaded Dice, you need to set the infill density to 95% for it to work, and there are six models in total, each favoring a different potential number. Given how light PLA is, it's not really obvious that these dice don't have a uniform weight distribution. But a much larger issue would be that the dice were 3D-printed in the first place. So it's not like you're going to surreptitiously switch these out for store-bought fair dice. That said, people are getting really good at processing 3D prints so that you can't even tell they were made with a 3D printer. ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 - Build Volume - 256 × 256 × 256 mm - Connectivity - Wi-Fi The ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 builds on the solid foundation of its predecessor and adds an affordable, effective multicolor system to the mix. - Heated Build Plate - Yes - Top Print Speed - ≤500 mm/s - Max Plate Temperature - 110°C - Max Print Temperature - 350°C - MULTICOLOR PRINTING - Yes A card shuffler that deliberately deals winning hands Though, to be fair, you need more than just a 3D printer for this one! You may have heard (as reported by the BBC) of those rigged high-stakes underground poker games involving NBA players and lots of high-tech cheating equipment. Well, if you look into it, you'll see that part of the scam involved a modified casino-grade card shuffler. This device is supposed to ensure a fair deal in games like Texas Hold'em, but by hacking and modifying the device, you can precisely determine where any given card is at any time. Now, that machine costs a fortune, and I guess those illegal modifications aren't cheap either, but as you can see above, a Reddit user used a 3D printer, a Raspberry Pi, and some other miscellaneous electronics and parts to make their own. It's an incredibly cool project, and it would make you the god-king of your local poker game, but I suspect it's going to be hard to convince your friends that they should use your homemade card shuffler when the next game night rolls around. Printing extra Scrabble pieces If you really need to get the last word in Some people take Scrabble far too seriously, and although this wonderful 3D model set of Scrabble tiles by jjpowelly are meant to let you replace lost tiles without buying a whole new box, clearly unscrupulous players could print out extra tiles and secrete them up a sleeve to gain an advantage. If you look closely at any of these tiles, it should be apparent that they are 3D-printed, but if you only slip in one or two letters, I bet you could get away with it. If you're playing with all 3D-printed tiles anyway, well, all bets are off, I guess. Printing your own tabletop miniatures is a gray area What would the emperor do? In the world of tabletop gaming, 3D printing has been rather controversial. This isn't about gaining an unfair advantage in the actual gameplay (which isn't how something like Warhammer works anyway) but more about copyright and intellectual property. With resin 3D printers and even modern FDM printers, you can create high-quality miniatures and then paint them. The tabletop community and the companies who sell official models to sustain themselves have had to reckon with this, and official games now have rules on what pieces may be 3D-printed, or how much of a given model is allowed to be 3D-printed. In the end, if you're using 3D printing as a way to avoid paying for (admittedly expensive) official models, there's certainly an ethical dimension to that. For no other reason than the hobby itself might disappear if this technology puts its custodians out of business. Follow your own conscience I can't stop you from printing whatever you want, and if you're just making stuff for your own personal amusement, there's no harm in it. However, with great power comes great responsibility. And owning a 3D printer gives you more than enough power to act in a fair and just manner.

item.title: This is the only podcast app that makes any sense in Android Auto
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.97
I always find that Android Auto is at its best when you keep it as stripped back as possible. It's great for navigation and music, but throw a podcast app into the mix, and it can quickly start to complicate things again. You don't want to be browsing through hundreds of episodes or fiddling with complicated menus while driving. Pocket Casts is the podcast app that gets the balance right. It's got a powerful phone app that you can use for organizing and queuing up your podcasts, but the Android Auto interface is focused purely on the essentials. In my experience, it's comfortably the best podcast app for Android Auto. Pocket Casts does the organizing before you get in the car Android Auto isn't the place for a complicated podcast app Pocket Casts maintains a clear distinction between Android Auto and phone, or between driving and not driving, that isn't replicated in other podcast apps like Spotify. The phone is where Pocket Casts really shines. The discovery features are excellent. You get top charts, curated lists, and assorted recommendations alongside the regular search function. This alone helped to make it my podcast app of choice some time ago. But what makes it especially useful for the car is its playlist features. It goes way beyond the normal Up Next queue, although you get that as well if you want to do it manually. What Pocket Casts offers is the Smart Playlist function that automatically updates with podcast episodes based on various criteria that you set. You can choose which podcasts you want to add them from, and narrow down the choices based on things like when the episodes were released, how long they are, and so on. It stops you from having to search through all your subscriptions to find things to listen to. As well as a dog-walking smart playlist that queues up the latest shorter episodes from my podcasts, I've got a "long drive" one that finds longer episodes. I queue it up when I get in the car, and I won't have to touch it again. Its Android Auto UI gets out of the way Simplicity is the key In the car, Pocket Casts becomes much simpler and is one of the best Android Auto apps. It isn't designed for browsing huge libraries, and that's a good thing. The features are still there if you really need them — you can discover new podcasts, for example — but that isn't the intended use. Pocket Casts notes that the Android Auto interface uses the standard Google UI templates, with a focus on simple navigation and a distraction-free experience. The buttons are big and obvious, and highly visible in case you ever need to press them. But this simplicity doesn't come at the expense of functionality. Smaller but no less important things like playback speed controls are still accessible, you just don't have to scroll your way through a huge app to find them. Other podcast apps that I've tested on Android Auto, like AntennaPod or Podcast Republic, often either lack the optimization you need when driving, or are stripped back but have a more limited Up Next feature that takes a lot more work to get sorted. For me, Pocket Casts' Smart Playlists make the app feel more like a personal radio station, serving up content for as long as I need it. Pocket Casts finds the right balance. It's very powerful and capable when you use it on the phone, but you interact with it as little as possible when driving. It stays in sync with your other devices Pick up exactly where you left off The other thing I like about Pocket Casts that's relevant when you're on the go is how seamlessly it moves between devices. It syncs your podcast list, playback status, and position within individual episodes so that it's accessible wherever you're listening (and the app works on pretty much any device or platform). So, I can start listening on my phone, continue in the car, and then pick up again later on a desktop without missing a word. It means that Android Auto doesn't feel like a separate part of my podcast setup. It's something more akin to a streaming app like Spotify than an app that's based around local files. Pocket Casts handles the Android Auto compromise well Finding the right balance in an Android Auto app must be quite difficult. You want it to be as simple and distraction-free as possible, but it still needs to be useful. Pocket Casts manages this by making intelligent choices about what you should do on your phone and what you should do on the big screen. Its automation means you can prepare everything in advance, then cut back on how much you ever have to touch the app while you're driving. But your listening remains completely seamless. That's what makes it Android Auto's best podcast app for me.

item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.50
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. He has been writing about consumer tech for as long as he can remember, and he has used a variety of Android phones since falling in love with Jelly Bean. Send him a direct message via X or LinkedIn. You must confirm your public display name before commenting Please logout and then login again, you will then be prompted to enter your display name.

item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.08
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. item.title: Ray-Ban Meta glasses update makes them more useful on the go
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.91
What you need to know - Meta AI glasses v28 update adds pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, expanded language support, and camera anti-tampering improvements. - With hands-free walking directions, you can ask Meta to navigate to nearby destinations, with driving directions sent to your phone for farther trips. - Spatial Audio makes listening richer and adds a more immersive layer to music and podcasts on supported Ray-Ban Meta glasses. Meta has been steadily expanding what its AI glasses can do, and the latest v28 update adds several practical upgrades, including pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, and broader language support. Perhaps the headline addition is pedestrian navigation. You can now ask the smart glasses to guide you on foot to nearby destinations using voice commands such as “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” If you’re farther away, the glasses can send driving directions to your phone. There’s also a new way to begin navigation from your phone: Find a destination in your mapping app, tap Share, and select Meta AI, and navigation will start on your connected glasses. The update also broadens where walking directions work. Meta says it now offers walking directions in the U.S., Puerto Rico, Canada, and some cities across the world. Audio gets an upgrade as well. Now, Spatial Audio can make a more immersive version of the stereo sound you’re already getting, whether that’s music or a podcast. You can find this option in Settings > Audio > Spatial. It works with Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 Optics and the Meta Glasses collection. Meta is also adding Mandarin Chinese (zh_CN) support across Device Controls, calls and messaging, media capture and music controls, Meta AI, and MMAI. Finally, v28 has ongoing anti-tampering improvements to protect the cameras on the glasses. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Earlier firmware releases introduced features like Conversation Focus, which uses the microphones in the glasses to help users hear nearby voices better, and deeper Spotify integration. Similarly, on Reddit, the response is pragmatic, with users mostly praising the glasses for hands-free photos, calls, podcasts, and open-ear audio, while battery life and Meta AI’s limitations remain common complaints.
