Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Intel Will Reportedly Increase CPU Prices by 10% Next Month
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.61
If you’re waiting for PC prices to drop, you may be in for a long wait. According to a new report from Chinese outlet Digitimes, Intel is set to raise its CPU prices for the third time this year. After increasing prices by 10% in Q1 2026 and by an unknown margin in July, the company is reportedly set to impose another 10% price hike on Oct. 5. Citing industry sources, Digitimes reports that Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is conducting a comprehensive review of CPU prices, gross profit, and manufacturing costs amid a global memory crisis and rising demand for some specific processors. As part of the plans, Tan may also consider discontinuing some low-margin product lines and letting go of a few more employees, the report adds. Intel’s headcount has been dropping steadily since 2024. The company cut 15,000 jobs that year and reduced its global workforce by another 15% the following year. A few more employees were laid off in July, and Intel is now planning to cut 5-10% more jobs soon, Digitimes says. The company is estimated to have about 75,000 employees. Qualcomm imposed a similar price hike on Sept. 1. Microsoft, too, is reportedly considering a price hike for Windows licensing fees. Whether PC manufactures absorb the rising costs or pass them on to consumers remains to be seen. According to June data from IDC, PC shipments are expected to decline by 11.3% this year, with Q4 projected to decline by 20% year-over-year. A recent survey by PCMag’s parent company, Ziff Davis, also found that 73% respondents were willing to hold on to their old devices for as long as they worked. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: AirPods 5 vs. AirPods Pro 3: Are Apple's Pro Buds a Big Upgrade or a Big Mistake?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.51
Table of Contents The first foldable iPhone might be the biggest news from Apple's September event, but that doesn't mean you should sleep on the new AirPods the company announced. The AirPods 5 come with active noise cancellation (ANC) as a standard feature, and they're waterproof—both qualities they share with the excellent AirPods Pro 3. The AirPods Pro 3 remain stunning in-canal earphones, but with the base model leveling up so drastically, it raises a massive question for your wallet: Is a single pair of AirPods Pro 3 actually worth two pairs of the new AirPods 5? Full Specs | Apple AirPods 5 | Apple AirPods Pro 3 | | |---|---|---| | Type | | | | Type | Open-style earbuds | In-Canal | | Wireless | | | | Wireless | | | | True Wireless | | | | True Wireless | | | | Connection Type | | | | Connection Type | Bluetooth | Bluetooth | | Water/Sweat-Resistant | | | | Water/Sweat-Resistant | | | | Active Noise Cancellation | | | | Active Noise Cancellation | | | Price: Pro Features at Half the Cost? At $129, the AirPods 5 rewrite the value equation by including active noise cancellation out of the box—eliminating the extra $50 tax Apple previously charged for ANC on non-Pro models. That slashes the price barrier in half compared with the $249 AirPods Pro 3, delivering flagship sound isolation without the premium markup. Winner: AirPods 5 Sound Quality: Open-Ear Fit vs. In-Canal Seal We can't evaluate how the AirPods 5 sound until we get them in for testing, but we can at least apply years of experience and the hard science of acoustics to compare them with the AirPods Pro 3. The AirPods 5, like all standard AirPods before them, are earbuds that rest against the ear canal but don't provide a seal as the in-canal AirPods Pro 3 do. There's a limit to how consistently earbuds can fit in the ear and how much deep bass they can produce without a seal, which can make a big difference in performance. To be fair, the AirPods 4 sound excellent even without a seal, but the AirPods Pro 3 are without a doubt superior. Apple claims the AirPods 5 have a revised internal acoustic design for better audio, but for clarity and power, you can't beat a physical plug that prevents frequencies from leaking into the open air. Winner: AirPods Pro 3 Noise Cancellation: Physics Always Wins As with sound quality, noise cancellation performance is something we have to test ourselves to be sure, but you can't get around the reality of acoustics. Because the AirPods 5 don't form a seal against the ear canal, noise can leak in, no matter how sophisticated the ANC processing is. Apple's claims are also pretty clear, by the numbers. The company says the AirPods Pro 3 provides "up to 3x more" active noise cancellation than the AirPods 5. Winner: AirPods Pro 3 Battery Life: Endurance and Wireless Convenience The AirPods Pro 3 double the endurance of the base model, delivering up to eight hours of ANC listening on a single charge compared with just four hours on the AirPods 5. The Pro 3 case also squeezes out extra overall juice—24 hours total versus 20—and includes wireless charging out of the box. To get wireless case charging on the AirPods 5, you have to shell out an extra $20. Winner: AirPods Pro 3 Durability: Same IP57 Rating, Half the Price The AirPods 5 play a surprising bit of catch-up here, thanks to their IP57 rating that matches the AirPods Pro 3. Both pairs are effectively dustproof and waterproof, and can even be submerged. It's far better than the water-resistant AirPods 4 with their IP54 rating, which means they can handle splashes, but not proper dunking. Winner: Tie Fitness and Health Features: Pro-Exclusive Sensors Take Over This is a category where the AirPods Pro 3 are miles ahead of any other AirPods. They can actually track your heart rate and integrate with Apple's Fitness app and Fitness+ subscription to help you stay in the right zone as you work out. Outside of fitness, the AirPods Pro 3 have a variety of hearing health features, including the ability to give yourself hearing tests, active Hearing Protection to shield you from loud noise around you, and a Hearing Aid mode that boosts voices around you. The AirPods 5 don't have any of those tricks. Winner: AirPods Pro 3 Controls: Swipe Gestures Finally Go Mainstream After years of being tap-only, the AirPods 5 now join the AirPods Pro 3 as swipe-friendly. You can adjust the volume on both sets of earphones by swiping up and down on the stems. Both also have hands-free Siri access to Apple's voice assistant. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Apple AirPods Pro 3 Despite being a year older and double the price, the AirPods Pro 3 comfortably retain their crown. Their physical in-canal seal, superior sound quality, vastly longer battery life, and exclusive health tracking justify the $249 investment for power users. However, the $129 AirPods 5 are the undisputed value champion. By bringing active noise cancellation and IP57 durability down to an aggressive price point, they deliver 75% of the Pro experience for half the cash. If you want top-tier audio isolation and fitness tracking, spring for the Pro 3; if you want maximum bang for your buck, the AirPods 5 are an excellent alternative.

item.title: iPhone Duo Is Apple's First Foldable Phone. Surprise, It's Expensive!
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.50
Apple was in no rush to launch a foldable phone, even as many of its rivals released various versions over the last eight years. But with John Ternus now at the helm, he kicked off his first Apple event as CEO by introducing a new form factor for the company: the foldable iPhone Duo. Though rumors suggested the device might be the iPhone Ultra, Apple likely opted for the Duo name to keep it short and snappy, aligning it with its other monikers, such as Air, Neo, and Pro. (Though it does have an Apple Watch Ultra, so who knows?) iPhone Duo Design and Display The Duo is a passport-style foldable phone, meaning it's shorter and wider than a lot of rivals. The inner display is 7.6 inches, while the outer display is 5.4 inches, with both sporting a 1:4 aspect ratio to help transitions between screens feel more seamless. The Duo is 11.3mm thick when closed and 5.2mm when open; during today's presentation, it was touted as the thinnest iPhone ever, though that's only when it's open, of course. (The iPhone Air is 5.64mm thick.) The left-hand corners of the outer display are right angles, while the right-hand corners are rounded to make it easier to use with one hand. It's unclear how easy that will be if you're left-handed, though. Touch ID is how you unlock the phone; it's built into the power button on the right-hand edge. On durability, Apple says it feels "exceptionally solid every time you use it." It's also IP68 for water and dust resistance, and there's a nano-texture finish on the display, designed to minimize damage on the inner screen. Apple says its hinge uses over 100 tiny components to close smoothly and last a long time, although it has yet to say how many folds it expects to handle over its lifetime. Apple's press release notes, "Internally, support ribs reinforce the structure for added stiffness, while antenna splits with ceramic fiber inserts enhance the frame’s rigidity." iPhone Duo Chip and Performance The iPhone Duo comes with a new A20 Pro chipset built on 2nm tech, enabling what Apple calls "upgrades across the entire chip," with up to a 50% increase in memory bandwidth. There's a 6-core CPU that's 20% faster than A19 Pro, a 7-core GPU with 40% faster graphics performance, and a 32-core Neural Engine. Plus, there's a larger vapor chamber for improved performance. The Duo has Apple's N1 wireless networking chip found in the iPhone 17 and Air, and the C2, Apple's next-generation cellular modem system (also in the iPhone 18 Pros), which brings AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability, as well as mmWave support in the US. iPhone Duo Camera Specs Foldable phones often fall short in their cameras, but Apple may have addressed this by including a 48MP Fusion Main rear camera and a 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide. That's one fewer than the iPhone 18 Pro series, so it may not be as capable as the brand's other top-end phones. The main camera uses the iPhone 18 Pro's Fusion tech, which includes a variable aperture that adjusts automatically to let in up to 50% more light. On the front of the phone is a 12MP selfie camera designed for video calls and for shooting when the phone is folded. iPhone Duo Battery Life and Charging Speed The phone is powered by two batteries, allowing for up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display or 44 hours on the outer display. We'll have to wait for our upcoming full review to know how long it lasts on a full day of use. New fast-charging features are also here, meaning the iPhone Duo gets from zero to 50% in around 20 minutes. If you're using a wireless charger, it takes 30 minutes to get to the same battery level. iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo The iPhone Duo will support an adapted version of iOS 27 for the wider, foldable screen. Apple detailed some of the changes during its launch, such as moving controls to the right-hand edge rather than at the bottom of the display. The software also shows whatever you were doing on the outer display when you move to the inner display. That includes access to the new AI-powered Siri for better assistant connectivity across Apple apps. Siri AI is rolling out with iOS 27 as a beta on Sept. 14 for users with a supported device set to English. (Support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish is coming in October; it's not coming to the EU and China.) The bendable screen also means new features such as dual-screen use for the camera, alongside innovations for running multiple apps at once across iOS. The iPhone Duo also works with the Apple Pencil USB-C version. iPhone Duo Price and Storage Options The iPhone Duo doesn't come in a 128GB option; it starts at 256GB of storage for $1,999. That's lower than some had expected, and only slightly higher than rivals; the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold are both $1,899.99. Here's the breakdown: - 256GB: $1,999 - 512GB: $2,199 - 1TB: $2,599 - 2TB: $3,199 If you want to test it out without dropping thousands, the Duo is available to lease via Apple Upgrade for $34.99 per month for a 24-month lease or $49.99 per month for 24 months. Meanwhile, if you were hoping to save some money and get a discount on the older iPhone, Apple has instead increased the starting price of the iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air by $100. iPhone Duo Release Date and Preorder Preorders for the iPhone Duo start on Oct. 16, and the official release date is set for Oct. 23. iPhone Duo Colors, Cases, and Accessories The phone comes in two colors: Night Sky, a black shade, and Star White, a light white option. There are also two official cases. The $129 iPhone Duo Folio comes in navy blue or taupe and features an integrated kickstand so you can place the phone on a desk. The $79 iPhone Duo Case comes in two parts, in either sand or navy blue. Both will be available to order on Oct. 16. The ongoing Apple launch just introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it's thought that it will skip the standard iPhone 18 to launch it early next year. Other new gadgets include an Apple Watch Series 12, an Apple Watch Ultra 4, and new AirPods 5. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: FCC: Satellite Constellations Don't Need Environmental Reviews
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.49
The FCC has decided to exempt satellites from federal environmental reviews, despite concerns about light pollution and potential effects on the atmosphere. The agency plans to make it official during its Sept. 30 meeting, where it will vote to reform its environmental regulations. “For too long, outdated and unnecessary environmental rules have slowed America’s builders down,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr wrote in a blog post on Tuesday. Specifically, the commission wants to revise its approach to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which requires federal agencies to “assess the environmental effects of their proposed actions prior to making decisions.” In his blog post, Carr cited the need to “cut billions of dollars in red tape" while clearing the way for more investment in new telecommunications infrastructure both on the ground and in orbit. “The decision will also clarify that bureaucratic NEPA reviews have no place across a range of innovative space-based activities regulated by the FCC.” The FCC plans on publishing the exact text of the reforms on Wednesday. That said, in a press briefing, a senior official noted they call for exempting the on-the-ground NEPA rules from satellite systems and other constellations in orbit. Historically, the FCC has refrained from conducting environmental reviews of satellite systems. But in 2022, the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) urged the commission to revisit its approach, given that tens of thousands of satellites, such as those from SpaceX, could be in orbit by 2030. “Stakeholders have expressed concerns about changes in the temperature of the upper atmosphere from emissions from launches or deorbiting of satellites and effects on astronomical research from radio transmissions or sunlight reflections. They have also expressed concerns about effects on amateur astronomy and astrophotography and the general public from changes to the night sky,” the GAO report said. Those concerns have only grown as SpaceX looks to launch another 100,000 satellites for Starlink and up to 1 million for its orbital data center system, Starmind. In 2024, a group of astronomers and space experts even called on the FCC to halt future Starlink launches so that the US could study the potential environmental effects, including whether retired satellites can harm the ozone layer when they burn up in the atmosphere. But a year ago, Carr’s FCC signaled it would continue excluding satellites from NEPA reviews when it kicked off a process to modernize its environmental regulations. In doing so, the commission described them as "'extraterritorial activities' with effects located entirely outside of the jurisdiction of the United States.” In July, the Commission also approved the US startup Reflect Orbital’s plan to launch a controversial satellite featuring a giant space mirror that reflects sunlight back to Earth during nighttime hours. Despite objections from astronomers and environmental groups, the FCC found the space mirror-related concerns “beyond the Commission’s authority,” involving NEPA. “The Commission’s authority pertains to the licensing and operation of a radio station using radiofrequency spectrum, and it does not have regulatory authority over the licensing and operation of a solar reflector,” the FCC said, noting it was merely clearing one satellite from Reflect Orbital. Although environmental groups are expected to object to the reforms, Carr's FCC has made maintaining US dominance in space and the satellite industry a major goal, citing the threat of China. "Our decision will ensure that outdated environmental rules do not hold back America’s space economy and the novel activities underway in orbit. It is time to build," Carr said. Meanwhile, SpaceX has long worked to prevent its satellites from causing light pollution. The company has also told the FCC it plans on starting small with its orbital data center project "to monitor actual atmospheric effects." About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Insta360 Luna Pro: Is Saving $170 Worth Losing the Ultra's Best Feature?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.25
It didn't take long for Insta360 to release a follow-up to its hot Luna Ultra ($769), our favorite vlogging camera for US creators, with a second, more affordable version. The new $599 Luna Pro is pretty much the same camera, minus the 3x optical zoom and 12x digital zoom functions. Both Lunas are built for handheld video recording, featuring a candy-bar-shaped body and top-mounted camera with 3-axis gimbal stabilization, similar in concept and execution to the popular DJI Osmo Pocket series. The lower price is appealing for sure, and puts just enough distance between the two Pro and Ultra to make you ask, "Is it worth it to spend more for the extra zoom power?" The Good News: It's 90% of the $769 Ultra Both the Luna Pro and Ultra were shown under frosted glass at the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) show back in April, so we knew a second camera was coming when the Ultra was unveiled in June. Today, it's here in the form of the Luna Pro, and as it turns out, the Pro is a lot like the Ultra. In fact, the two have far more commonalities than differences. For instance, the Luna Pro records video at up to 8K30 and 4K120, supports SDR, Dolby Vision HDR, and I-Log color profiles, and includes a large set of stylized color filters designed by Leica and Insta360. It also includes 47GB of built-in memory, and its buttons and screen pop out of the camera body for quick, seamless remote control—just like the Ultra. The control scheme is identical too. The Pro has a 2-inch OLED touch screen that rotates between landscape and portrait capture, a thumbstick to control the gimbal, a Record/Shutter button, and a rocker switch for digital zoom. The colors are the same, too, with the Pro and Ultra both available in your choice of black or white finish. The $170 Compromise: What Insta360 Removed So what's different? Well, the Luna Pro has one wide-angle lens with a lossless 2x digital and lossy 4x zoom, while the Ultra has two lenses—an identical wide-angle, plus a 3x optical with lossless digital zoom through 6x (120mm equivalent) and a lossy 12x option. The Luna Pro does one thing that the Ultra doesn't—it rolls 4K30 vertical video. The Ultra has less resolution in 9:16, but supports a faster maximum frame rate—3K60. Since most vertical video is viewed on 6-inch smartphone screens, I prefer the Ultra's 60fps capture. It has plenty of pixels, and pushing to 60fps lets you apply some slow-motion effects to your TikToks and Reels. There's also a change in accessories. The Ultra comes with a hard plastic case for protection when you're not using it, while the Pro comes with a rubber gimbal cover. The Pro is less expensive. It costs $599, a solid $170 less than the Ultra. Still, you're missing out on the Ultra's best feature if you decide to go with the Pro. The Ultra's second lens makes it a far more versatile creative tool than a single-lens vlog cam, and while $170 is not an insignificant amount of cash, it doesn't go as far these days as it used to. It's also a tougher sell versus the older, but still excellent, DJI Osmo Pocket 3, another single-lens gimbal cam that sells for $439. Yes, the Pocket 3 is a generation old, but it's the most recent version of the camera that US creators can get because of the FCC's late 2025 ban on newly introduced DJI products, and it remains a good performer and a good buy in the $500-or-less bracket. The Best Compact Vlogging Cameras I've Tested Is the Real Budget Luna Still Coming? I can't help but speculate about Insta360's plans for the future. I don't have any special insight, but given just how close the Luna Pro and Ultra are in features, I wonder if the company will eventually trot out an entry-level Luna that appeals to creators who don't want to spend $600 on a vlogging camera. Sure, bringing video down to 4K60 and dropping the clever removable remote control would likely be required to crack the $500 barrier, but I'm sure there are many creators who wouldn't mind losing some creature comforts to get a more affordable camera, and would put the company in a better position to compete against the value-priced DJI Osmo Pocket 3. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini Review: A Powerhouse Mini PC for Work and Play
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.21
This isn't your father's NUC—or even the NUC you may remember from five or 10 years ago. The PC industry keeps finding ways to pack beefier silicon into tinier and tinier machines. Case in point: the Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini. Our punchy test model (expected to sell for around $3,000), kitted out with an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H processor and 64GB of memory, is one of the most powerful mini PCs of its size class we've tested to date. It delivers enough CPU performance to handle tough workflows—managing complex datasets, casual content-creation work, even light AI development—while taking up almost no space on your desk. Plus, this NUC's integrated graphics can challenge an entry-level discrete GPU for graphics acceleration, and even gaming—outside of office hours, of course. Asus' individual pricing ranges wide: The base model, which is peppy in its own right, comes in at $559 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 CPU. (Mind you, that's a barebones model, so you'll need to add your own memory and storage, which are today's big-dollar components.) While our exact configuration was not yet available in the US as we published this (it's expected to show up in Q4), the highest-end build available at this writing still runs a sobering $2,799. If your workflows justify the payout, however, this NUC will deliver peak power per cubic inch. It displaces the Geekom A9 Max as our Editors’ Choice pick for the best overall Windows mini PC. The NUC 16 Pro comes in several configurations, all based on mobile (that is, laptop-grade) hardware. The base-level barebones model, as I noted, carries an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 chip that features four Performance cores (P-cores) and four Low-Power Efficient cores (LPE-cores) in the CPU portion, plus four Xe cores in its integrated graphics processor (IGP). The model I reviewed contains a far more powerful Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU. That "Panther Lake" chip features four P-cores, eight Efficient cores (E-cores), and four LPE-cores, making it significantly faster for CPU-intensive tasks. The Arc B390 IGP in the Ultra X7 358H processor also delivers a lot more graphics punch than the base model's chip, with a dozen Xe cores. It's a major advantage and one of the keys to this mini PC’s appeal. Our review model, available soon according to Asus, came with 64GB of LPDDR5X RAM, clocked at a speedy 9,600MHz and set in a dual-channel configuration. That setup will give you an abundance of memory bandwidth, boosting performance in demanding applications. It also boosts the IGPs performance with games. If you're looking to upgrade the machine, though, you're out of luck: The memory installed for the X7 chip (as well as for X9 models that Asus says will also come) is soldered to the motherboard; Asus says X7/X9 models with 16GB. 32GB, 64GB, and 96GB will be available. A 96GB memory allotment, paired with the X7 chip's robust neural processor (NPU) and IGP, would make for a lively, very small local-AI computing platform. This level of AI capability goes well beyond the Copilot PC functions that Windows 11 provides and can be useful even for AI product development. The appeal is that any sensitive AI work can be done directly on the device and stay off the cloud. The CPU also features hardware-based Intel vPro security options for managed environments. Asus also offers versions of the NUC 16 Pro Mini with ordinary Core Ultra 5 and Ultra 7 chips, and these rely instead on DDR5 SO-DIMMs (compact memory modules, the same kind some laptops use). The entry-level NUC model, with the Ultra 5 325 processor, is designed to be hands-on. As it's a barebones kit, you need to plug in your own SO-DIMMs, as well as an M.2 SSD, before you can fire up the system. (You’ll also need to install your own OS, in this case.) This model is worth keeping in mind if the NUC piques your interest, but a prebuilt model like our lavishly appointed tester is too expensive. As noted up top, the model with the Ultra 5 325 CPU starts at $559, which makes it far more affordable if you don't need that all the performance the X7 model packs. Bear in mind, though, that shelling out for the needed RAM, SSD, and operating system will set you back a few hundred dollars more. The top-most configuration available at this writing, at $2,799, has the same Intel Core Ultra X7 chip as in my test model, but with just 32GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. If you're buying as an IT fleet manager, you might have access to bulk pricing for this NUC, whether barebones or prebuilt, which will differ from these single-unit prices. All Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini models come with a three-year warranty that includes 24/7 support, which should appeal especially to business owners and IT buyers. The real selling point of a mini PC is the size, and the NUC delivers on that front, measuring just 1.65 by 5.7 by 4.6 inches (HWD). A sleek black exterior gives the system a premium sheen. Opening the case is simplicity itself: Press the latch on the bottom of the system and lift, and the bottom comes right off. You won’t need to open up a system like this often—unless you get the barebones model, of course—but on the rare occasions you do, accessing the hardware is a cinch. The exterior, meanwhile, delivers a plentiful array of ports for a machine this size. Up front, you get a 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C port and two 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A connections. Around back, the NUC gives you two more USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports, alongside a pair of Thunderbolt 4 connections that also support DisplayPort 2.1 video-out. You'll also find two HDMI 2.1 ports, two RJ-45 Ethernet jacks, and the DC-in power connection. It's an impressive spread that will satisfy most buyers, but particularly professionals. (For instance, those dual Ethernet jacks are useful for either connection redundancy or connecting to two networks separately, say, to isolate internal corporate and external net traffic.) This is a lot for such a small computer, and most of you will likely be happy with this configuration. I would have liked to see an SD or microSD-card slot, too, but that's just a quibble. A single fan handles active cooling inside the NUC 16 Pro Mini, pushing air out through two small heatsinks. These are connected to a few thin copper heat pipes. The whole works keeps operating noise exceedingly mum, even when you push the system. I never heard this NUC strain or whoosh while running benchmarks. Asus, in fact, rates its maximum noise generation at an impressively low 38dBA. To see how it stacks up, I sent the NUC head-to-head against the systems listed below, all of them mini PCs with relatively powerful hardware for their sizes. Among these peers was a $3,039 HP Z2 Mini G1a review configuration (the most powerful of the bunch, a compact workstation), as well as the Geekom A9 Max 2026 Edition ($2,079 as tested), an upgraded version of our previous Editors’ Choice pick for the best overall Windows mini PC. The words "previous pick" say a lot about which machine won these contests. Rounding out the list, we have the $1,699 HP Eliteboard G1A AI configuration we reviewed, and the ECS Liva Z11 Plus ($699 as tested) as a representative budget mini PC. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators gauges a PC's image-editing prowess in a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The NUC 16 Pro Mini beat the field in both PCMark 10 tests—showing it has a speedy SSD, too—as well as the single-core Cinebench test. It fell to second in Cinebench multi-core speeds, HandBrake, and the multi-core Geekbench test. Meanwhile, it placed technically third in single-core Geekbench speeds (though, really, second, third, and fourth were a virtual tie in this lot) and came in third in Photoshop. First place (or a near-tie for first) in most tests beyond the PCMarks went to the HP Z2 Mini G1a, which has the strongest multicore performance among the systems. These results suggest that power-user productivity performance is this NUC's forte. You can still see a clear step up for content-creation tasks with HP's workstation-grade Z2 Mini and its AMD Ryzen AI Max+ Pro 395. For all desktops we test, we challenge the graphics silicon with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first pair, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), uses the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The second set, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development, like Metal and DirectX 12, to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. The NUC 16 Pro Mini came in second in all of the 3DMark tests, with most of the other competing desktops trailing far behind. The HP Z2 Mini G1a, though, pulled ahead of the rest. Its processor tops the rest, and it has the punchiest graphics solution, too, AMD's Radeon 8060S. (The Radeon 8060S also distinguished itself in our recent review of the Asus TUF Gaming A14 gaming laptop, a rare gaming model with no discrete graphics chip.) Typically, for mini PCs, especially business units, our graphics tests end there. But I was curious to push its IGP further, given its promising results in the 3DMark trials. I ran some additional tests with the games Total War: Three Kingdoms and Shadow of the Tomb Raider. I ran these same tests on the Geekom A9 Max 2026 Edition, which employs a different flavor of Radeon integrated graphics. I didn’t have the other mini PCs I mentioned above available to test these games on them. Instead, I compared these game results against the IGPs from some other hardware that I had previously tested. I test the IGP on all desktop CPUs that I review with these two games, using medium graphics settings for Total War and low graphics settings for Shadow of the Tomb Raider. I also test all graphics cards with these games using Total War’s Ultra graphics preset and Shadow of the Tomb Raider’s Highest preset. So, I chose some representative desktop components for comaprison. Below, you can see how the NUC 16 Pro Mini's Arc B390 shapes up against the integrated graphics on these desktop CPUs: - AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (which uses integrated AMD Radeon Graphics) - AMD Ryzen 5 8500G (which uses an integrated AMD Radeon 740M) - Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus (which uses integrated Intel Xe LPG graphics) Also, you can see some comparisons against some of lowest-end graphics cards from the last five years: Here's how the NUC 16 Pro Mini shaped up in those face-offs... First off: I was surprised by how far behind the NUC the Geekom A9 Max performed in these tests. While I expected the NUC to be faster, I didn’t anticipate quite this difference. This is likely due, in part, to the different RAM supplied with these two mini PCs. The NUC’s RAM operates at 9,600MHz, while the Geekom’s DDR5 RAM is clocked far slower, at 5,600MHz. This is a massive difference in bandwidth, and GPUs are heavily reliant on memory bandwidth to maintain fast performance. This likely hampered the Geekom’s speed somewhat. Now let's look at the IGPs on the three desktop chips. Powerful IGPs are more common on mobile processors, used for PCs in which adding a graphics card is impossible. While desktop IGPs are capable of more than they are typically given credit for, they tend to struggle against the best of their mobile competition, and it showed here. Take the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus: It's equipped with the fastest IGP that Intel provides on a desktop platform, and it lagged far behind the NUC's Arc B390 IGP in both tests. That's despite this being a socketed desktop chip with much more aggressive cooling than the NUC. As for the comparisons against the low-end graphics cards, the Arc B390 was competitive with all three of the basic GPUs here in Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Meanwhile, it trounced them all in Total War, likely down to that game's heavy reliance on the CPU and the high memory bandwidth available to the NUC. (Plus, these three cards are all between four and seven years old.) This mini desktop isn't designed as a gaming PC, by any means, but it can hold its own against the low end of discrete graphics. I expect this will vary heavily by game, though. The size of this system would make it perfect for sitting on a TV stand in your living room. I could also see it as an attractive option for travel. While at a usability disadvantage against laptops, due to it lacking a built-in screen, a battery, a keyboard, and a mouse, its small size makes it a sensible option for, say, connecting to a TV in a hotel room, where maybe you want something faster to work on (or game on!) than a basic laptop can provide. Final Thoughts Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini, in the configuration that we tested or one like it, will set you back quite a bit when purchased individually. But the performance for the size is pretty impressive. It will power through any general office tasks you throw at it, as well as light content-creation work. It's also packed with features that IT managers and other business users will appreciate, like an extended warranty with direct support, hardware-level security, and deep AI development readiness. On top of that, its CPU and graphics speeds make it a capable pinch-hitter gaming PC. All of this comes in a compact package that's easy to tuck away on any desk. Among the mini PCs in our head-to-head tests, only the HP Z2 Mini G1a gave the NUC any real competition. The Z2 is technically a mini workstation with an even bigger price tag, making the pricey NUC 16 Pro Mini look even more attractive if you need density of performance at the smallest possible size. Even the more affordable version of the NUC should deliver good value for the price. It won’t be quite as fast, but that trade-off may well be worth it. For eclipsing the previous title holder, we give the Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini our Editors' Choice award among mini PCs. About Our Expert I have been interested in science and technology for as long as I can remember, spurred on by a fondness for video games. I learned to work in Windows and manipulate files to get buggy games to work, and I learned to build and upgrade PCs for better performance. In my role at PCMag for the past four years, I’ve deeply enjoyed the opportunity to share my knowledge and expertise. Before PCMag, I wrote for Tom's Hardware for three years, where I covered tech news, deals, and wrote some hands-on reviews. After working as a PCMag contributor for a time reviewing desktops, PC cases, budget processors, and motherboards, I now focus on testing and reviewing processors and graphics cards and sharing my insights on the industry.

item.title: Worried About Snooping Smart Glasses? This Startup's Tech Detects Nearby Specs
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.04
If you hadn’t already, add the military-industrial complex to the growing list of parties concerned by the potential for people wearing smart glasses to engage in clandestine recording. Bastille Networks, a startup specializing in wireless intrusion detection, announced Thursday what it called “first-of-its-kind software” to spot smart glasses at customer sites. The San Diego-based firm pitches this new solution, available to companies that already subscribe to its monitoring services, as going well beyond indie apps like Nearby Glasses and the cleverly named Zuckoff that scan for Bluetooth Low Energy signals from smart glasses. “Those other ones will tell you whether there are glasses within Bluetooth range of your phone,” Bastille CEO Chris Risley said in an interview on Thursday. “What we do is tell you within two to three meters where it is.” Risley said Bastille has neither received nor sought help from such smart-glass developers as Meta in developing its glasses-tracking tools. He added that Bastille’s systems, designed to look for rogue devices by sniffing across Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and cellular frequencies, also provide an audit trail. “We tell you the history of that device–when did it show up?” Risley said. “Has it ever been here before?” Bastille charges “hundreds of thousands” of dollars and up for its installations for national-security, military, and private-sector clients to spot Flipper Zero-like hacking tools as well as misplaced personal devices. “We’ve been in those facilities for years, and people know we’re in there,” Risley said. “And we detect new devices every day being brought in.” He added, “Everybody’s going to tell you they brought it in by accident.” A video on the company’s site depicts a more menacing scenario: someone masquerading as a job candidate hands over a phone at a security checkpoint but keeps his connected glasses on during a lengthy tour of the premises, allowing him to walk away with a trove of confidential footage. That raises a question: Do sensitive installations not already check for smart glasses? Shouldn’t they? “There’s just not sufficient awareness,” Risley said. But as sales of smart glasses from firms like Meta continue to climb—even as critics mock that eyewear as “pervert glasses”—stories of creepy behavior seem likely to keep coming. Venues from bars and theaters to courtrooms have banned smart glasses, and now Apple’s new Siri Recap feature for Apple Watches brings a whole new set of surveillance fears. Places that aren’t thinking about this problem will probably have to soon enough. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Forget the Overlay: 5 Game-Changing Siri Features Coming to Your iPhone Next Week
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.93
Apple’s hardware keynotes tend to focus on camera evolution and sleek titanium curves, but the reveal of the upcoming standalone Siri application stole the show for me. As someone who frequently uses Google’s advanced AI search models for daily research, I have spent years frustrated by how restrictive iPhone software is by comparison. That paradigm is finally shifting. When this massive overhaul drops alongside iOS 27 next Monday, it promises to bridge the gap between static web retrieval and an assistant that actually thinks ahead. As we prepare for the update to officially go live next week, here is an in-depth look at the five Siri AI features I'm most excited to incorporate into my daily routine, and how Apple is finally developing Siri into a truly agentic AI powerhouse. 1. Ditching the Overlay for a Dedicated Chatbot Application Whenever I activate Siri right now, the interface does what it has always done: It temporarily takes over the device. The screen triggers that familiar, glowing rainbow outline along the edges of the display, waiting for a single prompt. If you ask it a question, it drops a small answer window over whatever you are doing, provides a one-and-done response, and then vanishes. If you forget what it said, or want to follow up on a previous thought, you’re out of luck. You have to start the conversation over. The upcoming update fixes this by introducing a dedicated Siri app icon on the Home Screen—without sacrificing its system-wide integration. Instead of a temporary screen animation, Siri will finally have its own permanent workspace, functioning exactly like ChatGPT or Gemini. It means Siri will maintain a rolling, continuous conversation history. I’ll be able to look back at research threads from three days ago, type out a long-form prompt when I'm in a quiet public space, or pick up an active brainstorming session right where I left off. The new application interface also adds an attachment paperclip toggle. This will let you drag and drop PDFs, documents, or screenshots directly into a Siri thread to instantly generate summaries or isolate data. It moves the assistant out of the voice remote control era and into a true desktop-grade workspace. 2. True Screen Context: Pixels-Aware Intelligence Right now, if a friend texts you a photo of an ambiguous landmark and you want information on it, you have to leave the conversation, save the image, upload it to a third-party search app, or manually copy and paste text between split windows. Apple’s world-class silicon can read that data instantly, but the software is a bottleneck. The iOS 27 upgrade introduces Screen Context, enabling Siri to actively read and interpret the live pixels on your display. When this goes live, you’ll be able to pull up a text message, activate Siri, and simply say, "Where was this photo taken?" or "Summarize the key points of this article." Siri will read the active application canvas, parse the information dynamically, and give you a relevant breakdown without forcing me to switch apps or copy an ounce of text. It brings a native equivalent of Google's on-screen visual search tools directly into the core of iOS, which is a win for mobile efficiency. 3. Visual Intelligence via the Camera Viewfinder We have had tools like Live Text for a few generations now, which are great for pausing a video frame or opening a captured photo to copy text. But it is still a reactive system: You have to take the photo or freeze the screen first to extract the utility. The new Siri Mode inside the Camera app gives the assistant direct access to your lens. By swiping to Siri mode in the viewfinder and tapping the shutter, Siri freezes the frame and parses it. You can snap a photo of a dinner plate to get an instant, approximate nutritional breakdown, or a historical plaque to pull up a full background biography. It turns the iPhone camera into an active data scanner rather than just a memory catcher. 4. The Agentic Pivot: True Cross-App Workflow Execution Siri’s current app integration is essentially a system of simple triggers. You can tell it to "open Spotify" or "send a text to my wife," but you can't tell it to execute a multi-step workflow. If you want to move a file from your downloads, organize it into a folder, and email it, you have to click through each app manually. Apple is finally granting Siri the system permissions to execute deep, agentic workflows natively. This is the productivity leap I am most anxious to test. You will be able to give Siri a single complex command like: "Find the Nintendo Voice Memo I created yesterday afternoon, copy the transcript, paste it into an email, and mail it to my work email address." Instead of watching your phone open and close three different apps, Siri will handle the backend asset management silently, saving you dozens of manual taps throughout the workday. 5. Personal Context and Private Cloud Compute An AI assistant is only as useful as the data it has access to. If you ask Google's AI Mode, "What time does my mom’s flight land next week?" it will naturally fail because that data is locked away inside my private text threads, emails, and calendar entries. However, opening up my entire digital life to an AI model naturally triggers a wave of privacy anxiety. Apple’s solution is a Personal Context Index tied directly to a new architecture called Private Cloud Compute. Siri will securely scan your local data to build a personal timeline, allowing you to ask hyper-specific questions about my life, such as tracking down a confirmation code buried deep in your emails or cross-referencing text messages to remember your dinner reservation time. To protect your privacy, lighter tasks stay strictly on the iPhone's local chip. For heavier processing, data is routed to Apple's new end-to-end encrypted private cloud servers. The software ensures that your personal information is processed on custom silicon, where data is never stored and remains completely unreadable by anyone—including Apple. It provides the utility of a deeply integrated personal assistant without the paranoia about tracking. Will Your Phone Get Siri AI? The Device Divide Due to the intense computational demand, Apple is dividing the Siri upgrade into two distinct tiers: - On-Device (iPhone 18 Pro/Max, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 17 Pro/Max): With 12GB of RAM or more, these iPhones will run most complex AI models entirely locally. This means instantaneous response times and maximum local privacy. - Cloud-Assisted (iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, and the full iPhone 16 lineup): These older compatible models will still get access to the same feature list and Siri app layout. However, because they lack the raw on-board memory, they will offload heavier, complex computations to Apple’s secure Private Cloud Compute servers. If you're using a standard iPhone 15 or anything older, you'll get the iOS 27 system update on Monday, Sept. 14, but you'll be locked out of the new Siri capabilities entirely. I plan on testing all of Siri's new capabilities, so be sure to check back soon. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: We May Get the iPhone Ultra This Week. Every Rumor We Think Is Legit
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.86
It's no surprise that Apple is late to the folding phone party while its major rivals—Google, Motorola, and Samsung in the US, and many more abroad—take massive bites out of the hinged-handset pie. Apple has long taken a "wait and see" approach to emerging form factors. As a phone expert, I've tested intriguing foldables, from the not-so-great Microsoft Surface Duo to the more successful Samsung Galaxy Z Flip series, as well as the Google Pixel Fold and Motorola Razr lines. But where's Apple's fun and flexible iPhone Flip? I vividly remember when, in 2019, Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak told Bloomberg that "[Apple] is not the leader in areas like the folding phone, and that worries me because I really want a folding phone." Well, if the rumors are anything to go by, it looks like The Woz is finally getting his wish. Whispers about Apple's foldable project date back to 2016, but this year, reports have skyrocketed. As someone who's obsessed with both iPhones and foldables, I'm excited that these worlds may collide in an ambitious new piece of hardware that could make Apple's rivals sweat. Foldable iPhone: All the Credible Rumors So Far Given Apple's long-standing iPhone naming conventions, you may expect the company to announce the iPhone 18 Fold. However, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, one of the most credible Apple leakers, there may be a twist: Apple might go with iPhone Ultra, instead. Gurman claims the foldable is still on track for this fall, despite chatter about manufacturing snags. That said, the so-called iPhone Ultra is expected to launch at the Surprise and Shine Sept. 9 event, alongside the iPhone 18 series. What will Apple's foldable look like? Gurman called it "the most significant overhaul in the iPhone’s history and the first actual form-factor change." It won't open vertically like the Samsung Z Flip 7 or the Motorola Razr Ultra. Instead, it will open from side to side, like a book, revealing a larger display that's roughly the same size as the iPad mini. For reference, it won't be like the skinny Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7, which is thinner than some regular phones. According to a recent interview with Tom's Guide, Gurman said that the iPhone foldable will more closely resemble the Galaxy Z Fold 8, adopting a wider footprint for its inner display. Apple reportedly plans to pitch the iPhone Ultra as a device that's more beneficial for web browsing, framing subjects with a gigantic viewfinder, and most importantly, watching video. Samsung leaned heavily into the fact that the Z Fold 8 reduced letterboxing for a more pleasant streaming experience—Apple may roll out similar marketing plans. Gurman also expects the larger display to make the iPhone Ultra “awesome for gaming,” delivering a far more immersive experience similar to handheld gaming consoles. Having tested the Z Fold 8, I completely agree. Gaming on a wider foldable screen is glorious. For the first time in years, I actually want to play mobile games because I’m no longer confined to a cramped, narrow display. Similar to the Z Fold 8, the iPhone Ultra won’t have a dedicated telephoto camera, so you’ll miss out on the enhanced zoom capabilities Apple will likely offer on its iPhone 18 Pro models. The rumored Apple foldable may also lack Face ID, meaning users could have to rely solely on Touch ID for biometric security. Bloomberg's sources say Apple will introduce "apps [that] look more like iPad software" to accommodate the upcoming foldable. Similar to the experience you'd find on rival foldables, the foldable iPhone will reportedly launch side-by-side apps. However, unlike the iPad, it can't run multiple windows at once. Although Gurman's reports often liken the rumored iPhone Ultra to a tiny iPad, it's worth noting that it's expected to run iOS, not iPadOS. We've already seen early glimpses of foldable-friendly software at WWDC. Apple's documentation emphasizes to developers the importance of creating apps that support a "dynamic range of sizes and aspect ratios." As for the processor, there's speculation that the foldable iPhone will run on Apple's A20 Pro chip, which is also expected to power the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. The real question is, how does Apple plan to stand out from the crowd? As mentioned, the Z Fold 8 appears to be quite similar to the rumored iPhone Ultra. On top of that, Apple faces stiff competition from devices like the Motorola Razr Fold and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which we recently reviewed. Sources close to Apple's foldable project claim the iPhone Ultra will solve issues that other rivals struggle with, including that pesky crease in the middle of the display. Gurman acknowledged that Samsung has made “serious strides on the crease,” but told Tom’s Guide that Apple’s approach to tackling the center trench will be “a little bit better,” thanks to the stronger hinge rumored to be coming to the iPhone Ultra. Reportedly called Liquid Metal, the hinge is said to use a teardrop-shaped internal structure that helps distribute and reduce stress when folding. Another way the iPhone Ultra could stand out is with MagSafe. The iPhone Ultra will reportedly feature MagSafe support for case-free magnetic charging. Samsung’s foldables, on the other hand, aren’t quite there yet. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 support wireless charging, but without built-in magnets, you’ll need a compatible case to use magnetic chargers. The Cupertino company's forthcoming foldable is expected to be priced between $2,000 and $2,500, which is not a surprise for envelope-pushing tech or for Apple. Apple's Surprise and Shine event is set to kick off in Cupertino at 10 a.m. PT / 1:00 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Sept. 9. We'll be there to bring you all the news. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: Don't Miss These Still-Available Labor Day Deals on Laptops and Desktops
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.81
I spent the weekend tracking Labor Day sales across multiple retailers to spotlight the deepest discounts on laptops and desktops, focusing on top-rated machines that we've tested in the PC Labs. If you were too busy grilling and having a good time to get any shopping done, don't stress. Some—but not all—of the deals we found are still good as of Tuesday morning. We've still got Alienware gaming machines, mini desktops, all-in-ones, and everything else you could want at the summer's best prices, but there's no guarantee they'll stay discounted much longer. Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x Laptop Labor Day Deal For a solid budget-priced option, you can't go wrong with this $200 post-Labor Day discount on the capable Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x. While this isn't a portable that you're going to squeeze top-tier gaming performance out of, it's an absolutely dependable daily driver with excellent battery life thanks to the power-efficient Snapdragon X processor. We put it through its paces in a comprehensive review and overall felt positively about it, commenting that it felt solid and sturdy, ran for nearly 30 hours in our testing, and handled productivity tasks with ease. We did note that the keyboard felt a little cramped, one downside of the 15-inch form factor, but aside from that it was very pleasurable to use. Dell 2K Touchscreen Laptop Labor Day Deal For a budget-priced Windows machine, this Dell is an absolute steal. Typically portable PCs under $500 have dire loadouts and murky monitors, but this one is a full 2K IPS touch display with good color and contrast. Under the hood, you're getting great component value, with a peppy but affordable Intel Core i5 processor running the show and 512 gigabytes of internal storage. I would say that the 8GB of DDR5 RAM is slightly skimpy, but memory prices are absolutely out of control right now so it's not surprising. Just don't keep a million browser tabs open and you'll probably be fine. The keyboard and touchpad are both good-sized and well-built, and port selection is solid but not exceptional. Battery life is also a strong point, with fast charging taking you from zero to 80% full in just an hour. Lenovo Legion Pro 5i Gen 10 Gaming Laptop Labor Day Deal For something with a little more horsepower, Lenovo's delivering a discount of over a thousand dollars on its Legion Pro 5i gaming laptop. We gave this one an Editors' Choice award in our review, with our expert Charles Jefferies declaring that it "offers compelling value for gamers" thanks to a solid component loadout, including a Blackwell-series RTX 5070 graphics card, tons of system memory, and top-flight connectivity with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. Although some versions of this laptop ship with an OLED display, this particular offer has an IPS screen, which is not as high-end but still quite good, with 500 nits of brightness and a 240Hz refresh rate. Because it's a Lenovo, the keyboard and touchpad also both feel spectacular. Alienware 16 Aurora Gaming Laptop Labor Day Deal Here's a huge deal that's still good post-Labor Day. Dell is offering $900 off of an entry-level Alienware 16 Aurora laptop, and just from sheer component value you're getting your money's worth. While it's not pushing the envelope in terms of resolution, the RTX 5050 graphics card is more than capable of whip-fast framerates to the crisp 2560x1600 display. We have a review of the similar 16X Aurora, where it took home an "Excellent" rating for its sturdy but compact design, with no thermal shelf for a more modest profile, along with a well-considered port selection. While Alienware machines typically land on the higher end of the price spectrum, this discount cuts it down well into a more competitive bracket. Asus ROG Strix G16 Gaming Laptop Labor Day Deal For a gaming portable with a little more juice to squeeze, this is a very nice 28% discount on a midrange Asus that brings the heat. We have an extensive review of this model, awarding it an Editors' Choice nod for its 165Hz ultra-high refresh rate Nebula display, lightning-fast performance both in synthetic benchmarking and real-world testing, and surprisingly long battery life. The RTX 5060 graphics card is one of the best current-gen options for gaming laptops, easily keeping up with the 1200p screen. Visually, it's a treat as well, with a full-sized RGB backlit gaming keyboard, attractive styling, and plenty of ports. This bundle comes with a wireless gaming mouse and headset.
