item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.97
Apple rolled out the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 at its “Surprise and shine” event. The new watches feature sizable improvements to their health sensors and tracking, plus the ability to create brief audio transcriptions and summaries, plus a ceramic case option for the Series 12. Despite the new features, the watches start at the same base prices as their previous iterations. The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399 for the aluminum version without cellular, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799. How the new Apple Watches compare to the last-gen models Apple’s newest watches sport new features like Audio Intelligence, but how do they stack up against the older models? The biggest differences between the models are new features powered by the S11 processor. It supports the new Apple Intelligence features as well as more detailed health and fitness programs. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also has longer battery life, up to 50 hours on a single charge, up from 42 on the Ultra 3. All the watches are slightly heavier, with the heaviest ceramic Apple Watch Series 12 sitting at 42.8 grams for the 42mm version and 52.9 grams for the 46mm version. The heaviest Apple Watch Ultra is 63.1 grams, up from 61.8 grams on the older model. Make sure to check out our hands-on if you’re curious about the full scope of the changes. item.title: Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K is over half off at under $20
item.description:

Looking to take full advantage of your 4K television, but your current streaming stick doesn’t have the right features? Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K is over half off at under $20 With bonus deals on Resident Evil Requiem for PC, a two-pack of Ring alarm sensors, and a Lenovo Android tablet. Read our review. - You can grab a two-pack of Ring Alarm Contact Sensors at Amazon for $20, a $10 discount compared to what they usually cost (but half off their original price). item.title: Electric air taxis get the green light for test flights in Texas
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.85
A new federal program to test the feasibility of electric, hybrid-electric, and autonomous aircraft kicks off today in Texas — before the rules governing this new technology have even been finalized. Electric air taxis get the green light for test flights in Texas The flights will be conducted under the White House’s new pilot program to test out electric, hybrid, and autonomous aircraft. Earlier this year, the Federal Aviation Administration’s Advanced Air Mobility and Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing (eVTOL) Integration Pilot Program (eIPP) selected eight state-led projects to serve as some of the first public tests of these new aircraft. The first one kicks off today in Texas, featuring three eVTOL companies: Joby, Beta, and Wisk. For the next week, these companies will conduct test flights demonstrating future routes between cities and regional airports, including Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. The aircraft won’t carry any passengers, but regulators will be keen to see how the state’s air traffic control system handles the uptick in flight traffic. The companies, meanwhile, are eager to prove to the federal government that their aircraft deserve to be awarded type certification, which is required before any of them can carry passengers commercially in the US. But type certification can take years to attain, which led to the White House to create this pilot program allowing these companies to demonstrate their new technology — even before the regulatory process has concluded. Through the eIPP, the companies hope to accelerate their path to market by getting a head start on data collection that will be needed for certification. Data from the program will also be used to “develop new regulations that safely enable this futuristic technology at scale,” the White House said earlier. The companies say they are thrilled to demonstrate the future of electric and autonomous flight, which they argue will help reduce car traffic in cities and open up new mobility opportunities for consumers. “I’m incredibly excited by the potential for vertical lift in Texas, a state with the infrastructure, expertise, and partnerships to help lead the next era of American aviation,” JoeBen Bevirt, Founder and CEO of Joby Aviation, said in a statement. Several of these companies have conducted public test flights before — Joby’s egg-shaped aircraft demonstrated its future route between Lower Manhattan and JFK Airprot earlier this year — but these will be the first official flights under the White House’s new pilot program. Additional tests are being planned in New York, Utah, Pennsylvania, Louisiana, Florida, North Carolina, and New Mexico. Legal in-fighting, however, could muddy the picture for electric aviation. Joby and one of its rivals, Archer, are currently suing each other for stolen trade secrets and corporate espionage. Technology limitations, including battery weight and sensor decisions, could also hamper the rollout.

item.title: Drama swirls around OpenAI’s legendary mathematical milestone
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.84
OpenAI says it found a solution to a major math problem that has remained unsolved for around 90 years, as reported earlier by The New York Times and Wired. In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI announced that it discovered a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem — which relates to the flow of liquid and gas — using an internal AI model more powerful than the newly released GPT-6 Astra alongside 10,000 concurrent agents. The Navier-Stokes problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million reward for solving. Drama swirls around OpenAI’s legendary mathematical milestone OpenAI’s breakthrough with a 90-year-old problem is challenged by researchers who solved a related problem the day before. OpenAI says it started training the internal AI model on August 28th, which has “exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics.” The solution is a big breakthrough for the mathematics community, but it doesn’t come without controversy. Just one day before OpenAI’s announcement, New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster published findings on a related problem in partnership with Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic. When announcing these findings, Buckmaster claims he contacted OpenAI after learning the company had heard about their progress. However, Buckmaster found that OpenAI had produced a proof for the Navier-Stokes equation using a route he and Alpöge had been working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. In his statement, Buckmaster raises concerns about whether OpenAI had accessed their Codex data to get closer to the Navier-Stokes solution. “I asked whether the model had been trained on, or had access to, our sessions in Codex, into which we had been putting all our drafts for the whole of this project,” Buckmaster writes. “I was told the model did not look up user data. I asked again, about training, and I did not get an answer.” OpenAI is now attempting to squash these suspicions with its Tuesday announcement, saying “no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem.” It adds that “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.” When reached for comment, OpenAI pointed The Verge to its statement on X, which echoes its blog post. Sebastien Bubeck, a member of technical staff at OpenAI, similarly said: “We did not see any of their [Buckmaster and Alpöge’s] work until they released it publicly last night. One can in hindsight see that our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different.” Meanwhile, Buckmaster responded to this in a post on Mastodon, claiming that OpenAI is “openly admitting they used training data from a period after we found our result.” OpenAI says it doesn’t plan on taking the $1 million prize.

item.title: Razer’s ANC-equipped gaming headset for PS5 and Xbox is almost $100 off
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.49
It’s rare to find high-end features like active noise cancellation in a gaming headset under $200, so we’re thrilled that the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro on sale at Woot for $164.99. At just $35 more than current sale price for the BlackShark V2 Pro, the newer headset adds ANC and simultaneous audio between the 2.4GHz and Bluetooth connections, although you only get a 90-day Woot warranty with this deal. Razer’s ANC-equipped gaming headset for PS5 and Xbox is almost $100 off The BlackShark V3 Pro gaming headset features a clear microphone, ANC, and crisp spatial audio. The BlackShark V3 Pro’s main connection mode is with its low latency 2.4GHz transmitter, which plugs into your console or PC via USB. Fans of Riot’s soon-to-be-retired fighting game, 2XKO, can save an extra $15 for a special edition version of the BlackShark V3 Pro that’s $149.99.

item.title: The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.35
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has pulled off a familiar trick. It arrives into a mature Android foldable market with a handful of hardware features we’ve mostly already seen elsewhere, but paired with a level of software polish that makes a lot of them feel new again. It’s those software flourishes that have me excited to try the iPhone Duo when it launches next month, but I’m less convinced that its hardware will be anything special. The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be Android foldables have done most of this before, but rarely looked so good doing it. If Apple had gotten there first, the Duo’s biggest surprise would have been its squat, wide, passport-inspired shape. But its slow-moving supply chain meant that Huawei, Samsung, and Xiaomi all managed to beat Apple to market with similarly sized rivals, so the unusual design already feels fairly familiar — helped by Samsung’s aggressive efforts to market its new design. More has been made of Apple’s efforts to eliminate the foldable display’s crease, which seem to have been largely successful. Apple attributes it to a 100-component hinge, custom adhesives that allow the display layers to “glide” over one another, and a matte finish that reduces glare and reflections to make the crease harder to spot. Trying the phone at Apple’s event yesterday, Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel said that you can’t really see the crease, but that “if you go looking for it, you can definitely feel one.” It sounds, and looks, impressive, but Apple is far from the first to do it. Samsung made great strides in eliminating the crease on its Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra thanks to new titanium display layers. Before that, Oppo all but eliminated its Find N6 crease by using 3D printing to fill the minute gaps across the hinge. I’d have to see all those phones side by side to see which crease is subtlest, but even if Apple does win, it won’t be by much. None of the iPhone Duo’s other standout hardware features are true firsts either. Google beat it to an IP68 rating, now even surpassed by Honor’s IP69. Samsung, Oppo, and Honor have all offered stylus support before — though Samsung has since dropped it. Samsung also moved on from the under-display selfie camera, which has always been hamstrung by poor photo and video quality and a distractingly visible patch on the screen. In other ways, the hardware even feels behind the competition. The Duo is the thickest of this new wave of wide foldables, though at 5.2mm when open it’s still thinner than the iPhone Air. The weight is a more obvious issue: The 254g Duo is 26 percent heavier than the Z Fold 8 — a 53g difference — which is going to be pretty noticeable. You have to go back to 2022’s Z Fold 4 to find a Samsung foldable that’s heavier, TriFold excluded. There’s also no evidence that Apple has adopted silicon-carbon batteries yet, which have allowed Samsung, Motorola, and other Android manufacturers to fit bigger capacities into the smaller spaces of foldable phones. Apple says the phone should still deliver a full 24 hours of regular use, but Honor’s Magic V6 uses silicon-carbon to deliver two days of life. The rear cameras are pretty basic too, with a pair of 48-megapixel shooters and no telephoto. That’s almost an exact match for the cameras on the Z Fold 8, but Google, Motorola, Xiaomi and others are now providing capable triple cameras across their foldable lines, and the iPhone Duo already lags behind. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them None of this is to say that the Duo looks like a bad piece of hardware. Every foldable phone is a compromise, and Apple has picked a similar set of compromises to Samsung in order to get this phone out the door at $1,999. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them. Where that might change is the software. Google has made an effort to make Android more flexible and adaptable to suit folding phones, while OEMs deliver custom solutions to push things further, but none have rewritten the rulebook quite like Apple. The version of iOS 27 running on the iPhone Duo isn’t the same as on other iPhones, but it doesn’t match the iPad either. The biggest change takes the dock from the bottom of the display and lays it out vertically along the right-hand side. The Dynamic Island is turned vertical and thrown in here too, while the status bar collapses into a small circular icon in the top-right corner. This big change is bolstered by clever little touches throughout, like a dynamic blur effect that shifts as you open the screen, creating a fluidity no Android foldable has so far matched. It’s a total transformation of the iOS layout that specifically has foldables in mind. The point of all that change is to ensure consistency between the outer and inner screens. Open the iPhone Duo on the homescreen and almost everything will stay in place, making the move between screens feel seamless. That effect won’t hold in full-screen apps of course, which will adapt to fill the space, but that right-hand UI rail will be fixed. Locking the whole phone interface to the right-hand edge doesn’t sound great for left-handed users though, who are likely to find the Duo unusually awkward to use unless Apple adds the option to flip everything to the other side. StandBy mode has also been retooled for the Duo. Prop the phone down half-open and it will enter StandBy, letting you use it as a digital photo frame, smart display, or just get quick access to a few key widgets, like the clock. Finally, the $2,000 alarm clock you’ve always dreamed of. Not everything is as ambitious. Multitasking looks limited so far, with the option to run two apps in split-screen, including two windows of the same app, and save pairs to reopen together. Android rivals offer similar, but support three split-screen apps at once, and often more sitting in flexible, resizeable floating windows. But Apple’s software power doesn’t only lie in its OS. It’s the only phone manufacturer with the influence to shift the app ecosystem at large, and with the Duo it hopes to push third-party developers to adopt its best foldable features. It already showed off Netflix, Slack, and Zoom apps with custom Duo support, in some cases adapting dynamically depending on how flexed the hinge is. Android foldable features are still rare, with most apps simply changing size to fit the varying screens. Even that has its limits — I found a few apps ran awkwardly on the Fold 8’s short outer display. Apple is likely to have an easier time ensuring developers optimize their apps to suit both of the Duo’s displays. Most apps do little else to take advantage of dual displays, multiple cameras, or semi-open states like a tented mode. A few video apps adapt their playback controls when foldables are half-open, but that’s about it so far. Of course, some of those app developers might take their iOS foldable features and eventually roll them out to Android too, so Apple’s advantage might not last forever. It’ll take more time with the Duo to see exactly how it stacks up against the latest models from the Android side of life. So far it doesn’t look like Apple has surpassed its rivals on the hardware side, but its total control of software may give it an edge regardless.

item.title: Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.14
Marvel’s Wolverine captures just how angry its lead character is. The latest PS5 exclusive from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, Wolverine is a straightforward action game that is at its best when you’re (literally) slicing through enemies or thrust into a sequence pulled from a blockbuster movie, like climbing the fuselage of a plane as it careens toward land or racing a motorcycle across rain-slicked city streets. It’s the kind of game that can really get your heart rate rising, and keeping Logan mad is a key part of the strategy. In many ways, it’s a throwback to straightforward action titles of the past — and it’s a refreshing change of pace in a medium saturated with live-service and open-world games. Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game The next few months are packed with new games, and PlayStation goes old-school to cut through the noise. Though it comes from Insomniac, Wolverine is very different from Spider-Man, which thrust the web-slinger into an open-world version of New York City. Instead, this is a much more linear experience that feels like a combination of two other PlayStation staples: God of War and Uncharted. Rather than follow Wolverine as a member of the X-Men, the story instead has him as an often reluctant member of Team X, a mercenary group with similar pro-mutant aims but a much more violent approach. Instead of heroes like Cyclops and Professor X, Wolvy is joined by more villain-adjacent characters like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Nathaniel Essex, before eventually connecting with Jean Grey. The story pulls Logan and his companions across the globe, but it starts out relatively simple, as they investigate a rash of mutant disappearances connected to a billionaire arms dealer. The most important thing about both Wolverine the character and Wolverine the game is fighting. This is a hairy little dude who loves to scrap, and his mutant powers — healing and sharp claws — make it so that he is very good at it, able to both take a huge amount of damage and dish it out. And the best part of the game is how Wolverine-specific the action is. The combat is fast and violent and forces you to be aggressive. Wolverine can leap huge distances to take out foes and use his claws to both repel attacks and slice at enemies, often with very gruesome results. (At the end of a battle he’s usually coated in blood.) An important part of this is Wolverine’s rage level, which increases the more you fight. As his rage grows, it allows you to do two things: go absolutely berserk and kill a rash of enemies with a single blow, and use your healing power as a sort of extra life in case your health depletes. It’s a clever system that means you can’t sit back and play it safe. Wolverine isn’t chill, and you can’t be either. That’s the God of War side of Wolverine. The Uncharted side comes in the form of all of the over-the-top set-pieces you’re thrown into. I’ll refrain from detailing some of the best ones for spoiler reasons, but I’ll say that, just like in Uncharted, these moments make it feel like you’re playing out a wild sequence from an action movie. There are chases across the rooftops of Tokyo, massive boss battles against some iconic comic book villains, and scenes where Wolverine is literally being ripped apart as he fights for survival. The flip side is that, because of this setup, Wolverine is also much more restrictive than most of its contemporaries. In some ways this is a good thing; it’s refreshing to play a game that isn’t trying to do everything. But there are still some awkward elements. For instance, much like in Spider-Man, there are lots of collectibles that will reveal new bits of story or unlock new suits for Wolverine to wear. But exploration outside of the main path is extremely dull, so the only reason to track these down is if you have a completionist mindset. It’s also disappointing that Wolverine’s closet of outfits is much less fun than Spider-Man’s, and they often feel out of place with the game’s attempt at a more gritty tone. Making matters worse is that, despite a promising start, the story ends up in a largely forgettable place, with few surprises, particularly if you have an even slight knowledge of the X-Men universe from comics or the animated series. Outside of combat and set-pieces, Wolverine skews generic AAA game; the voice acting, the cutscenes, and even some of the missions feel like standard video game fare, many of which seem out of place. Wolverine is amazing when you’re surrounded by ninjas trying to kill you. But when Logan is in a tux trying to spy on a fancy party? Not so much. All that said, Wolverine’s return to a simpler and smaller style of action — I beat the game in around 13 hours — is still notable, particularly from Sony, which has had a rough few years after placing many ill-fated bets in the live-service space. But much like last year’s Ghost of Yōtei, Wolverine shows that PlayStation is still capable of the single-player blockbusters the platform is best known for. It’s also launching at perhaps the busiest video game release period in recent memory, going up against major titles including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Control Resonant, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Gears of War: E-Day, Silent Hill: Townfall, Star Wars: Zero Company, and, soon enough, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Grand Theft Auto VI. In that company, despite occasionally skewing generic, Wolverine’s bloodthirsty focus on action is something that makes it stand out. Marvel’s Wolverine launches on September 15th on the PS5.

item.title: Rivian spinout Also apologizes for delays in shipping futuristic e-bikes
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.13
Rivian’s futuristic e-bike is delayed, and customers are not happy. Rivian spinout Also apologizes for delays in shipping futuristic e-bikes The TM-B from Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also was supposed to reach customers by spring 2026. But after months of delays, the company is opening up about the challenges it’s facing. Last year, Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also unveiled a new, software-controlled electric bike called the TM-B that immediately set the e-bike world ablaze. With USB-C chargeable battery, removable seat post, and software-controlled pedal-by-wire system, the TM-B set itself apart with a totally unique approach to electric bicycle design. It’s not an exaggeration to say that nothing else looked like this bike. But that list of high-tech features is creating unexpected bottlenecks for Also’s product team. The company had originally said customer deliveries would start in spring 2026, and then later summer. But now, with fall approaching, the TM-B has yet to reach any customers — and several reservation holders are making their frustrations with the delays known on Reddit. This past weekend, Also went the unique route of responding to those criticisms on Reddit. Saul Leiken, Also’s product manager, posted a 661-word letter apologizing to customers for the delays, attributing the hold-up to strict quality standards rather than rushing an unfinished product. Leiken attributes the delay to “significant supply chain challenges” as a result of the AI boom. Specifically, the company has struggled to find enough printed circuit board (PCB) and integrated circuit (IC) materials for its software-powered e-bike. In some cases, Also’s team has had to find new materials that deviate from the original design, which requires more engineering and testing work to make sure its the right fit. TM-B’s battery has also presented some hurdles. The batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, which is forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish “new safety and testing protocols,” Leiken says. Lastly, Also may have bitten off more than it can chew with the DreamRide drivetrain system. It’s a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive. But the system requires “high-precision manufacturing,” Leiken admits, which has led to “a slower production ramp-up to ensure quality.” Rivian’s Also set out to build one of the most high-tech, complex e-bikes ever made. So it shouldn’t necessarily come as a shock to anyone that it’s taking a while to get the manufacturing and production process just right. You could certainly argue that Rivian should have been more clear-eyed about the challenges it would likely face given the complexity of the bike. And to his credit, Leiken does admit they could have done a better job at communicating those delays to customers, and for that he apologizes. “With any complex and technology-laden product, we have a choice,” he said. “As we ramp production we can relax standards against an original timeline or we can hold to a high standard and face potential delays. We believe our decision to hold that standard was, and is, the right one. And, at the same time, we agree that we should have been more communicative along the way.”

item.title: Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg placed on leave
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 2.96
Matt Mullenweg, the CEO of WordPress.com owner Automattic, has been placed on a paid leave of absence, as reported earlier by 404 Media. In an internal message by the outlet, Mullenweg claims Automattic chief financial officer Mark Davies “conspired” with board members to place him on leave. Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg placed on leave Mullenweg claims Automattic’s CFO ‘conspired’ with board members to put him on a leave of absence, 404 Media reports. “They voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that,” Mullenweg wrote, referring to Davies, along with Automattic board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker, 404 Media reports. Mullenweg, who also co-founded WordPress.org, has headed up Automattic since 2014. In 2024, Mullenweg waged a public pressure campaign against a prominent WordPress host, a move that divided the open-source community and ignited a legal battle that’s still going on today. Automattic spokesperson Megan Fox confirmed the company’s decision in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” Fox writes. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.” Mullenweg will remain on Automattic’s board, 404 Media reports. “Automattic’s board has decided to ask Matt to step away from his CEO role and take a leave of absence,” Schneider said on the company’s internal message board, according to 404 Media. “We have asked Mark Davies to assume the interim CEO role while Matt is out. We’ve worked closely with Mark over the years and we’re confident he will steer the ship well while Matt is away.” Update, September 9th: Added Automattic’s statement.

item.title: OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 6.58
OpenAI is announcing security updates following the July news that its AI broke out of a sandboxed environment and accidentally hacked Hugging Face, including improvements to its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques. The company had already put the brakes on a new model, Astra, that it thinks could have “critical” cybersecurity capabilities, and the company says it instituted a two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on its “latest models intended for deployment” while it tightened up security. The company’s “largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold.” OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face OpenAI is updating its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques to avoid another security fiasco. For its frontier model research, OpenAI now requires stronger sandboxes for workloads that “execute model-generated or otherwise untrusted code,” and has more controls to “isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet.” It has also updated its research environment to “remove potentially vulnerable shared services, reduce standing privileges, and improve security and trust boundaries.” As part of the company’s expanded monitoring setup, OpenAI now aims to issue an alert “within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced,” OpenAI says. If the people paged after an alert can’t “conclusively” determine whether an alert is a false positive within 30 minutes, “those teams are expected to pause the activity.” OpenAI also says that it’s applying “our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process,” including reward models that “better detect and discourage unsafe behavior” and training models “to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations.” Since the discovery of the Hugging Face breach, Anthropic and Meta have also found that their AI models had hacked other organizations.

item.title: Ring says its new encryption limits what it can give police
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 4.67
Ring has a new way to protect your videos. It’s developed an encryption method called TAKE, short for Throw Away the Key Encryption, that the Amazon-owned company says will protect your videos without traditional end-to-end encryption. TAKE limits when and why Amazon’s cloud can access those videos, while still providing features like smart alerts for people and packages, AI-powered video search, and video descriptions. Ring says its new encryption limits what it can give police The ‘Throw Away the Key Encryption’ (TAKE) method will become the default on all Ring cameras The feature is rolling out gradually starting in September, regardless of whether you have a subscription, and will become the default encryption for all Ring customers. TAKE arrives during a year of intense scrutiny for Ring, driven by its ties to law enforcement and the privacy implications of its AI-powered Search Party feature. Ring says TAKE changes what the company can hand over to law enforcement. “Ring will only be able to provide non-video information … and encrypted video files in response,” Ring spokesperson Sam McGee said in an email to The Verge. However, it doesn’t completely eliminate the privacy trade-off of cloud-based cameras. Ring says TAKE uses unique, rotating encryption keys for your footage, stored in a secure enclave and accessible only under strict conditions — based on the features you enable on your account. Currently, footage captured by Ring cameras is encrypted in transit to the cloud and at rest, and then decrypted for Ring to process for those smart features. With TAKE, the encryption keys change for every five minutes of footage. Ring stores copies of those keys to decrypt the footage, but throws away each copy within 24 hours, “leaving you with the keys and full control of your videos,” according to Ring. TAKE was developed using Messaging Layer Security, an open standard from the Internet Engineering Task Force, according to Ring. The company says it is “inspired by the privacy principles of E2EE (end-to-end encryption),” which Ring offers on some of its cameras. However, the two systems work differently. With E2EE, Ring never has the keys and can’t process your video for cloud-based features. Both options are available on newer cameras that encrypt on-device, and you can switch between the two. Older cameras encrypt at cloud ingress and only support TAKE. According to a white paper the company published today, Ring’s copy of those keys is managed inside an AWS Nitro Enclave, to which Ring’s access is restricted by “access controls, cryptography, and hardware isolation.” The company claims there is no persistent storage and no way for a Ring employee to access it. The stored keys can only be unlocked by the enclave through cryptographic attestation that proves it’s running the exact software image Ring approved. The enclave releases a temporary key when an enabled service requests it. Each key is permanently deleted after 24 hours — a window McGee told The Verge allows for processing its current cloud-based features — and no backups are kept. To view older footage, an authorized device running the Ring app (such as your phone or computer) must send the keys back to Ring for that session. Ring claims key delivery is push only, meaning Amazon’s servers can’t force devices to hand over your keys remotely; only you can request one. If you lose access to your device, Ring says there are several recovery methods, all of which are only accessible to the customer. These include cloud backup via your phone, a passphrase, passkey, another authorized device, and camera-based recovery. If all those fail, you won’t be able to access encrypted content. The white paper details how the keys are generated and how Ring continuously “throws away” your old keys. Ring says it’s continuing to harden this architecture: Deletion is continuous rather than a single event at the 24-hour mark. Content encryption keys rotate every five minutes, and as each key ages past 24 hours, CMMS [Cloud Member Management Service] ratchets forward the corresponding intermediary secret in the key derivation hierarchy. Ratcheting applies a one-way key derivation function to overwrite a managed secret with its derived output and discards the original, making it cryptographically infeasible to reconstruct. […] The CMMS database is configured with no backups. This deletion is designed to be irreversible. TAKE isn’t E2EE, but it limits Ring’s access Ring says that “only you retain the keys to your video” with TAKE. But TAKE isn’t E2EE. Ring has access for up to 24 hours and can receive keys again when you pull up older videos. You can also share the keys with others when you add authorized users. With E2EE enabled on Ring cameras, none of that is possible, making it the stronger privacy option. Ring’s main reason for developing TAKE is to preserve cloud-based features you lose with E2EE. But as the footage goes to Amazon’s servers for processing, it still has the privacy trade-off of cloud-based cameras. Cloud processing can deliver more sophisticated features, but basic on-device intelligence can still alert you to people and packages. “Where TAKE is enabled, Ring will only be able to provide non-video information (such as basic subscriber information) and encrypted video files in response to the valid legal process.” — Sam McGee Competitors including Reolink and Eufy offer cameras and hubs that can store and process footage locally, so it doesn’t need to be done in the cloud. Ring also has local processing through Ring Edge on its Ring Alarm Pro hub, but that doesn’t work with E2EE. Ring says many of its features can’t run locally. “Features that require cloud processing include Unusual Event Alert, Video Descriptions, Smart Alerts, and Video Search, for example,” McGee said. “These features rely on models and infrastructure that cannot run locally on camera hardware.” The Verge also asked McGee about concerns users might have regarding how TAKE processes videos in relation to privacy and law enforcement access: What happens if Ring is subpoenaed by law enforcement? Does TAKE prevent law enforcement and others from accessing footage? “Where TAKE is enabled, Ring will only be able to provide non-video information (such as basic subscriber information) and encrypted video files in response to the valid legal process. We have updated our Law Enforcement Guidelines to reflect this change.” “Community Requests remains a transparent way for local public safety agencies to request footage from customers to support an official investigation. Customers always choose whether to respond to a Community Request and what they share. If they choose to ignore a request, the Requesting Agency is never notified. TAKE does not change this.” Do governments have a backdoor into TAKE? “No. Building a backdoor would undermine the enhanced security and privacy that we designed TAKE to deliver.” Does Ring train on any data or metadata from users’ Ring devices? “Ring only trains on video recordings that have been made publicly available, or on recordings from users who have given Ring explicit permission to use them for this purpose. Users can revoke permission at any time.” When asked if TAKE had been independently evaluated, McGee said, “TAKE is built on Messaging Layer Security, an open standard developed and reviewed through the IETF. We are publishing a detailed technical whitepaper explaining how the system works.” The Verge asked the Electronic Frontier Foundation to review the white paper. Thorin Klosowski, a security and privacy activist at EFF, said that while TAKE provides some “incremental improvements” to Ring’s current system, it adds a false sense of security. “TAKE provides some incremental improvements to Ring’s current system, but also introduces a false sense of security where the privacy protections Ring claims to be adding requires putting a lot of trust in the company, as opposed to just using what we know works, end-to-end encryption,” said Klosowski. “Even taken at face value, one of the most concerning details is that TAKE doesn’t offer strong protections against law enforcement requesting access to future videos, and doesn’t seem to protect against access and additional data derived from those videos, like text descriptions of the content.” Ring’s TAKE addresses concerns around cloud processing in an attempt to balance security, privacy, and convenience, especially compared to E2EE, which gives you privacy but not the Ring features you probably bought the cameras for. But while TAKE is built on a standard, Ring developed the parts that involve throwing away the key itself. Ultimately, you still have to trust Amazon and Ring. Updated August 28th: Added a statement from EFF.

item.title: Apple Event Live Updates: New Foldable iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and More
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 4.39
Apple has officially launched a foldable iPhone, and to no one’s surprise, it’s the most expensive iPhone yet. Wirecutter was on the ground in Cupertino, California, to report on Apple’s annual product-launch event on September 9, where the company also announced a revamped iPhone 18 Pro, plus new Apple Watches and AirPods. It’s been an interesting year for Apple, one in which new CEO John Ternus took the helm from Tim Cook on September 1. The tech industry is also facing a shortage of components such as memory and storage, which are being funneled to AI data centers. That’s caused prices on many products to increase in recent months, including Apple’s latest iPhones. We’ll dive into longer reviews of Apple’s new gadgets after spending hands-on time with them, but until then, here are the big takeaways from the Apple event. - There’s now a foldable iPhone. The iPhone Duo folds in half to fit in your palm or unfolds so you can view and use two apps at once. Starting at $2,000, it’s the most expensive iPhone yet. - The new iPhone Pros represent an iterative update. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have better battery life and cameras, plus more powerful chips that help run AI features, but their designs are otherwise mostly the same. - The latest Apple Watches have new health features. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 now measure your heart rate every five seconds, deliver a daily health score, and can listen to conversations to deliver an AI-generated recap. - The new AirPods are better at noise cancellation. The active noise cancellation in the AirPods 5 set is supposed to be up to 50% better, and these earbuds are also better at helping you hear exterior noise when it’s time to have a conversation. iPhone Duo Apple announced its long-awaited foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. The Duo has a passport-style design with rounded corners. The cover display measures 5.9 inches, while the inner display is 7.6 inches (80% larger than that of the iPhone 18 Pro). Unfolded, it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. The cover and inner displays share the same aspect ratio, and the inner camera is hidden beneath the display, appearing only when you need it for FaceTime calls. For multitasking, you can view and use two apps simultaneously, and the iPhone Duo’s surface also supports the USB-C Apple Pencil. With an IP68 rating, the foldable iPhone is fully dust- and water-resistant, and it has Ceramic Shield on both the front and back for extra protection. As for cameras, it comes with 48-megapixel dual-fusion cameras on the back and a 12-megapixel front-facing camera on the cover display. It adds a few camera options that other iPhones don’t have, including an AI feature that snaps a picture only once everyone has posed, the ability for multiple people to join a FaceTime call from both sides of the phone, and a stand-up feature using the phone’s folding design. Under the hood is the same new A20 Pro chip that appears across Apple’s latest iPhones. It delivers faster CPU and GPU performance, and it has two neural engines (Apple’s AI-specific processors), allowing for a 50% increase in memory bandwidth — all of which help power AI-based features and tasks. The iPhone Duo also has a C2 modem for 50% faster uploads. The foldable iPhone comes with batteries on each side that work together for all-day battery life, which Apple claims reaches up to 31 hours on the inner display and 44 hours on the outer display. It offers up to 24 hours per charge when you’re using both screens equally. Though we haven’t yet put the phone to the test, the displays impressed in demos. In one video, Netflix previews on the cover display seamlessly transferred to the interior display when the phone was opened. The iPhone Duo appears to combine the best of a phone and a tablet in one device. The iPhone Duo will start at $2,000, with storage ranging from 256 GB up to 2 TB. It will come in two colors: Star White and Night Sky. It will be available for preorder on October 16 and will go on sale October 23. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max This year’s iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade over its predecessor, with the addition of the new A20 Pro chip, longer battery life, and improved camera features. The design is the same as that of last year’s model, but it comes in a few new color options: Black, Glacier, and Burgundy, plus Silver (each with a color-matched back). Apple also redesigned the Dynamic Island (the cutout at the top) to be smaller, but it now supports up to three apps simultaneously. Apple increased the battery life, promising up to 36 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro and up to 45 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro Max — the longest battery life for the Pro and Pro Max models yet. Apple reports that the iPhone 18 Pro charges to 50% in as fast as 15 minutes. The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max both get big camera upgrades, as well, including a new 48-megapixel camera sensor with variable aperture that better balances light and depth of field. It adjusts automatically based on the scene; in dark environments, for example, it lets in around 50% more light. iPhones also now “sign” the images they take, so it can be proven whether an image is original or has been altered. Apple will also add support for SynthID, which can identify pictures made or modified by AI. With these models, Apple is emphasizing Siri AI, its more intelligent voice assistant. The company says Siri will draw from messages, emails, photos, and what’s on the device’s screen to give more personalized answers. New AI-powered software features will be available in iOS 27 on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer, so you don’t need to upgrade to get access to them. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,200, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,300, which amounts to $100 more than last year’s models. Both phones will come in 256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, and 2 TB versions. They will be available for preorder starting September 12, with full availability on September 18. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 The latest Apple Watch models, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, measure your heart rate every five seconds, 60 times more frequently than prior models. The watches will now be able to display a real-time heart rate on the watch face, and heart-rate variability, which the watches use to help measure stress and recovery, is sampled up to every five minutes. Apple claims that the Apple Watch has the most accurate heart-rate sensing of any wearable device. In addition to continuous heart-rate monitoring, the Apple Watches have a new Readiness feature similar to those offered by Whoop and Oura. Every morning, your watch will give you a score from 0 to 10 and advise you on how to proceed with exercise: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. The advice then updates throughout the day. A new Insights tab in the redesigned Health app, which is coming later this year, offers AI-powered recommendations based on your activity and data. The Health app will also use your data to display your Health Age and measure your Longevity. You’ll be able to see how your data compares to clinical recommendations and integrate your lab results. Both new watches have a new S11 chip that powers AI features, which Apple calls Audio Intelligence. Audio Intelligence uses AI combined with the watches’ built-in microphones for a few different purposes. For starters, it can listen for sounds and then notify you when, for instance, someone rings the doorbell, which will be particularly useful for those who are deaf or hard of hearing. Another Audio Intelligence feature is Siri Recap, which takes notes from your conversations and creates an AI-generated summary. You can enable it and choose to always have it on, or you can schedule it to offer recaps at specific times of day. You can turn it on or off at any time. Audio is not recorded or stored and can’t be accessed by anyone, including Apple. The recaps are end-to-end encrypted, and speakers aren’t identified. The $400 Apple Watch Series 12 comes in 42 mm and 46 mm sizes in Space Gray, Black, Light Gold, and Dark Bronze aluminum. The cases have Ceramic Shield 2, similar to the iPhone. Series 12 is also available in a ceramic finish in Pearl White and Night Blue. Battery life remains unchanged at a day long, though this watch charges faster and lasts longer than previous models did when used outside. The $800 Ultra 4 gets more than two days of battery life, charges faster, and lasts longer outside. Its Max Extended Mode can help you eke out 45 hours on a charge. It comes in black or natural titanium in a 49 mm size. Both watches are available to preorder today, and they go on sale September 18. AirPods 5 Apple’s latest earbuds, the AirPods 5, emphasize better sound quality and more effective background noise reduction. With a new acoustic architecture, the AirPods 5 set offers up to 50% more noise reduction than its predecessor. The earbuds can also automatically adapt between active noise cancellation and transparency depending on the background noise. This year’s model also gets up to four hours of listening with ANC and up to 20 hours with the charging case. Apple also introduced the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case set, which lets you swipe on the stem of the AirPod to adjust audio levels. This set has longer battery life (up to five hours with ANC) and comes with a wireless charging case that’s compatible with Apple Watch and Qi chargers. The new AirPods are also better at letting in external sounds when wanted, and they lower the volume on music and other audio automatically if the wearer starts speaking. You can speak with Siri via the AirPods, too, and you can shake your head yes or no to respond to Siri. In addition, Siri can translate speech in another language or interact with the apps on your phone for you. The standard AirPods 5 set will cost $130, while the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case set will cost $150. They are both available for preorder starting today and will go on sale September 18. This article was edited by Jason Chen.

item.title: After a Mat, These Cork Blocks Are the Yoga Props Worth Investing In
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 3.27
If you’ve ever attended a class at a yoga studio, you’ve probably seen yoga blocks. These rectangular props are intended to provide additional support and reach, making some poses more accessible to people with varying skill levels and physical abilities. Experts say that after a reliable mat, yoga blocks (ideally two, so you have one for each arm or leg or to stack, if desired) are the equipment most likely to elevate your practice. If you want to invest in a set for use at home, we’ve determined that the Manduka Cork Yoga Block is the one to get. Everything we recommend What to consider - Cork or foamYoga blocks made of cork tend to be heavier, stiffer, and especially supportive. Foam blocks are lighter, softer, and less stable. - Size and weightMost yoga blocks are around 9 by 6 by 4 inches. Foam blocks are usually lighter than cork ones. - Your practiceCork blocks are better for balancing and standing. Foam blocks are preferred for restorative poses. - Two > oneGenerally, two blocks will serve your practice best. Some poses require only one. Top pick This block’s edges are nicely rounded, and its sides have an extra-grippy texture, reducing slippage. It’s on the heavier side, however. With its rounded edges and a satisfyingly grippy texture, the sturdy but comfortable Manduka Cork Yoga Block is exceptionally versatile, supporting bodies in all manner of standing/balancing and restorative poses. At about 2 pounds, it’s among the heaviest cork blocks available, lending additional stability but adding heft. Runner-up Although this block is lighter than our pick, it stably supports bodies in balancing poses. Its texture also provides good grip. The JadeYoga Large Cork Yoga Block is a lighter alternative to our pick, so it’s easier to move around during practice (or to travel with). It’s also narrower, which may appeal to those with smaller hands. Because its edges aren’t as rounded as those of our pick, this block is somewhat less comfortable to use in reclined positions, such as under the sacrum in a bridge pose. Why you should trust us To learn all we could about yoga blocks, we spoke with yoga instructors, yoga therapists, and block manufacturers. - I’m a longtime yoga enthusiast, and in 2023, I completed 200-hour yoga teacher training with Three Sisters Yoga. It was during this training that I embraced using yoga blocks. I’ve also contributed reporting to our yoga mats guide and reviewed hot yoga towels. - Like all Wirecutter journalists, I review and test products with complete editorial independence. I’m never made aware of any business implications of our editorial recommendations. Read more about our editorial standards. Who this is for Contrary to popular belief, blocks aren’t just for beginners. They’re for anyone and everyone who practices yoga, and they can be especially useful to people with physical limitations or injuries. Using blocks is not a sign of being “bad” at yoga. Blocks are useful for balancing, standing, stretching, and restorative yoga poses, among other things. The experts we consulted explained that blocks can serve various purposes beyond providing additional reach and support, making them arguably the most versatile yoga props. They aid in deepening stretches, bringing the ground closer, and getting into proper alignment without compromising your body (especially the spine, knees, and hips). You can even use them for core-strengthening exercises. Yoga therapist and author Jenny Clise emphasized that you can use a block for assistance in getting into a challenging pose. The block serves to reduce fear or to form muscle memory. The use of blocks involves “curiosity and investigation,” Clise said. How we picked and tested Yoga blocks can be made of wood, bamboo, cork, or foam. Blocks made of maple or bamboo are gorgeous, but they’re not the most economical or practical (slippage is common). For this guide, we focused on blocks made of cork and foam, two comparatively less expensive materials that provide better grip. Altogether, we tried nine top-rated best-sellers. In choosing what to test, we considered: - Weight: A good cork block should be sturdy and stable in standing/balancing poses. If it’s too heavy, however, it won’t be comfortable to move around during your practice or to carry outside the home. Foam blocks, usually made of EVA foam, will be lighter but should still be stable enough to hold some weight. The cork and foam blocks we tested ranged from 0.4 pounds to 2.4 pounds each. - Size: The standard block (whether cork or foam) is roughly 9 by 6 by 4 inches. All of the blocks we tested were about this size. - Material quality/texture: The cork should provide good grip and a comfortable surface. There should be little to no cork shavings that rub off during practice — at least in the beginning, before heavy use. Foam will naturally have a little more cushion, so we preferred high-density foam blocks that felt soft but were still durable. - Edge design: Some blocks are well rounded; others have a more pointed edge. Rounded edges add extra comfort. I used a set of two blocks for each practice because many poses require two blocks for balance. I did the same poses with each of the block sets, including downward dog, triangle, half moon, reclining bound angle, and bridge pose. We also sought feedback from people who have used our picks longer term — in some cases, for years. We’ll continue to long-term test our picks and report back on their longevity. Our pick: Manduka Cork Yoga Block Top pick This block’s edges are nicely rounded, and its sides have an extra-grippy texture, reducing slippage. It’s on the heavier side, however. Sturdy and long-lasting, the Manduka Cork Yoga Block has the grippiest texture and the most comfortable edges of all the blocks we tested. It’s ideal to use for standing and balancing poses, but it can also be used for restorative ones. Cork is long-lasting and has natural cushion that’s not too soft. Cork blocks tend to last a long time, even if shavings inevitably rub off over the years. Krissy Jones, cofounder of Sky Ting Yoga in New York, said she’s been practicing at home with her Manduka cork blocks for about eight years. “They seem totally fine. I don’t think I need to replace them anytime soon.” The block’s sides and ends are grippier than those of other, similar blocks. So there will be less slipping while balancing or being supported in stretches. The texture of the cork on the sides of this block is somewhat rough but still plenty comfortable against the skin. The faces of this block have a slightly smoother surface, which you can use while in downward dog. According to Deanna Green, owner of Shambhala Yoga & Dance Center in Brooklyn, New York, cork blocks are better than foam for downward dog or plank. If your hands don’t have a little warmth to them, you may feel the slightest slip in downward dog while using two of these blocks. As your hands progressively develop a little more moisture, the blocks work better to keep you from slipping. This added height from the blocks may be beneficial for those who have a hard time holding downward dog or want to practice at an elevated height. This 2-pound block remains stable while balancing. It didn’t budge while I balanced, and I had no issue using it for incorporated core exercises. In fact, that extra weight feels like you’re getting a more vigorous workout. Its rounded edges are very comfortable. They felt better than those of any other cork block we tested. Along with the thickness, the rounded edges make the blocks comfortable to grab or lean on — even in reclining hero pose. Dimensions: 8.75 by 5.75 by 3.88 inches Weight: 2.16 pounds Material: cork Flaws but not dealbreakers The Manduka cork blocks are among the heaviest we considered — yet they are still easy to move around during practice. They also may feel a bit too wide for people who have smaller hands. Runner-up: JadeYoga Large Cork Yoga Block Runner-up Although this block is lighter than our pick, it stably supports bodies in balancing poses. Its texture also provides good grip. The JadeYoga Large Cork Yoga Block is a solid block that performs almost as well as our pick and generally costs a bit less. Its edges are rounded, but not as prominently as those of the Manduka cork block. The cork has a good grip. We found that this block did not slip when we used it. However, unlike those of the Manduka cork block, the faces and sides of the JadeYoga block don’t feel any different, so this block is slightly less satisfying to use. The faces are not as smooth as those of our main pick, and the sides aren’t as grippy. The weight feels just right. At 1.74 pounds, the JadeYoga block has the most comfortable weight of all the blocks we tested. It’s lighter than our pick but remains stable throughout practice. This block is a tad slimmer than our pick. So people with smaller hands may prefer it over the Manduka cork block. Dimensions: 8.75 by 5.75 by 3.75 inches Weight: 1.74 pounds Material: cork Another yoga block worth considering If you want a lighter, softer block that’s ideal for restorative yoga: The Calia Foam Yoga Block is lighter than our cork picks (just 0.8 pounds), yet it’s surprisingly stable, including for standing poses. Compared with the firmer, heavier cork blocks we recommend, this foam block is a better choice for restorative poses. The Calia block, made of EVA foam, is comfortable to sit on and to use in reclining positions. Its surface and edges are pleasantly smooth and soft, but still plenty firm and supportive. The blocks we tested had visibly uneven texture — like all foam blocks it is subject to indentation and scratches. And while EVA foam can be recycled, it’s not particularly easy to. The competition The Alo Uplifting Yoga Block feels rough and is quite hard for a foam block. The Bala Building Block’s edges are not as comfortable as those on other foam blocks we tested, and its overall width makes this block more difficult to grasp. At about 2 pounds, the Calia Cork Yoga Block is stable and hefty. The edges of this block are rounded, but overall it’s neither as smooth nor as grippy as our picks. Gaiam’s Cork Yoga Block is exceptionally sturdy (and the thickest block we tested). But it’s 2.4 pounds, which we found was too heavy for comfort. Hugger Mugger’s Cork Yoga Block has a nice, grippy texture, but it’s a little too slim, and it wobbles more easily than our picks. The Hugger Mugger 4-Inch Foam Yoga Block’s beveled edges can feel a little sharp in reclined poses. Note that the marble-patterned version of this block was far too light to feel stable, and it weighs around half what the solid-color version does (they were supposed to weigh the same, according to the company’s marketing). We chose not to test both the Lululemon’s Lift and Lengthen Yoga Block and Inner Flow Yoga Block Marble. The former is thinner and lighter than the Manduka Recycled Foam Yoga Block we previously recommended, making it less versatile and potentially less stable. The extra rounded edge is less suitable for restorative practices; this block would likely be best for balancing poses. Some cork from the Yoga Accessories 4” Cork Yoga Block rubbed off on our mat during practice. Yoga Hustle’s The Block, made of EVA foam, comes in fun patterns. It performed nearly the same as the Calia Foam Block we recommend, with similar weight and dimensions. At the time of publication it was out of stock. This article was edited by Tracy Vence and Kalee Thompson. Sources - Krissy Jones, cofounder of Sky Ting yoga studio, phone interview, April 5, 2023 - Deanna Green, owner of Shambhala Yoga & Dance Center, phone interview, April 6, 2023 - Eyal Shifroni, founder of the Iyengar Yoga Center of Zichron Ya’akov and author of the book series Props for Yoga, email interview, April 10, 2023 - Chuck Blumenthal, president at Bean Products, email interview, April 13, 2023 - Jenny Clise, C-IAYT yoga therapist and author of Blockasanas, Zoom interview, April 18, 2023 Further reading - by Seth Berkman After testing 49 yoga mats and using our picks for years, we’ve determined it’s worth investing in a quality mat that will last. The JadeYoga Harmony Mat is our top pick. - by Katie Okamoto Since I first discovered the grippy JadeYoga Harmony Mat in yoga teacher training a decade ago, I’ve bought four, swapping out new mats every couple of years.
